Caveat / follow-up: Occurrence ranges are compiled from prior studies and vary by targets, sampling and region; verify originals before citing as a standardized comparative dataset.

Adsorbent / material: Multiple adsorbent classes in HWW studies
Experimental design / conditions: Table 3 summarizes conventional, advanced and adsorption methods; materials and waters vary across cited studies.
Reported result: The review table gives broad adsorption antibiotic-removal efficiency around 70–90%; it also discusses MBR, membranes, AOPs, UV, chlorination and other treatments with their own ranges and trade-offs.
Caveat / follow-up: The 70–90% value is not a controlled meta-analysis or guaranteed HWW performance. It must not be compared directly to one specific adsorbent study without tracing conditions.

Adsorbent / material: Zeolite and silica aerogel examples summarized by review
Experimental design / conditions: The main text summarizes a zeolite study on HWW and a silica-aerogel study using HWW spiked with doxycycline.
Reported result: Review-reported removals: zeolite 60.7% AZM, 75.6% OFL, 43.6% SMX with listed concentrations 391 ng/L, 378 ng/L and 78.6 ng/L respectively; silica aerogel 98.5% removal from HWW spiked with 10 mg/L DOX.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 11; text on HWW/municipal wastewater studies; supplementary Table S5 cited
Evidence status: Secondary evidence; original papers not checked in this batch
Caveat / follow-up: Spiked HWW at 10 mg/L is very different from naturally observed ng/L feed; verify the original study, dose, analytical limits and actual matrix.

Target / co-contaminant: SMX, erythromycin, carbamazepine and other pharmaceuticals
Adsorbent / material: Bagasse fixed bed; PAC/GAC and PAC-UF systems
Evidence domain: Pilot/full-scale case studies and implementation gap
Experimental design / conditions: Review discusses pilot-scale sugarcane-bagasse columns and full-scale PAC/GAC polishing systems, including municipal WWTPs linked to hospitals/clinics.
Reported result: Sugarcane-bagasse SMX example reported 73.3% removal and 0.23 mg/g in lab column, 78.79% and 0.163 mg/g in pilot column; matrix must be confirmed in original source. A hospital-connected municipal wastewater PAC/GAC contextual example and a 227,000 m³/day reclamation plant with GAC reportedly removed erythromycin 74% and carbamazepine 88%. Review states PAC/GAC are the adsorbents used at full scale while many advanced materials remain lab-stage.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not label municipal/hospital-connected effluent as pure HWW. Examples combine different contaminants and treatment trains; verify primary studies before quantitative comparison.

Continuum stage: Secondary review — deployment and matrix factors
Experimental design / conditions: Review discusses pH and speciation, adsorbent PZC/functional groups, coexisting salts/organics, dosage, adsorption isotherms/kinetics, and chemical/thermal/mechanical regeneration.
Reported result: Main practical gaps are variable high-organic-load matrices, competition, regeneration costs and secondary eluent waste, material loss, limited long-term real-HWW data, hospital space constraints and little full-scale use of advanced materials. The review suggests adsorption may be integrated with degradation as a separate unit operation.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not treat generic mechanism descriptions or hybrid degradation as evidence of mechanism/destruction in a particular adsorbent; SI Tables S1–S6 are not in the uploaded PDF.

Adsorbent / material: Spent brewery grain biochar BC-SBG, microwave-pyrolysed without activation
Experimental design / conditions: Spent pilsener-brewery grains dried/ground; microwave-pyrolysed at 800 °C for 20 min under N2 62 mL/min, ramp 15 °C/min; washed with ~1.2 M HCl then water to neutral; washed leachate neutralized with NaOH; dried 100 °C for 24 h. Yield 23%. Granular media 0.5–1 mm, batch powder ≤180 μm.
Reported result: Granular BET 281 m²/g, pore volume 0.12 cm³/g, micropore volume 0.11 cm³/g, density 0.87 g/cm³, PZC 4.0; powder BET ~312 m²/g, pore volume 0.14, micropore 0.12. No chemical or physical activation.
Caveat / follow-up: Yield and processing route reported, but full production inventory and total LCA metrics are in SI; acid/base wash use and drying electricity become environmental hotspots.

Experimental design / conditions: Effluent collected May 2024 at outlet of Ílhavo urban WWTP receiving primary and secondary biological treatment; 0.45 μm filtered, autoclaved 120 °C for 15 min and stored at 4 °C up to 3 weeks. Conductivity 3.3 mS/cm, pH 7.8±0.1, DOC 31 mg/L.
Reported result: This is a real secondary WWTP effluent but was filtered/autoclaved before experiments. Feed antibiotic solutions were controlled at 20 μmol/L and pH 8; therefore the experiment assesses matrix effects on spiked/controlled antibiotic feeds, not native untreated effluent concentrations.
Caveat / follow-up: Call it filtered/autoclaved real WWTP effluent; not raw wastewater. Matrix chemical composition and sterilization can affect transferability to live untreated flows.

Experimental design / conditions: Single antibiotic feed 20 μmol/L, pH 8, 25.0±0.1 °C, 80 rpm; kinetic dose 0.75 g/L in buffered water and 1.5 g/L in wastewater; sampled 5–240 min. Equilibrium tests after 240 min with dose 0.25–3.75 g/L in buffered water and 0.80–3.80 g/L in wastewater.
Reported result: Equilibrium within 60 min. Langmuir fitted q_m in buffered water: TMP 18±1 μmol/g, CIP 16±1 μmol/g, SMX 7.1±0.1 μmol/g. PFO and PSO both fit; PSO generally R²≥0.97 and Syx≤0.83. In wastewater, fitted q_m of SMX/CIP were ~7%/11% lower; TMP ~38% lower.
Model / metric: Fitted Langmuir q_m; kinetic fit statistic
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 4–6; Figs. 1–2; Table S5/S6 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Keep fitted q_m separate from fixed-bed experimental q_s/qTH/qY. PSO fit is not standalone proof of chemisorption.

Adsorbent / material: Granular BC-SBG in jacketed glass column
Experimental design / conditions: Column 13 cm long, 1.0 cm ID, bed depth 4.4 cm, ~2.00±0.01 g biochar, 25 °C; feed 20 μmol/L, pH 8. Flow rates 0.042, 0.083 and 0.167 L/h in buffered distilled water.
Reported result: Authors select 0.083 L/h (~1057 L m−2 h−1 reported) as compromise between throughput and adsorption. At 0.042 L/h, Thomas-model q_TH values: SMX 11.4±0.2, TMP 33±1, CIP 18.9±0.2 μmol/g. Increased flow shortens residence time and reduces uptake/breakthrough time.
Caveat / follow-up: q_TH is a fitted dynamic parameter, not batch qmax; keep model name, flow and single/mixture context visible.

Experimental design / conditions: Table 3 gives fixed-bed breakthrough threshold C/C0≈0.1 at the stated flows, using ~2 g biochar.
Reported result: In buffered-water single-solute tests at 0.042 L/h: SMX tb 14.4 h and Vb 0.6 L; TMP tb 64.8 h and 2.7 L; CIP tb 38.4 h and 1.6 L. At 0.167 L/h, tb was 0.6 h SMX, 6.6 h TMP and 4.8 h CIP.
Caveat / follow-up: A C/C0 threshold of 0.1 is the operational breakthrough definition; not equivalent to complete treatment or final effluent removal.

Experimental design / conditions: Single-solute fixed-bed tests compare buffered water and filtered/autoclaved wastewater at 20 μmol/L, pH 8, 25 °C, 0.083 L/h, bed depth 4.4 cm.
Reported result: Yan-model q_Y in buffered water→wastewater: SMX 7.8→4.15 μmol/g; TMP 32.3→7.8; CIP 18.1→3.33. Experimental saturation q_s from Table 3 for lower flow tests: buffered→wastewater approximately SMX 7.3→2.2, TMP 46.7→2.8, CIP 28.7→2.5 μmol/g. Breakthrough becomes markedly steeper in wastewater.
Model / metric: Model-derived q_Y and experimental q_s, kept distinct
Caveat / follow-up: q_Y and q_s come from different fitting/experimental contexts; do not merge into one capacity field. Real effluent had DOC 31 mg/L and was filtered/autoclaved.

Target / co-contaminant: SMX, TMP, CIP in ternary mixture
Experimental design / conditions: Feeds were 20 μmol/L each in single or combined ternary solutions; pH 8, 25 °C, 4.4 cm bed, flow 0.083 L/h, buffered water or filtered/autoclaved wastewater.
Reported result: Ternary feeds showed steeper breakthrough and lower q_Y. In buffered water ternary q_Y: SMX 5.4, TMP 17.7, CIP 17.4 μmol/g. In wastewater ternary q_Y: SMX 3.61, TMP 6.0, CIP 5.80 μmol/g. SMX had strong competition in buffered water; all three were affected in wastewater.
Model / metric: Yan-model fitted capacities under mixture conditions
Caveat / follow-up: Do not use single-solute batch capacity as a guarantee for multicomponent column service life.

Experimental design / conditions: After TMP fixed-bed saturation, regenerate under N2 at 600 °C, ramp 15 °C/min, residence 20 min; reuse for two further TMP fixed-bed tests.
Reported result: BET increased 281→380→462 m²/g (fresh, first, second regeneration); pore volume 0.12→0.21 cm³/g after second cycle; micropore volume 0.11→0.19 cm³/g. Yan q_Y 32.3→94.9→114 μmol/g; experimental q_s 38→55→68 μmol/g. Reported regeneration efficiency ~118% and 146% defined as q_regenerated/q_initial×100%.
Model / metric: Two regeneration cycles for TMP; q_Y vs q_s distinct
Caveat / follow-up: Efficiency above 100% means post-regeneration uptake exceeded fresh capacity; not percentage of antibiotic desorbed. No full antibiotic fate/emissions mass balance during 600 °C treatment.

Target / co-contaminant: Production of 1 kg BC-SBG; environmental impacts
Adsorbent / material: Spent brewery-grain biochar production, lab-scale process
Experimental design / conditions: LCA follows ISO 14040, Ecoinvent 3.9.1, ReCiPe 2016; functional unit 1 kg BC-SBG; includes 30 km truck transport and stages of collection, microwave pyrolysis, HCl/NaOH wash/neutralization, drying; electricity estimated from laboratory equipment/time/capacity; flue emissions measured/estimated via FTIR.
Reported result: Fig. 7: washing contributes 45% of global warming and 46% fossil-resource scarcity; drying contributes 41% to both. Washing contributes 82% mineral-resource scarcity (HCl/NaOH). Pyrolysis contributes 63% ozone formation (human health) and 39% terrestrial acidification; wash adds 36% acidification. Collection, water and wastewater each contribute <3% to listed emissions categories.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 4, 12; Fig. 7; §2.6/§3.4; SI Table S4 cited
Evidence status: Extracted; total impact magnitudes in SI unavailable
Caveat / follow-up: Lab-scale production boundary, not cradle-to-grave column operation or spent media. Do not claim total life-cycle superiority; washing chemicals, drying electricity and pyrolysis emissions are the hotspots.

Adsorbent / material: Wood-apple-shell carbonized char (CNB) then H3PO4-activated ACNB
Experimental design / conditions: Wood-apple shell sun-dried 5 d, oven-dried 100 °C/1 h, carbonized 250 °C/3 h; char washed and dried at 100 °C/12 h. 33.372 g carbonized material mixed with 50 mL H3PO4, stirred 24 h at 35 °C, filtered, washed to pH 7 and dried at 100 °C/3 h.
Reported result: BET: raw shell 69.03 m²/g, CNB 274.735 m²/g, ACNB 547.36 m²/g, commercial AC 643.97 m²/g. Paper labels material “activated N-biochar”, but the described preparation contains no intentional external N-doping step; N is reported at 0.12 wt%. Iodine value 485 mg/g vs 500 mg/g commercial AC.
Caveat / follow-up: Reported micropore volume is 1.76 cm³/g and is unusually large relative to other values; verify against SI/source table before quantitative comparison. Yield/mass balance not reported.

Experimental design / conditions: Batch variables included pH 2–10, initial ENF 2–50 mg/L, dose (ranges vary by article section), 15–40 °C and 2–30 h. Main reported optimum: pH 6, C0 10 mg/L, dose 2 g/L, contact 24 h, 25 °C.
Reported result: Reported maximum removal 96.5% under pH 6, 10 mg/L ENF, 2 g/L ACNB, 24 h, 25 °C. At pH 6, ENF is around the pKa transition/zwitterionic regime, and ACNB is above pHPZC 4.
Caveat / follow-up: Abstract says dose range 0.2–1 g/L, methods say 0.45–1.5 g/L, results say max at 2 g/L. Do not silently reconcile these ranges.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic/optimization tests used batch ENF solutions; equilibrium series run with pH 6, dose 2 g/L and 24 h. Initial concentrations vary by test; article states 2–50 mg/L broadly, but isotherm plot includes a distinct series.
Reported result: Langmuir isotherm reported best fit R²≈0.966, fitted Qmax 54.94 mg/g, RL=0.118; PSO kinetic fit R²≈0.999 and Elovich R²≈0.991. Report Qmax as fitted capacity, not direct uptake at the 10 mg/L optimum feed.
Model / metric: Langmuir fitted Qmax; kinetic model fit
Evidence status: Extracted; fit parameters partly shown in figure/paragraph
Caveat / follow-up: Model fit alone does not prove chemisorption. SI model descriptions/parameter details are not retrieved.

Experimental design / conditions: pHPZC≈4; ENF pKa reported as 6.09 and 7.91; FTIR/EDX/XRD evaluated before/after adsorption. Table 4 tabulates thermodynamic quantities for 288–313 K.
Reported result: Authors report ΔH°=−0.735 kJ/mol, ΔS°=−0.107 kJ/(mol K), but Table 4 lists ΔG° from −3825 to −4089 kJ/mol. Using their stated ΔG°=ΔH°−TΔS° relation at 288 K yields roughly +30.1 kJ/mol, not −3825 kJ/mol. This is a major internal arithmetic/unit inconsistency; do not use ΔG numbers as valid evidence for spontaneity.
Caveat / follow-up: Need source correction/author clarification before citing thermodynamic values. PSO and apparent activation energy also do not uniquely prove a molecular mechanism.

Adsorbent / material: Spent ACNB and treated/untreated ENF solution
Continuum stage: Stage 3 — regeneration and limited toxicity indicator
Evidence domain: ENF desorption used 40% (w/v) ethanol; desorbed media dehydrated and tested for reuse. DNA test used 8 μL 0.02 mM ethidium bromide, 80 μL 0.2 mM calf-thymus DNA, 10 ppm treated/untreated ENF solution, incubation 34 °C for 30 min, fluorescence excitation 471 nm and emission measured.
Experimental design / conditions: ACNB reported 81.47% ENF removal efficiency after four cycles. DNA fluorescence assay showed changes between control, treated and untreated samples, interpreted by authors as reduced DNA-intercalation effect.
Reported result: % removal after 4 cycles; ppm; °C; min
Value / units: Four-cycle reusability and specific DNA-binding fluorescence assay
Evidence status: This is not a broad ecotoxicity/genotoxicity test of actual wastewater or transformation products; do not claim the treated water is universally safe for reuse from fluorescence alone.

Adsorbent / material: ACNB, lime/water/cement immobilization for spent media
Evidence domain: Laboratory cost breakdown; spent ACNB mixed with lime, water and cement then dried/solidified and landfilled.
Experimental design / conditions: Reported material production cost INR 239.22/kg (cost table includes 8.57 INR carbonization electricity, 102.84 INR drying electricity, 97.50 INR H3PO4, 8.57 INR drying and 10% overhead). Authors compare four-cycle cost with local commercial activated charcoal, claiming 16.7-times lower treatment cost.
Reported result: INR/kg as reported; INR per table entries
Value / units: Laboratory production-cost estimate and proposed disposal
Evidence status: Yield/mass basis and scale of H3PO4 amount are not transparent; regeneration/treatment and effluent costs not harmonized; no full LCA. Authors themselves note long-term leachate implications need more study.

Target / co-contaminant: PCG, AMP, CAZ, MEM, SMZ (paper label), CIP
Adsorbent / material: Six commercial GACs: Co-U, Co-A, Co-E, Co-P, Coal-K, Coal-C
Experimental design / conditions: GAC particles 1–2 mm washed and dried at 150 °C/12 h. Table 1: BET area Co-U 847, Co-A 592, Co-E 574, Co-P 594, Coal-K 893, Coal-C 1106 m²/g; mean pore size 2.9, 2.9, 2.8, 2.7, 2.7, 1.9 nm. Co-U water contact angle 78° and total acidic groups 0.2 mmol/g.
Reported result: Coconut-shell GAC Co-U (not the highest BET-area GAC) showed highest overall antibiotic adsorption and highest hydrophobicity/lowest oxygenated acidic group density. Authors attribute performance to surface hydrophobicity, pore access and functional-group interactions.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2, 5; Table 1; Fig. S4 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Table's “SMZ” label should be preserved unless the original antibiotic identity in the methods/supplement is separately confirmed; do not automatically relabel it SMX.

Target / co-contaminant: PCG, AMP, CAZ, MEM, SMZ, CIP
Adsorbent / material: Co-U GAC among six commercial GACs
Experimental design / conditions: Initial concentration 100 μg/L, GAC dose 1 g/L, 10 mM phosphate-buffered solution pH 7, 25 °C. Real chlorinated hospital wastewater (C-HWW) used as background matrix for batch kinetics/isotherms.
Reported result: In single-solute C-HWW linear isotherms, Co-U Kp values (L/g): PCG 0.3778; AMP 0.8379; CAZ 0.3916; MEM 1.5674; SMZ 0.7876; CIP 0.4157. PCG/AMP showed lowest overall adsorption; MEM highest Kp among the six.
Model / metric: Linear isotherm distribution coefficient, not Langmuir qmax
Caveat / follow-up: The study deliberately operates at low μg/L levels; do not directly rank its Kp values against high mg/L batch qmax values.

Target / co-contaminant: PCG, AMP, CAZ, MEM, SMZ, CIP mixed feed
Experimental design / conditions: Single/mixed six-antibiotic isotherms in actual C-HWW background, pH 7, 25 °C, dose 1 g/L; concentration range 50–200 μg/L.
Reported result: In the mixed solution, Kp values (L/g) for PCG/AMP/CAZ/CIP were 0.2996/0.5292/0.3770/0.1738; MEM and SMZ were not adsorbed/fitted. At Ce=50 μg/L, AMP and CIP capacities fell ~37% and ~58%; CAZ slightly increased, PCG changed little. MEM and SMZ were outcompeted despite stronger single-solute adsorption.
Model / metric: Linear isotherm Kp and single-vs-mixture effect
Caveat / follow-up: The mixed-feed effect is important for engineering relevance; keep the paper's antibiotic labels and actual C-HWW matrix attached to the values.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic feed 100 μg/L, dose 1 g/L, pH 7, 25 °C, background C-HWW; sampled 0–12 h. MEM and SMZ omitted from kinetics because they were not adsorbed in mixed-solute conditions.
Reported result: CAZ/CIP reached plateau around 300 min after fast first 45 min; PCG around 200 min and AMP around 400 min. LDF/HID kinetic model RRMSE was reported as approximately 1.35–4.37 μg/g; Biot analysis suggests external-film and intraparticle diffusion both contribute.
Model / metric: Linear driving force / homogeneous intraparticle diffusion
Caveat / follow-up: Not a high-concentration capacity study. Model fit describes transport but should not be turned into a chemisorption claim.

Target / co-contaminant: Residual antibiotics/intermediates in S-HWW and C-HWW
Adsorbent / material: GAC treatment after secondary hospital-wastewater treatment
Experimental design / conditions: S-HWW is non-chlorinated secondary effluent; C-HWW is chlorinated secondary effluent (residual free chlorine 0.5 mg Cl2/L). Toxicity assessed by growth of E. coli ATCC 25922, compared to DI-water control.
Reported result: DI water supported log 9.4 CFU/mL; S-HWW and C-HWW log 7.2 and 6.7. GAC treatment gave only log 6.7–7.8 for S-HWW but log 9.2–9.5 for C-HWW. Authors associate the latter response with chlorination reducing intermediate diversity and improving adsorption of remaining intermediates.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 5–6; Fig. 1; Fig. S6 cited
Caveat / follow-up: This is an E. coli growth response, not full ecotoxicological clearance or proof all antibiotic/intermediate toxicity is eliminated in every assay.

Continuum stage: Stage 4 — GAC column and spent-media risk
Experimental design / conditions: Glass column 2.5 cm ID × 15 cm high, bed depth 15 cm, 20 g dried Co-U, 5 mL/min, EBCT 25 min. Operated 45 days (~4402.5 bed volumes); HT-qPCR panel 43 target genes, 32 detected across samples.
Reported result: Column passage reduced relative abundance of many detected ARGs in effluent, but some microbial taxa/genes increased in used GAC samples, including reported Firmicutes and efflux/chlorine-resistance-related genes under certain conditions. Authors conclude used GAC may acquire resistant bacterial strains and requires appropriate disinfection before disposal.
Value / units: days; bed volumes; mL/min; 20 g; gene detections
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–4, 10–13; Figs. 5–7; Table S13 cited
Evidence status: Extracted; SI gene-abundance tables not uploaded
Caveat / follow-up: Removal from water does not equal gene/organism destruction; some biology may accumulate on spent GAC. Waste media must be treated as potentially infectious/resistome-bearing.

Adsorbent / material: Phosphoric-acid-activated banana-peel activated carbon (BPAC), selected at 450 °C
Experimental design / conditions: Banana peels washed, cut to 2 cm, dried 100 °C/24 h, ground/sieved <0.150 mm; 25 g BP soaked in 500 mL 25% v/v H3PO4 solution at 80 °C/4 h; dried 110 °C/6 h; carbonized 350/450/550 °C for 30 min; washed to pH 6–7, dried at 105 °C. BPAC chosen at 450 °C.
Reported result: BET area 911.59 m²/g, pHPZC 5.005, total acidic groups 0.711 mmol/g, basic groups 0.143 mmol/g. Fixed carbon increased from 0.67 to 74.07%; volatile matter 82.53→16.90%; moisture 11.37→4.08%. Raw BP BET 0.650 m²/g.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3–5, 10–12; Figs. 2–4; Table S1 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Only amoxicillin should count toward antibiotic-only synthesis; carbamazepine is a non-antibiotic co-contaminant. No product yield, numerical cost or full LCA is reported.

Experimental design / conditions: Main condition: 150 mL mixture, initial concentration stated as 25 mg/L, 0.18 g BPAC (=1.2 g/L), pH 5, 25±2 °C, 150 rpm, 120 min. Dosage series 0.3–1.5 g/L; tests triplicate with CV≤2.64%.
Reported result: Increasing BPAC from 0.9 to 1.5 g/L raised amoxicillin removal 84.07→96.02% and carbamazepine 87.04→90.62%; authors selected 1.2 g/L because further gain was marginal. Contact-time tests reached plateau at 120 min. Amoxicillin removal decreased from 99.43% at 10 mg/L feed to 91.54% at 25 mg/L.
Caveat / follow-up: The paper's concentration description refers to the mixture; don't assume each analyte starts at 25 mg/L unless its method/figures confirm it.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherm feed 5–120 mg/L, 0.18 g BPAC in 150 mL, pH 5, 12 h, 25±2 °C. Kinetic tests 25 mg/L, pH 5, contact 10–120 min; triplicate.
Reported result: Langmuir model best by SSE; fitted Qmax 393.70 mg/g amoxicillin and 338.98 mg/g carbamazepine. PSO R²=0.992 amoxicillin and 0.984 carbamazepine; PFO R²=0.909 and 0.977, respectively.
Model / metric: Langmuir fitted qmax and kinetic fit
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 5–6, 16–17; Fig. 7; Table S2 cited
Evidence status: Extracted; detailed model-parameter table is SI-dependent
Caveat / follow-up: Fitted capacities are not observed uptake under optimum 25 mg/L mixed-feed conditions. PSO fit does not prove chemisorption.

Experimental design / conditions: pH series pH 2–10; pHPZC 5.005. FTIR before/after adsorption; XRD reportedly showed no tangible change.
Reported result: Amoxicillin removal rose from 80.43% at pH 2 to 91.42% at pH 4, then reduced at alkaline pH, reaching 50.65% at pH 10. Carbamazepine removal rose from 61.22% at pH 2 to 87.63% at pH 4 and about 90.54% around pH 5. Authors propose electrostatic effects, hydrophobic and π–π interactions, pore filling/intraparticle diffusion and surface groups.
Caveat / follow-up: Specific mechanism is interpretive; do not treat PSO or D–R energy as definitive proof of chemisorption.

Experimental design / conditions: Desorption in 25 mL water at pH 7 or ethanol, 150 rpm for 6 h; post-run sorbent dried at 105 °C for 24 h.
Reported result: Ethanol desorption rates: 76.83% for amoxicillin and 72.41% for carbamazepine. Water showed poor desorption.
Caveat / follow-up: Desorption is not equivalent to full media restoration or destruction of the contaminant; ethanol regenerant contains pollutant and needs downstream management.

Adsorbent / material: BPAC used in Milli-Q, Lake Balaton and wastewater samples
Experimental design / conditions: Optimized adsorption conditions applied to MQ water, lake water and wastewater without adjusting pH. Source paper refers to an earlier work for full water-matrix characterization.
Reported result: Initial-cycle removal reported: MQ water 91.63% amoxicillin/90.29% carbamazepine; lake water 86.63%/83.29%; wastewater 82.34%/81.51%. By cycle 7, MQ-water removal 41.43%/37.84%, lake-water 25.43%/15.84%, wastewater 20.43%/12.09%, respectively. The article reports mean cycle-4 removal >86.06% MQ, 74.57% lake and 63.89% wastewater.
Model / metric: Observed water-matrix performance and reuse decay
Caveat / follow-up: Strong decline in complex-water reuse. Matrix characterization is not fully included in this PDF; no unit cost/LCA or fully validated spent-media route.

Adsorbent / material: Melia azedarach raw sawdust and four modifications: CaCl2, NaHCO3, HCl, FeCl3/HCl
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — raw lignocellulosic waste and simple chemical modification
Experimental design / conditions: Sawdust washed, dried at 80 °C/3 h, sieved to 40–60 mesh. MS(I): 5 g in 100 mL 200 mg/L CaCl2, 2 h; MS(II): 5 g in 100 mL 0.7 M NaHCO3, 4 h; MS(III): 5 g in 100 mL 10% v/v HCl, 80 °C/1 h, neutral wash; MS(IV): 5 g MS(III) in 100 mL 0.75 M FeCl3 in 3 M HCl, 4 h, then 100 °C/12 h and neutral wash.
Reported result: Compared raw and chemically modified sawdust. FeCl3/HCl-treated MS(IV) performed best; no BET area, Fe leaching or complete preparation mass balance reported.
Model / metric: Preparation protocol and qualitative modification comparison
Caveat / follow-up: Chemical inputs/neutralization burden and the possibility of residual iron are not quantified; do not infer iron doping chemistry beyond the reported method and characterization.

Adsorbent / material: Raw sawdust (RS), MS(I) CaCl2, MS(II) NaHCO3, MS(III) HCl, MS(IV) Fe-modified sawdust
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — raw waste vs modified biomass
Experimental design / conditions: Initial comparison at TC 10 mg/L, dose 3.0 g/L, 22±2 °C, 100 rpm, contact time 0–120 min; pH 4, 7.5 and 9.5 (Fig. 1).
Reported result: Raw sawdust removal generally <10%; CaCl2-modified material generally ~20–40%; NaHCO3 generally <20%; HCl-modified material mostly 20–40%, maximum 41.50% in one condition. Fe-modified material exceeded 60% at pH 7.5 and 9.5 after >60 min; ranking MS(IV)>MS(III)>MS(I)>MS(II)>RS.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not treat this screening comparison as an equilibrium capacity ranking; each point is removal under a selected dose, pH and time.

Experimental design / conditions: Central composite design / response surface methodology with 30 runs; C0 5–25 mg/L, pH 3–12, dose 1–5 g/L, time 15–120 min. Measured design responses were 18.60–93.52%.
Reported result: RSM predicted optimum 98.40% at C0 12.5 mg/L, pH 7.9, dose 4.8 g/L and time 118.3 min (Table 4). Separate validation scenarios in Table 5 reached measured removal up to 92.37%; the listed validation runs do not reproduce the exact predicted optimum.
Caveat / follow-up: The 98.40% value is model predicted, not directly measured at the exact optimum. Avoid conflating it with the highest listed validation result.

Experimental design / conditions: C0 5–30 mg/L, dose 4.0 g/L, 90 min, pH 7.8; nonlinear Langmuir/Freundlich fits. Fit comparison used adjusted R², SSE and AIC.
Reported result: Freundlich preferred by AIC: adjusted R² 0.9891, SSE 0.16, AIC −12.62; Langmuir adjusted R² 0.9802, SSE 0.28, AIC −8.42, fitted Qm 5.41 mg/g and RL 0.19.
Model / metric: Fitted isotherm results; Langmuir Qm not directly observed capacity
Caveat / follow-up: Freundlich is the better reported model; retain Qm as fitted model parameter rather than a measured saturation loading.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic tests: C0 20 mg/L, pH 7.8, dose 1.5–4.5 g/L and time 0–120 min; PFO and PSO evaluated with R² and AIC.
Reported result: PFO R² values 0.991–0.997 and PSO 0.989–0.996; AIC −18.74 for PFO and −18.32 for PSO. The authors concluded both described the data well; PFO was marginally preferred by AIC. In a separate condition at C0 15 mg/L, pH 7.5, 3 g/L, removal rose from 50.97% at 15 min to 67.66% at 120 min.
Caveat / follow-up: The paper notes the contact-time trend was still rising at 120 min; do not claim verified equilibrium at 120 min.

Adsorbent / material: TC-loaded Fe-modified sawdust, regenerated with acidic water or methanol
Experimental design / conditions: Loaded sorbent prepared using 5 g sorbent and 100 mg/L TC for 24 h; compared 10 regeneration liquids, including water pH 4/7/10 and multiple solvents. Regenerated sorbent then tested at dose 3 g/L, pH 7.5 and 120 min against 10–25 mg/L TC.
Reported result: Acidic distilled water (pH 4) and methanol gave best post-regeneration performance; methanol was slightly better but considered more costly/toxic. At 3 g/L adsorption dose and 25 g/L regeneration-stage dose, authors calculated 88% water reclaimed, i.e. 12% of treated effluent volume is used in regeneration. This 88% is water-volume reclamation, not antibiotic desorption efficiency.
Caveat / follow-up: Only single-stage regeneration was conducted. Do not report 88% as TC desorption or multi-cycle efficiency; methanol creates a solvent-management burden.

Experimental design / conditions: Hospital wastewater from Imam Reza Hospital, Mashhad, Iran; initial TC 0.25 mg/L. Reported treatment condition pH 8.3, dose 3.6 g/L and contact time 53 min.
Reported result: TC decreased from 0.25 mg/L to not detectable by HPLC under the stated conditions.
Value / units: mg/L; g/L; min; pH; HPLC non-detect
Model / metric: Observed real-matrix result; below detection is not zero
Caveat / follow-up: Numeric HPLC LOD/LOQ is not reported in this study text. Authors also explicitly identify non-conformability between synthetic and real-water concentrations as a limitation; no column/pilot or iron-leaching study.

Target / co-contaminant: Eight tetracycline antibiotics plus five metabolites
Adsorbent / material: Purified Na+-homoionic stevensite from Moroccan Rhassoul clay
Experimental design / conditions: 30 g washed clay in 1 L water, stir 30 min; add 1 M HCl until carbonate CO2 release stops; treat with 1 M NaCl for 12 h to Na+ homoionic form; isolate particles <2 μm by Stokes-law sedimentation; dry 50 °C/24 h and grind.
Reported result: BET area 147 m²/g, pore volume 0.122 cm³/g, mean pore diameter 3.32 nm, type-II N2 isotherm (some numeric characterization is in SI Table S1). Material is purified size fraction of a natural stevensite-rich Rhassoul clay; this is not synthetic functionalization.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3–4, 17–18; Fig. 1–4; SI Table S1 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Acid/salt consumption, wastewater and purification yield/cost are not quantified in a TEA/LCA.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, CTC, MNC, DMCC, DC, OTC, TGC, MTC plus ETC, ATC, EATC, ECTC, EOTC
Experimental design / conditions: Main methods state 10 mL target solution, 20 mg ST (2 g/L), 350 rpm, room temperature, general initial concentration 2 mg/L; contact time swept from 5 s to 24 h. Abstract says dose 2 g/L and concentration 5 mg/L; another kinetic passage seems to print 2 mg/mL. Selected later contact time 30 min.
Reported result: Most compounds exceeded 80% adsorption within 0.5 min; the kinetic discussion says equilibrium reached in <5 min for all selected tetracyclines, while abstract/conclusion say equilibrium within 30 min (30 min used for subsequent tests). At conditions reported in abstract, >99% removal is claimed at acidic pH.
Value / units: mg/L vs mg/mL; g/L; rpm; seconds/minutes
Model / metric: Kinetic/observed removal result with condition discrepancy flagged
Caveat / follow-up: Initial concentration is inconsistent across abstract/methods and a kinetic passage has a likely unit typo. Do not combine concentration-dependent q values unless the exact protocol is confirmed.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherm concentration range 0.25–100 mg/L; Langmuir and Freundlich fitted by nonlinear optimization. Kinetic Table 1 reports experimental qe about 0.983–1.575 mg/g for analytes under the main low-concentration protocol.
Reported result: Freundlich fit R² range 0.817–0.968 was generally better than Langmuir (R² 0.755–0.908). However, the narrative states qmax over 200,000 mg/g for TC in one passage (and TGC in the conclusion); Table 2 gives TGC 86.1 mg/g, TC 1000 mg/g, with several fitted qmax values exactly 1000 mg/g. These values are internally inconsistent and the extreme narrative figure is physically implausible.
Model / metric: Fitted isotherm values; source inconsistency flagged
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 8–10; Fig. 6; Tables 1–2; SI Table S2 cited
Evidence status: Extracted; qmax not accepted as reliable comparison
Caveat / follow-up: Do not use the >200,000 mg/g narrative value. Even Table 2 values appear capped/implausibly high relative to qe exp (~1–1.6 mg/g); quantitative qmax should be excluded pending clarification.

Experimental design / conditions: pH sweep 2–9; TC compounds have pKa values reported about 3.3, 7.7 and 9.6. Surface charge changes with pH. Most compounds >99% across wide pH range except extreme conditions.
Reported result: Best adsorption generally pH 3–6. At pH 2, most compounds showed lower removal (with exceptions), and the authors note some tetracyclines may degrade under highly acidic conditions; at pH 9 some compounds may also degrade to a lesser extent. Reported performance is a combination of adsorption and possible analyte transformation at extremes.
Model / metric: Observed pH response and author interpretation
Caveat / follow-up: Apparent disappearance at pH 2 or 9 may include degradation, not adsorption alone. Do not claim every loss as adsorption without target/product mass balance.

Experimental design / conditions: Humic acid/DOM was varied; relevant effect discussion reports up to 25 mg/L humic acid for the compound-specific discussion, while Methods says 0.5–10 mg/L for the planned range.
Reported result: DOM generally had little influence. OTC removal changed by about 0–3% as DOM increased; EOTC by about 0–1.5%; most other compounds remained >99% in the discussed conditions.
Caveat / follow-up: Main methods and results describe different DOM test ranges; verify supplementary table/figure before a strict quantitative matrix comparison.

Experimental design / conditions: NaCl varied from 0 to 4% (described in text as %); adsorption response evaluated across the target panel.
Reported result: As salinity rose 0→4%, OTC removal fell about 50%, EOTC about 30–40%, TC/ETC/ATC/ECTC roughly 20%, and several other analytes about 10%. The authors attribute this to competitive interactions/ionic strength and Na+-tetracycline complexation.
Caveat / follow-up: Salinity considerably affects results for some analytes; maintain the target compound and concentration in any comparative plot.

Target / co-contaminant: Eight tetracyclines and five metabolites in real water matrices
Experimental design / conditions: Tap water, surface/river water, influent wastewater and effluent wastewater filtered through 1.2 μm glass microfiber filters and spiked at 2 mg/L; matrix-matched LC-MS/MS calibration. The full initial test is a spiked matrix, not native trace concentrations.
Reported result: Removal was >99% for most compounds; general trend distilled water > tap > surface water > effluent wastewater > influent wastewater. Example reported reductions: OTC 99.98→99.82%, MTC 99.98→99.9% as matrices got more complex.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 14–16; Fig. 9; Fig. S10 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Real matrices are spiked at 2 mg/L, well above many environmental trace levels; don't describe as unspiked native wastewater remediation or field-scale treatment.

Adsorbent / material: Purified stevensite regenerated with McIlvaine buffer/acetone
Experimental design / conditions: Five adsorption-desorption cycles. Each cycle used 5 mL McIlvaine buffer/acetone mixture (7:3 v/v) at pH 4, followed by DI water wash, centrifugation and drying at 40 °C. Article says desorption efficiencies >99% after four cycles and >90% capacity retained after the fifth cycle.
Reported result: Authors report retained adsorption capacity >90% after five cycles, and desorption efficiencies >99% after four cycles. Suggested mechanisms are acidic eluate weakening electrostatic binding and acetone assisting solvent-mediated release.
Caveat / follow-up: Acetone-containing regenerant and concentrated antibiotic eluate require solvent recovery/waste treatment; no cost/LCA or dynamic-column validation reported.

Adsorbent / material: Apple-branch biochar (BC), ball-milled control QBC and ammonia-assisted N-doped QN7.5BC
Experimental design / conditions: Apple branches dried 80 °C; pyrolysed under N2 at 700 °C for 2 h; ground/sieved 100 mesh. Modified material: 2 g BC + 15 mL 25 wt% ammonia solution + zirconia balls (three sizes; stated ratio 1:10:11), 300 rpm for 24 h with direction reversal every 30 min and 5-min pauses. QBC is milled without ammonia.
Reported result: QN7.5BC BET area 206.8825 m²/g, total pore volume 0.2951 cm³/g, micropore volume 0.03822 cm³/g (13% total), pore diameter 11.8834 nm. After TC adsorption: 144.4029 m²/g, 0.2532 cm³/g total pore volume and 0.01082 cm³/g micropore volume. N species included pyrrolic, graphitic and pyridinic N.
Evidence status: Extracted from uploaded ACS Omega PDF
Caveat / follow-up: Abstract gives total pore volume as 276 cm³/g, conflicting with detailed result 0.2951 cm³/g; use detailed main-text value and flag abstract error. No yield, milling energy, unit cost or LCA.

Experimental design / conditions: Adsorption test at selected conditions, 30 mg/L initial TC, dose 0.5 g/L, solution native pH unless pH-specific experiment; tests in independent triplicate.
Reported result: TC removal: pristine BC 6.6%, ball-milled QBC 43.8%, N-doped ball-milled QN7.5BC 95.7%. The comparison supports separate contributions from mechanical milling and ammonia-assisted N modification.
Model / metric: Observed batch removal under selected condition
Caveat / follow-up: A high first-cycle synthetic-water removal result does not establish real-wastewater/column performance, and does not by itself quantify the separate causal effects of pore changes vs chemistry.

Experimental design / conditions: Langmuir/Freundlich isotherms evaluated at 298, 308 and 318 K; nonlinear model fits.
Reported result: QN7.5BC fitted Langmuir Qm: 155.7405 mg/g (298 K), 219.8073 mg/g (308 K), 400.0180 mg/g (318 K), with R² 0.9983, 0.9931, 0.9793. Ball-milled QBC Qm: 29.9875, 32.1855, 41.7961 mg/g at those temperatures (QBC fit weak at 298 K, R² 0.7781).
Caveat / follow-up: Qm is a fitted equilibrium model parameter and temperature-dependent, not a directly observed real-water working capacity.

Experimental design / conditions: Dosage varied 0.2–0.5 g/L and beyond; initial TC 10–50 mg/L; pH 3–12. Native pH used except pH-specific tests. Isoelectric point pHIEP≈6.
Reported result: Removal rose from ~65% to >95% when dose rose 0.2→0.5 g/L, then plateaued. For C0 10–30 mg/L removal >95%; at 40 and 50 mg/L it fell to 91.2% and 89.5%. pH 3–9 removal >90%, peak 95.1% at pH 8; it fell to 83.5% at pH 10–11 then recovered to 89.9% at pH 12.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7–8; Fig. 3b–c; Fig. S6/S7 cited
Caveat / follow-up: High-dose and synthetic-feed results should not be substituted for trace-level capacity or natural wastewater.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic Qe experimental 64.49 mg/g under kinetic study; PFO, PSO and intraparticle-diffusion models fitted; isotherm temperatures 298–318 K.
Reported result: PSO R²=0.9998 and calculated Qe 64.94 mg/g; PFO R²=0.8576 and Qe,cal 65.16 mg/g. Reported ΔG −1.77, −2.91 and −4.40 kJ/mol (298/308/318 K), ΔH +37.24 kJ/mol, ΔS +130.69 J/(mol K). Paper proposes pore filling, H-bonding, π–π/EDA and pH-dependent electrostatics; PSO fit alone is not independent proof of chemisorption.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 8–9; Fig. 3f–g; SI Tables S4–S5 cited
Caveat / follow-up: Text's interpretation calls process chemisorption-controlled but describes strong noncovalent interactions; retain as author interpretation, not a proven unique mechanism.

Target / co-contaminant: TC under ions/DOM and tap/river water
Experimental design / conditions: 30 mg/L TC at reported selected conditions; ions up to 20–80 mmol/L, humic acid 0–8 mg/L, natural water tests with DI, tap and river water.
Reported result: Cl−, NO3−, SO42− and HCO3− had negligible effects with removal >86%; H2PO4− and CO32− reduced removal to 83.9% and 75% at high concentrations. Mg²⁺ most inhibitory, 69.8→56.3% as concentration rose 20→80 mmol/L. DI water 95.7%, tap water 89.2%, river water 92.5% TC removal.
Model / metric: Ion competition and real-water matrix effects
Caveat / follow-up: Natural waters are batch tests; not native-concentration analysis or continuous-flow validation.

Target / co-contaminant: TC; OTC and non-antibiotic dyes in a separate screen
Adsorbent / material: QN7.5BC regenerated using DI water, 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaOH wash sequence
Evidence domain: Six adsorption-desorption cycles; spent material washed sequentially with DI water, 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaOH (3–5 times) and dried before reuse. Separate broad-target test includes OTC, methylene blue, malachite green, rhodamine B and Congo red.
Experimental design / conditions: TC removal declined from 95.6% in cycle 1 to 54.6% in cycle 2 and 40.6% by cycle 6. Article attributes loss to irreversible binding, pore blockage and incomplete desorption. Separate tests report >95% removal of several other pollutants; LMG was highest at 99.7%, not an antibiotic.
Reported result: cycles; % removal; mol/L
Value / units: Regeneration decay; broad-spectrum screen kept separate
Evidence status: Reuse is a major weakness despite first-cycle performance. Do not imply excellent sustained reusability, and keep dyes separate from antibiotic evidence.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics and heavy metals in binary/multicomponent systems
Adsorbent / material: Review of CNTs, graphene, resins and carbon-based nanocomposites
Continuum stage: Stage 4 context — carbon nanomaterials; review-level source
Experimental design / conditions: Review article covering antibiotic–heavy-metal co-removal in water–soil systems; literature trend analysis covers 2010–2023.
Reported result: Useful context for the review's competition/matrix-effects and engineered-carbon sections. The article identifies bridging, electrostatic shielding, competition and spatial site-blocking as important interactions in combined systems. It is secondary literature, not a new independent experiment.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not count this review's summarized experiments as independent primary studies or transfer its numerical values into the primary-data synthesis without tracing the cited source papers.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics plus HMs (e.g., CIP–Cu/Zn, TC–As, etc.)
Experimental design / conditions: The review synthesizes binary-system adsorption where an adsorbent, metal and antibiotic can form ternary bridges; alternatively, antibiotics and metals can compete for active sites, displace adsorbates or block access spatially.
Reported result: Mechanisms can promote, inhibit or have negligible net impact on adsorption. The article says bridging and electrostatic shielding often promote co-adsorption, while competition and spatial blocking often inhibit it; outcomes are material- and chemistry-dependent.
Caveat / follow-up: These are hypotheses/synthesis across different systems; don't apply one mechanism universally to single-antibiotic wastewater without direct evidence.

Experimental design / conditions: Review summarizes regeneration agents and cycle performance across sources; proposes adsorption cost as Energy cost + Chemical cost + Transportation cost + Capital cost. Lab-scale chemical and energy costs can account for more than 80% of carbon nanosorbent production cost in the cited literature.
Reported result: The review emphasizes that regeneration efficiency, solvent/eluent handling, separation from water, downstream treatment of regenerant and spent solids, factory operation and disposal must be included. Adsorbent cost-performance is framed as dollar cost for producing/using sorbent to remove a unit mass of contaminant.
Caveat / follow-up: Exact cost values in the review depend on its cited sources and supplementary calculations; not a harmonized, independently reproduced TEA. Trace any quantitative comparison to the original paper and original cost boundary.

Target / co-contaminant: Sulfamethoxazole (SMZ), levofloxacin (LVX), clindamycin (CLI), tetracycline (TC), penicillin G (PEN), chloramphenicol (CHL)
Experimental design / conditions: Graphite oxidized with concentrated HNO3/K2S2O8/P2O5 at 80 °C/6 h, then concentrated H2SO4/H3PO4/KMnO4 oxidation at 35–60 °C and 98 °C, H2O2 quench and HCl wash; exfoliated by 100 W ultrasound 30 min. GO dispersed in water, ammonia added, autoclaved 180 °C/24 h, then washed and dried at 60 °C/12 h. XPS reported pyridinic N 50.91%, pyrrolic N 26.49%, graphitic N 22.60% of N 1s contributions.
Reported result: N-rGO surface was wrinkled/folded with C, N and O signals. Chemistry involves strong oxidants/acids, repeated washing, ultrasonic treatment, and a 180 °C, 24 h autoclave step; no material yield, reagent recovery, energy/cost estimate or LCA reported.
Caveat / follow-up: Clearly distinguish N-rGO from N-doped biochar: this is a graphene-derived nanosorbent. Scale-up chemical, washing-water and hazardous-reagent burdens are not quantified.

Target / co-contaminant: SMZ, LVX, CLI, TC, PEN, CHL
Experimental design / conditions: Each antibiotic solution: 80 mL plus 20 mL N-rGO dispersion reported as 0.5 mg/L; 120 rpm and 25±1 °C. Initial concentration series 0.1, 1, 10 and 20 μg/L; pH 3–12; reported N-rGO dosage range 40–400 μg/L. Figure 2 kinetic comparison at C0=10 μg/L; equilibrium/kinetics differed by compound.
Reported result: Authors state removal >80%, TC adsorption fastest (within 30 min), clindamycin slowest (within 90 min), and the adsorption process generally completed within 60 min. Table 1 reports experimental qe 80.58–90.21 mg/g at the kinetic conditions.
Model / metric: Observed removal/time and qe as reported
Caveat / follow-up: The stated volumes, N-rGO dispersion concentration, trace feed concentrations and Table 1 qe need to be reconciled. For the example 80 mL of 10 μg/L feed plus 20 mL at 0.5 mg/L N-rGO, complete uptake implies a maximum qe of about 80 mg/g; some Table 1 qe values exceed this. Verify unit basis before quantitative comparison.

Target / co-contaminant: SMZ, LVX, CLI, TC, PEN, CHL
Experimental design / conditions: Concentration series reported as 0.1–20 μg/L; adsorption isotherms fitted to Langmuir/Freundlich. Table 2 reports Langmuir q_m and fitted R².
Reported result: Reported Langmuir q_m: SMZ 574.71, LVX 561.80, CLI 1265.82, TC 662.25, PEN 917.43, CHL 662.25 mg/g; Langmuir R² 0.9989–0.9996. Authors favour Langmuir. These q_m values are extrapolated fits at an extremely low stated concentration range.
Caveat / follow-up: Fitted saturation capacities greatly exceed the loading range implied by the reported trace concentration and adsorbent doses; treat these q_m values as unreliable for cross-paper ranking unless the concentration/dose units are clarified.

Experimental design / conditions: pH 3–12 and temperatures 288.15, 298.15, 308.15 and 318.15 K; starting conditions and antibiotic dosage as described in Methods.
Reported result: Authors report antibiotic structure/speciation influences pH response; adsorption/removal generally decreased as temperature rose, interpreted as exothermic. The reported ΔH entries are negative and ΔG values are negative in Table 3.
Model / metric: Observed effects and author thermodynamic interpretation
Caveat / follow-up: Thermodynamic constants inherit the same unit/concentration concerns as the adsorption model; use qualitatively unless source arithmetic and dimensions are independently checked.

Target / co-contaminant: Six target antibiotics with coexisting ions and natural organic matter
Experimental design / conditions: Ions listed: Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, Cl−, HCO3−, CO3²− and NO3− at reported 100 mmol/L in coexistence tests; humic acid 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6 and 10 mg/L.
Reported result: Authors report that tested ions had little inhibitory effect, but increasing humic acid reduced antibiotic adsorption; at 10 mg/L humic acid, capacity decreased by up to 30%. Coexisting six-antibiotic tests also show competition effects in the figure.
Caveat / follow-up: The reported ion concentration (100 mmol/L) is high relative to many natural waters; describe as a controlled interference test rather than proof that all natural-water ions never inhibit adsorption.

Experimental design / conditions: 0.1 mol/L HCl used to elute saturated N-rGO; 0.1 mol/L NaOH used for regeneration, followed by DI-water washing. Figure 3e reports cycle response.
Reported result: Authors state adsorption capacity decreased by no more than 25% after eight cycles. They attribute some decrease to changes/agglomeration in the rGO interlayer structure and loss of active sites.
Caveat / follow-up: Regenerant volumes, concentrated antibiotic eluate treatment, material loss and cost were not quantified. The favourable cycle claim does not offset the q_m mass-balance concern.

Experimental design / conditions: Rice husk collected in Al-Mishkhab, Najaf Governorate, Iraq; washed repeatedly with DI water and air-dried at room temperature for 24 h; sieved to 1–2 mm and stored. Reported BET/surface area 0.328 m²/g; real density 1.48 g/cm³; bulk density 0.11 g/cm³.
Reported result: The study uses raw husk with no pyrolysis or chemical functionalization. SEM shows grooves/rough aggregates; FTIR bands shift after LEV adsorption and authors assign roles to OH, carboxylic/C–O, aliphatic C–H and aromatic groups.
Caveat / follow-up: Surface area is low as reported, so report the modest fitted qmax with the very high practical doses tested; no complete cost model or leaching assessment.

Experimental design / conditions: Parameter ranges included pH 2–8, initial LEV 25–100 mg/L, RRH mass 0.5–12 g per 100 mL (=5–120 g/L), particle sizes 0.25, 1 and 2 mm, 150 rpm, usually room temperature. Particle-size comparison: 50 mg/L LEV, pH 5, 3 g/100 mL, 3 h.
Reported result: Reducing particle size increased removal; the paper reports removal rising approximately 56%→87% across the particle-size comparison. Raising RRH dose from 5 to 120 g/L raised removal from 27.8% to 93.8%.
Caveat / follow-up: 120 g/L is an exceptionally high adsorbent dose; high removal at that loading must not be presented as an inexpensive or practical result without a dose-normalized cost and sludge/solid-handling assessment.

Experimental design / conditions: Time and initial-concentration tests: C0 25, 50, 75 and 100 mg/L, up to 3 h; dose/particle size/pH otherwise held as selected in each test. Authors report fast initial uptake during first ~10 min and equilibrium around 120 min.
Reported result: Removal efficiency decreased from about 99% to 90% as C0 increased from 25 to 100 mg/L; the paper says removal increased with time, then plateaued around 120 min. A separate dose sweep reports 93.8% at 120 g/L; headline 99% should remain attached to its specific condition rather than generalized.
Caveat / follow-up: Different figures use different parameter sets, and the headline 99% is not a universal result. Do not combine the best percentage with the dose from a different figure unless conditions match.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherm tests: initial concentration 25, 50, 75, 100 mg/L, pH 5, 9 g RRH per 100 mL (=90 g/L), 150 rpm and 3 h. Langmuir/Freundlich fits evaluated.
Reported result: Langmuir preferred by reported R² 0.95 (Freundlich R² 0.93); Langmuir fitted qmax 2.47 mg/g and b 0.073; Freundlich K 0.18 and 1/n 0.763. The abstract reports up to 99% removal, but optimum conditions and dose must remain explicit.
Caveat / follow-up: A low qmax paired with very high sorbent doses is central to the continuum argument. Do not use 99% as evidence of low cost or high uptake.

Experimental design / conditions: Thermodynamic tests at 298, 303, 308, 313 K; time tests to 3 h. Tested kinetic models included PFO, PSO, intraparticle diffusion and Elovich.
Reported result: Authors report intraparticle diffusion best fit, R² 0.96, with ERRSQ 0.01, ARE 0.25 and χ²≈0.00; Langmuir fitted qmax 2.47 mg/g. ΔH°=+37.117 kJ/mol, ΔS°=+125.134 J/(mol K), ΔG° −0.197, −0.823, −1.312 and −2.188 kJ/mol at 298/303/308/313 K. Positive ΔH is interpreted as endothermic adsorption.
Value / units: R²; mg/g; kJ/mol; J/(mol K); K
Caveat / follow-up: The best intraparticle-diffusion fit alone does not prove intraparticle diffusion is the sole rate-limiting step; kinetic table formatting/parameter labels should be checked before reproducing individual rates.

Experimental design / conditions: Batch tests in prepared LEV solutions; no real wastewater/column/pilot test, no adsorbent regeneration test, no numerical production cost or LCA reported in the uploaded article.
Reported result: The article positions raw rice husk as low-cost/sustainable, but the highest reported dose sweeps reach 120 g/L and fitted qmax is 2.47 mg/g. No empirical regeneration, real-water testing or cost comparison is presented.
Caveat / follow-up: Keep the authors' sustainability claim separate from demonstrated evidence: the paper gives no measured unit cost, regeneration, real-water validation, or solid-waste management assessment.

Experimental design / conditions: 1 g alginate in 50 mL water; add 0.5 g additive, stir 12–24 h; drop into 2% CaCl2 and crosslink 24 h.
Reported result: BET area increased from 7.08 m²/g for ALG to 42.04 m²/g for ALG_Hal@MIP.
Caveat / follow-up: Chitosan comparators are drawn from an earlier study; no cost/LCA.

Experimental design / conditions: 20 mg beads/10 mL, 298 K; pH tests 25 mg/L TC, pH 3–9; concentration series 5–700 mg/L. pHPZC was 6.15 for ALG and 6.72–6.95 for additive beads.
Reported result: Abstract reports observed maximum 281 mg/g for ALG_Hal@MIP. Table 1 fitted Langmuir qm: ALG 83.68; ALG_Hal 216.5; ALG_MIP 552.5; ALG_NIP 145.8; ALG_Hal@MIP 339.0; ALG_Hal@NIP 174.8 mg/g.
Model / metric: Observed capacity distinct from fitted qm
Caveat / follow-up: The paper generally prefers Freundlich fits for composite beads; do not merge measured and fitted capacities.

Experimental design / conditions: Time series at C0 500 mg/L, 20 mg beads in 10 mL, pH 6, 298 K; time to equilibrium varies by bead.
Reported result: Equilibrium: ALG ~8 h, ALG_Hal ~18 h, ALG_Hal@MIP/Hal@NIP ~24 h, free-polymer systems ~48 h. Table 2 reports q_exp=277.6 mg/g for ALG_Hal@MIP, but stated 500 mg/L × 10 mL / 20 mg yields a maximum 250 mg/g.
Caveat / follow-up: Reported q_exp exceeds the mass-balance ceiling implied by the stated inputs.

Experimental design / conditions: Ethanol with 1 h ultrasound and water rinse; five adsorption-desorption cycles.
Reported result: Authors propose pore filling, electrostatic effects, calcium complexation, H-bonding and π–π interaction. After 5 cycles ALG fell to ~63% initial efficiency; composite alginate beads remained >80%.
Caveat / follow-up: PSO fit alone does not prove unique chemisorption; eluent management not costed.

Experimental design / conditions: Water samples filtered and spiked to 500 mg/L TC; 20 mg beads/10 mL, pH 6, 48 h, 298 K.
Reported result: ALG_Hal@MIP reported q_e (mg/g): demineralized 277.6; four-solute mixture 187.2; TC+CF 210.8; TC+DX 201.8; TC+VN 223.5; tap water 253.8; lake 219.6; river 212.5.
Caveat / follow-up: 500 mg/L is a high spiked feed, not trace-level wastewater. Doxorubicin is an anticancer drug, not an antibiotic.

Experimental design / conditions: 1 g soil + 20 mg beads in 50 mL TC at 0.2 or 0.5 mg/L in 0.005 M CaCl2, 48 h; soil pH not optimized.
Reported result: Alginate generally outperformed chitosan; halloysite-containing beads reduced TC desorption from soil; pure chitosan beads increased it relative to the soil control.
Caveat / follow-up: Lab soil test; no field remediation validation.

Adsorbent / material: Magnetic Se-MOF/Fe3O4 embedded in chitosan/alginate beads (MSCA)
Experimental design / conditions: Fe3O4 precipitated from Fe(III)/Fe(II) salts under N2 at 80 °C, pH ~10; Se-MOF synthesized using 2-aminoterephthalic acid and SeCl4 in methanol at 120 °C; beads CaCl2-crosslinked and hardened in 25% epichlorohydrin for 48 h.
Reported result: BET area 420 m²/g, pore volume reported ~5.1 cm³/g, pore size 8.88 nm, pHPZC 5.64, magnetization 42.4 emu/g.
Caveat / follow-up: No Se/Fe leaching, production yield, environmental safety, cost or LCA tested; synthesis uses SeCl4, methanol and epichlorohydrin.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherms: 0.02 g MSCA in 25 mL CIP, C0 15–550 mg/L, pH 8, 200 rpm, 25 °C. pH test at C0 400 mg/L; kinetic test at C0 300 mg/L, pH 8, 250 rpm, 25 °C, 0–100 min.
Reported result: Capacity reached ~380 mg/g at pH 8 and ~420 mg/g near 80–100 min; removal exceeded 95% below 100 mg/L initial concentration and fell to ~62% at 600 mg/L.
Caveat / follow-up: Tests use mg/L feeds, not native trace concentrations or continuous-flow operation.

Experimental design / conditions: Langmuir/Freundlich fitted; Box–Behnken design used dose, pH and contact time with 17 design runs.
Reported result: Langmuir qm=442.4 mg/g; experimental q_m=439.2 mg/g; KL=0.031 L/mg; RL=0.12. RSM optimum: 0.02 g, 100 min, pH 8; predicted q_e=440.84 mg/g; R²=0.9918, adjusted R²=0.9812, predicted R²=0.8682.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 4, 12–15, 22–23; BBD Table 1, ANOVA Table 2
Caveat / follow-up: BBD table labels its response “Yield (mmol/g)” although other sections report capacity in mg/g; retain as source inconsistency.

Experimental design / conditions: FTIR/XPS before and after adsorption; NaCl interference tested from 0–50 g/L; filtered wastewater was spiked at 10, 50, 100 mg/L CIP.
Reported result: Authors propose electrostatic attraction, coordination, hydrogen bonding, π–π interactions and pore filling. Reported removal falls ~98% (0 g/L NaCl) to ~52% (50 g/L). Spiked wastewater results are described as “recovery” rates 94.6%, 88.5%, 77.8% at 10/50/100 mg/L.
Caveat / follow-up: Retain the paper's term “recovery”; don't silently relabel as removal efficiency. Spiked CIP is not native trace concentration.

Evidence domain: 50 mL solution at 100 mg/L CIP treated with 0.02 g MSCA at pH 8 for 100 min; elute for 1 h at 25 °C using ethanol:HCl 7:3 v/v, wash and dry at 65 °C.
Experimental design / conditions: Capacity retention cycles 1–5: 96.4%, 94.2%, 91.8%, 88.6%, 82.5%. XRD reportedly showed structure retained after five cycles.
Reported result: % initial capacity; cycles; °C; h
Evidence status: No leaching, regenerant pollutant mass balance, cost, LCA or spent-media fate assessment.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, CIP, SMX; IBP is a non-antibiotic co-contaminant
Adsorbent / material: Sunflower seed-husk SF-600 biochar and H3PO4-activated PSF
Experimental design / conditions: Raw husk dried 105 °C/24 h, ground <500 μm. SF-600: 5 g pyrolysed at 600 °C/2 h under N2 (10 °C/min; 100 mL/min), washed and dried. PSF: impregnate with 85% H3PO4 at biomass:acid 1:3 w/w, dry 105 °C/12 h, pyrolyse, rinse thoroughly.
Reported result: BET area increased 6.2→378.8 m²/g and pore volume 0.012→0.206 cm³/g. SF-600 pHPZC=3.6; PSF was negatively charged across pH 3–11.
Caveat / follow-up: No product yield, acid/water balance, cost or LCA. IBP is ibuprofen, an NSAID rather than an antibiotic.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, CIP, SMX; IBP is non-antibiotic
Experimental design / conditions: Tests in 40 mL, [PSF] = 25 mg/L, 10 mM NaNO3, 298 K; isotherm/table fitting is reported for initial 1–20 mg/L for TC/CIP/SMX and 5–25 mg/L for IBP. The main text describes kinetic tests at C0=20 mg/L and pH 7, followed for up to 24 h, with equilibrium reported around 6 h. Caveat: Fig. 2 caption associates the 1–20 mg/L/fixed-6-h series with panel (a) but identifies (a) as kinetic; it associates 20 mg/L/5–1440 min with panel (b) but identifies (b) as isotherm. The condition labels for panels (a) and (b) therefore appear swapped or internally mismatched.
Reported result: Table 2 Langmuir fitted qm (SF-600→PSF, mg/g): TC 228.3→429.3; CIP 80.8→361.6; SMX 129.1→251.3; IBP 135.8→251.1.
Caveat / follow-up: Only TC/CIP/SMX count in antibiotic-only synthesis; fitted Langmuir qm is model-derived, not real-water working capacity. Fig. 2 caption appears to mismatch kinetic versus isotherm panel conditions (see source location); use main text and Table 2 for the reported fitted values and do not reconstruct the precise panel-condition mapping from the caption alone. Supplementary material is referenced but was not supplied in the PDF.

Experimental design / conditions: Example kinetic conditions: C0=20 mg/L, pH 7; tests used 40 mL solution, PSF 25 mg/L, 10 mM NaNO3, 298 K.
Reported result: Equilibrium reported around 6 h. PSO fitted qe (mg/g): TC 415.2, CIP 321.7, SMX 207.9, IBP 206.7; PSO R²=0.741, 0.917, 0.976, 0.990, respectively. Elovich R²=0.946 for TC and 0.920 for CIP.
Caveat / follow-up: Keep fitted kinetic qe separate from Langmuir qm; model fit alone does not prove a unique mechanism.

Experimental design / conditions: pH tests pH 3–11, 40 mL, PSF 25 mg/L, 10 mM NaNO3, 298 K, 6 h, initial target concentration 20 mg/L.
Reported result: TC capacity peaked near pH 7 at 437.6 mg/g; authors report compound-dependent pH effects related to target speciation and the negative PSF surface at pH 3–11.
Caveat / follow-up: The pH optimum is target-specific; do not generalize TC behaviour to all antibiotics or mixed real wastewater.

Experimental design / conditions: Cl−, NO3−, HCO3−, CO3²− and SO4²− tested at 10 mM; PSF 25 mg/L, 40 mL, 298 K, 6 h, target concentration 20 mg/L.
Reported result: Fig. 4 reports nitrate as promoting uptake in these tests; monovalent ions generally had a smaller effect than divalent ions, with carbonate and sulfate showing stronger inhibition.
Caveat / follow-up: Controlled 10 mM ions do not establish that all natural-water ion mixtures are harmless; retain specific target/anion conditions.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, CIP, SMX with IBP as non-antibiotic co-solute
Experimental design / conditions: Mixture test used equal 0.025 mM concentrations; PSF 100 mg/L, 40 mL, 10 mM NaNO3, 298 K, pH 7, 6 h.
Reported result: Reported uptake order: IBP < SMX < CIP < TC. Authors discuss hydrophobicity alongside H-bonding, electrostatic, pore-filling and π–π interactions.
Caveat / follow-up: IBP is ibuprofen, a non-antibiotic NSAID; do not call this a four-antibiotic mixture.

Experimental design / conditions: Article tests synthetic solutions, controlled anions and mixed feeds; no regeneration cycles or actual wastewater tests reported.
Reported result: Authors state future work should develop regeneration to reduce operating and maintenance costs for long-term continuous use. No product yield, unit cost, LCA, fixed-bed/pilot data or spent-sorbent management route supplied.
Caveat / follow-up: Waste feedstock and a claimed low-cost activator do not prove economic/environmental superiority without mass, chemical, energy, water and waste balances.

Adsorbent / material: Commercial MWCNTs functionalized with eucalyptus-leaf extract and iron particles (MWCNT-E)
Experimental design / conditions: Commercial MWCNTs reported with ~9% hydroxyl/carboxyl groups. Iron sulfate heptahydrate (1.5% w/v) and eucalyptus-leaf extract used for functionalization; extract made from 30 g leaves with ultrapure water, 1 h at 80 °C. CNTs, extract and metal solution mixed 160 rpm/25 °C/24 h; wash, centrifuge 4000 rpm for 10 min and dry 50 °C.
Reported result: MWCNT-E contains eucalyptus-extract-derived surface functionality and iron particles. Authors report post-adsorption changes in FTIR/XPS and elemental composition; SEM shows changes in aggregation/dispersion.
Caveat / follow-up: “Green” describes functionalization; original MWCNTs were commercially sourced. No quantitative CNT/Fe leaching or life-cycle assessment.

Experimental design / conditions: 10 mL antibiotic solutions; C0=0.05–1.5 mmol/L; MWCNT-E 1.5 g/L; agitation 200 rpm for 6 h; 25, 35 and 50 °C; concentration measured by HPLC.
Reported result: Table 3 q_exp (mmol/g): CIP 0.361, 0.360, 0.433 at 25, 35, 50 °C; OFL 0.413, 0.416, 0.457. Langmuir fitted q_max: CIP 0.397, 0.358, 0.440; OFL 0.407, 0.419, 0.439 mmol/g. Sips model was reported as best fit based on R²/AICc; Langmuir q_max was closer to q_exp.
Model / metric: Observed q_exp distinguished from fitted q_max and Sips capacity
Caveat / follow-up: No real wastewater, regeneration/cycling, fixed-bed test or measured unit cost reported. Maintain source units unless performing an explicit conversion.

Experimental design / conditions: Binary system CIP:OFL molar fractions 1:1, 1:3 and 3:1; total initial concentration 0.1–3.0 mmol/L; tests at 25, 35 and 50 °C under the single-system operating protocol.
Reported result: At 50 °C reported mixture uptake: 0.958 mmol/g CIP and 0.872 mmol/g OFL; at 25 °C: 0.909 and 0.850 mmol/g, respectively. Authors calculate qe'/qe of 2.2 (CIP) and 1.9 (OFL), interpreting net behaviour as synergistic, while also describing competition and stronger affinity for CIP. Langmuir–Freundlich was selected for binary isotherms. ANFIS reported R≈0.9999 (CIP), 0.9998 (OFL) against the study data.
Model / metric: Binary uptake, equilibrium model and internal ML validation
Caveat / follow-up: No external ML validation or real-water generalization. Do not imply all mixture fractions show simple synergy: authors also identify competition/site affinity and model-dependent behavior.

Adsorbent / material: Iron-modified biochar: nZVI@BC, iron (hydro)oxide@BC and mixed-metal/iron-oxide biochars
Evidence domain: Secondary synthesis: mechanisms, preparation routes and environmental risk
Experimental design / conditions: Review compares synthesis routes and textural data (Table 1) and compiles adsorption capacities/conditions/mechanisms/models from primary literature (Table 2). It separately reviews Fenton-like and photocatalytic degradation (Table 3).
Reported result: Mechanisms summarized include π–π EDA, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic effects, hydrophobic interactions and pore filling. Iron modification can add magnetic recovery, but iron particles may also block pores or reduce surface area. The review flags possible desorption/secondary pollution, used-media disposal and need for environmental safety assessment. It cites <5% adsorption decline after 10 cycles for doxycycline/CIP in a referenced study.
Value / units: Review; mechanism categories; cycle figure cited second-hand
Model / metric: Secondary review evidence; not an independent primary dataset
Caveat / follow-up: Do not add review-table observations as independent experimental records or combine degradation/oxidation results with adsorption-only capacities. Verify any numerical primary data against the cited original paper.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, norfloxacin, SMX, sulfamethazine and other antibiotics
Continuum stage: Adjacent technology — membrane separation, outside adsorption-capacity matrix
Evidence domain: Membrane rejection, electro-driven cleaning and simulated wastewater
Experimental design / conditions: UiO-66/CNTs synthesized in DMF at 120 °C/48 h, washed six times with DMF/ethanol. Nanofillers embedded in PVDF via nanobubbles-mediated NIPS; selected membrane 48.7 wt% nanofiller and 400 μm active layer.
Reported result: Reported TC rejection 99.3%, permeability 101.3–105.7 L h−1 m−2 bar−1, MWCO 375 Da and mean effective pore size 0.32 nm. Simulated municipal effluent tests tracked antibiotics at 5 μg/L over 260 h; surface water was also tested for 7 days. Electricity-driven self-cleaning used 2 mA/cm² for 5 min; authors report 77% lower energy and 72% lower cleaning cost than NF270 for the membrane process.
Value / units: % rejection; L h−1 m−2 bar−1; Da; μm; μg/L; h; mA/cm²
Model / metric: Membrane rejection/permeance and cleaning metrics, not adsorption capacity
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; exclude from core adsorptive-capacity synthesis
Caveat / follow-up: Primary metric is membrane rejection via size exclusion/Donnan effects, while ROS-mediated degradation cleans foulants. Do not convert rejection % into mg/g or call self-cleaning antibiotic adsorption. Use only as an adjacent technology comparator if needed.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics compiled from cited studies
Adsorbent / material: Magnetic biochar (MBC; multiple biomass and sludge feedstocks)
Experimental design / conditions: Narrative review of MBC preparation and antibiotic-removal literature; preparation conditions are study-specific and not normalized by the review.
Reported result: Review describes impregnation-pyrolysis, hydrothermal treatment, co-precipitation and ball milling. Modification routes include element doping, acid/alkali treatment, nanoparticle loading and organic-compound modification. Feedstock and preparation temperature affect surface area, pore structure and magnetic phase.
Caveat / follow-up: Use to map processing routes, not to imply a single energy, yield or cost profile. Numerical performance claims in the review must be traced to their cited primary studies.

Target / co-contaminant: SMX, TC, CIP and other antibiotics compiled across studies
Experimental design / conditions: Review-level compilation across different feedstocks, concentration ranges, material formulations and test designs; the review's abstract gives an overall reported range.
Reported result: Abstract reports MBC adsorption capacities spanning 5–900 mg/g and states that MBC commonly removes >90% within 60 min. Examples in the narrative include Fe/Zn sludge biochar with fitted maximum capacities of 145 mg/g for TC and 74 mg/g for CIP, and microwave-hydrothermal magnetic water-hyacinth biochar with reported TC maximum capacity of 202 mg/g and BET area 2097 m²/g.
Value / units: 5–900 mg/g (review-level range); examples: 145 mg/g TC, 74 mg/g CIP, 202 mg/g TC; >90% within 60 min
Model / metric: Mixed reported capacities/removal percentages; not a harmonized comparison
Caveat / follow-up: Do not treat the 5–900 mg/g range or >90%/60 min claim as a comparable benchmark: studies differ in antibiotics, C0, adsorbent dose, conditions and fitted versus observed metrics. Confirm numeric claims in original papers before ranking.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics; adsorption and catalytic-degradation applications distinguished
Adsorbent / material: Magnetic biochar; reused adsorbents and catalyst-support systems
Evidence domain: Regeneration, degradation separation, feasibility and risks (secondary synthesis)
Experimental design / conditions: Review compiles regeneration examples and discusses separate adsorption and catalytic oxidation/degradation pathways.
Reported result: The review reports one cited TC example in which removal after five cycles was 19% following water washing, versus 64% after ethanol extraction and 73% after NaOH desorption. It identifies high preparation costs, possible secondary pollution, unclear mechanisms and toxicity of degradation by-products as practical issues.
Value / units: After 5 cycles: 19% (water washing), 64% (ethanol), 73% (NaOH) in a cited study
Model / metric: Secondary reported regeneration example; not an independent result from this review
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 13–15; regeneration discussion and Section 7 conclusion
Caveat / follow-up: Verify the regeneration figures in their cited primary study. Keep adsorption-only results separate from PMS/PDS or other catalytic degradation; removal by destruction is not adsorption capacity.

Target / co-contaminant: Quinolones, tetracyclines, macrolides, sulfonamides and other antibiotic classes in cited studies
Adsorbent / material: Biochar and modified biochars; review-level scope
Evidence domain: Compiled adsorption-capacity range and experimental concentration context (secondary synthesis)
Experimental design / conditions: Review compiles literature spanning antibiotic concentrations of 0.003–200 mg/L; underlying conditions and material types vary among cited studies.
Reported result: The review reports maximum adsorption capacities of 0.3–612.2 mg/g across biochar studies. It describes biochar as a potential low-cost biomass-waste valorization route but emphasizes antibiotic-class and material-dependent behavior.
Model / metric: Review-reported maximum capacities; not a standardized or independently measured range
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 3 (journal p. 1259); Section 3; Figure 1; Table S2 cited by article
Caveat / follow-up: Do not compare this range directly against the magnetic-biochar review's 5–900 mg/g range as if they came from the same dataset. Trace quantitative examples to primary papers and preserve C0, dose, material and metric.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics across quinolone, tetracycline, sulfonamide, macrolide and β-lactam classes
Adsorbent / material: Biochar; mechanisms summarized across cited literature
Experimental design / conditions: Review synthesizes mechanism reports by antibiotic class and discusses antibiotic speciation (pKa/charge), solubility, hydrophobicity and biochar properties.
Reported result: The review identifies π–π electron donor–acceptor interactions and hydrogen bonding as commonly reported for sulfonamides, tetracyclines and quinolones; it describes electrostatic interactions as predominant in cited macrolide and β-lactam cases. It emphasizes that pH-dependent antibiotic speciation and biochar surface chemistry shape observed adsorption.
Value / units: Qualitative synthesis; no single shared experimental condition
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanism frequencies and class-level tendencies are not universal laws for every material. Treat mechanisms as study-supported hypotheses and verify direct characterization/control evidence in primary papers.

Adsorbent / material: Biochar used as adsorbent, microbial shelter/carrier and electron mediator
Evidence domain: Biotic roles and engineering deployment (secondary synthesis)
Experimental design / conditions: Review discusses microbial interactions and deployment options rather than conducting a new common-condition experiment.
Reported result: Biochar can serve as a microbial shelter/carrier and redox/electron mediator; cited studies include improved antibiotic biodegradation. Engineering strategies include fixed/packed-bed columns, granular biochar, support media, sachets/bags and biochar-immobilized-cell bioreactors. The review notes trade-offs such as inability of adsorption-only beds to destroy retained antibiotics, clogging, unstable immobilization, or high capital/operating costs in some configurations.
Value / units: Qualitative synthesis; individual cited studies have different conditions
Model / metric: Secondary synthesis of biotic mechanisms and engineering options
Caveat / follow-up: Keep sorption and biodegradation endpoints separate. Statements about removal or ARG response should be tied to the specific cited study and measured endpoint; deployment examples do not establish field-scale economic feasibility.

Target / co-contaminant: SDZ, SMT and SCP, tested individually
Adsorbent / material: Pine bark (<0.63 mm), “oak ash” (boiler combustion residue), and uncalcined mussel shell
Continuum stage: Stage 1-adjacent — low-processed/waste-derived by-products; oak ash is a combustion residue
Evidence domain: Primary batch adsorption/desorption design and operating conditions
Experimental design / conditions: Seven listed initial concentrations: 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 µmol/L; 24 h shaking at 50 rpm; 25 ± 2 °C, in the dark; CaCl₂ background electrolyte; triplicate tests; HPLC-UV measurement. Pine bark and oak ash: 0.5 g in 10 mL (nominal dose 50 g/L). Mussel shell: 2 g in 5 mL (nominal dose 400 g/L). Contact-solution pH was measured but not adjusted or buffered; blank losses were <3%.
Reported result: The source reports different adsorbent doses and natural material pH conditions, making this a material-by-product comparison rather than a standardized equal-dose comparison.
Value / units: 50 g/L (pine bark and oak ash); 400 g/L (mussel shell); 24 h; n=3
Model / metric: Batch equilibrium uptake from initial-minus-equilibrium concentration; separate desorption test
Caveat / follow-up: The abstract says the concentration range starts at 1 µmol/L, while Methods lists 2.5 µmol/L as the lowest of seven concentrations. SI files were not supplied. Unequal doses and unbuffered pH must be disclosed; no column, real-water, cost/LCA or multi-cycle regeneration test was reported.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark (<0.63 mm); high-organic-matter acidic by-product
Evidence domain: Observed adsorption uptake and percentage removal
Experimental design / conditions: Individual batch tests, C0 up to 50 µmol/L, 24 h at 25 ± 2 °C; 0.5 g pine bark in 10 mL (nominal 50 g/L); pH not adjusted/buffered.
Reported result: At C0=50 µmol/L, amounts adsorbed were 780 µmol/kg SDZ, 890 µmol/kg SMT and 870 µmol/kg SCP. Pine bark adsorbed >70% of each antibiotic across the tested concentration range; SDZ reached up to 90% at the lowest concentration and SCP reached up to 95% at the two highest concentrations.
Value / units: 780 µmol/kg (SDZ); 890 µmol/kg (SMT); 870 µmol/kg (SCP) at C0=50 µmol/L; reported removal >70%, maxima as stated
Model / metric: Observed uptake and percentage adsorbed; not a Langmuir qmax
Caveat / follow-up: Do not relabel the reported µmol/kg amounts as mg/g or fitted maximum capacity. Performance is tied to acidic pine bark and unbuffered batch conditions; no actual wastewater was tested.

Adsorbent / material: “Oak ash” from oak-chip combustion; reported pHw 11.31 and organic matter 13.23%
Continuum stage: Stage 1-adjacent — waste-derived mineral/ash by-product; combustion residue
Evidence domain: Observed adsorption uptake and low-retention comparison
Experimental design / conditions: At C0=50 µmol/L; 0.5 g ash in 10 mL (nominal 50 g/L); 24 h, 25 ± 2 °C; contact pH not adjusted/buffered.
Reported result: At C0=50 µmol/L, adsorption amounts for each of the three sulfonamides were below 150 µmol/kg. Results text reports adsorption percentages below 40% for oak ash; Fig. 2 shows the concentration-dependent values. Authors relate lower uptake to strongly alkaline conditions and antibiotic speciation.
Value / units: <150 µmol/kg for each antibiotic at C0=50 µmol/L; <40% as stated in Results text
Caveat / follow-up: The abstract states adsorption is <45%, whereas Results text gives <40%; retain this discrepancy or report values from Fig. 2 rather than choosing an unsupported single threshold. Mechanism is inferred from pH/speciation and cited literature.

Adsorbent / material: Uncalcined mussel shell; reported pHw 9.39 and organic matter 11.43%
Evidence domain: Observed adsorption uptake and low-retention comparison
Experimental design / conditions: At C0=50 µmol/L; 2 g shell in 5 mL (nominal 400 g/L); 24 h, 25 ± 2 °C; contact pH not adjusted/buffered.
