Reported result: At C0=50 µmol/L, uptake for each sulfonamide was below 20 µmol/kg. The abstract and one Results passage give adsorption below 15%, while a later passage states adsorption was always below 10%; Fig. 2 shows values around the single-digit range.
Value / units: <20 µmol/kg for each antibiotic at C0=50 µmol/L; source text gives <10–15% depending on passage
Caveat / follow-up: Record the source's <10% versus <15% wording discrepancy. The shell had a much larger nominal dose (400 g/L) than pine bark/oak ash (50 g/L), so avoid a simplistic equal-dose ranking. No real-water test was reported.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash and mussel shell
Experimental design / conditions: Adsorption residues were resuspended in 0.005 M CaCl₂ for desorption; Table 2 reports values at initial antibiotic concentrations of 2.5–50 µmol/L.
Reported result: At C0=50 µmol/L, desorbed amount (% of previously adsorbed): mussel shell — SDZ 5.2 µmol/kg (67%), SMT 5.1 (63%), SCP 9.8 (79%); oak ash — SDZ 18.8 (15%), SMT 21.9 (15%), SCP 15.0 (11%); pine bark — SDZ 40.2 (5%), SMT 33.6 (4%), SCP 32.6 (4%). Across the tested range, desorption was 19–81% for mussel shell, 0–49% for oak ash and <11% for pine bark.
Model / metric: Desorption amount and percentage; not regeneration-cycle retention
Caveat / follow-up: The desorption assay is evidence of retention/reversibility under the stated CaCl₂ test, not proof of multi-cycle regeneration, treated-water safety or contaminant destruction. Desorbed antibiotic remains in a secondary stream.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash and mussel shell
Experimental design / conditions: Equilibrium data for seven C0 levels fitted to Linear and Freundlich models; triplicate tests. The paper does not fit a Langmuir model.
Reported result: Both models fit reported adsorption data with R²=0.98–1.00. Across materials/antibiotics, Kd ranged 0.17–253.67 L/kg, Freundlich KF 0.14–202.76 (units reported by the paper as concentration- and n-dependent), and Freundlich n=0.81–1.28. Highest Kd/KF were pine-bark/SCP: Kd=253.67±11.82 L/kg (R²=0.989); KF=202.76±20.42 (n=1.28±0.09; R²=0.984).
Model / metric: Linear Kd and Freundlich KF/n; no fitted qmax
Caveat / follow-up: Do not report Kd or KF as a Langmuir qmax or compare their numerical magnitudes to mg/g capacities. The source notes the Freundlich coefficient's units depend on n; preserve source units.

Target / co-contaminant: SDZ, SMT and SCP; mechanism explanation is interpretive
Adsorbent / material: Pine bark (48.7% organic matter; pHw 3.99), oak ash (13.23%; pHw 11.31), mussel shell (11.43%; pHw 9.39)
Evidence domain: Material properties and proposed adsorption mechanism
Experimental design / conditions: Material characterization values are cited from supplementary material / previous characterization; the uploaded PDF did not include the supplementary file. The study measured contact-solution pH but did not buffer/adjust it.
Reported result: Authors associate pine bark's comparatively high retention with its high organic-matter content and acidic character. They propose electrostatic interaction between cationic sulfonamide species and deprotonated carboxyl groups at acidic pH, and discuss SCP's greater hydrophobicity as a contributor. High pH for ash/shell is proposed to favor anionic species and reduce retention.
Model / metric: Mechanistic interpretation from batch trends and referenced literature
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3–5; Fig. 1–2; Section 3.2 and Conclusions
Caveat / follow-up: Treat the mechanism as the authors' interpretation, not a directly proven unique mechanism from spectroscopy in this experiment. Supplementary Table S1/S2 was not supplied; exact surface characterization and antibiotic properties could not be checked.

Adsorbent / material: Fe/Cu clay-nanosheet (CNS) nanocomposite embedded in alginate–carboxymethyl cellulose (CMC) beads and chitosan-coated (NBs)
Continuum stage: Engineered biopolymer/mineral–metal nanocomposite; adjacent high-processing class rather than a simple unmodified biopolymer
Experimental design / conditions: CNS prepared by ultrasonication, then Fe/Cu nanoparticles dispersed by in-situ reduction. Alginate (5 wt%) and CMC (2 wt%) were dissolved in water at 40 °C; nanocomposite loading varied; droplets gelled in 2 wt% CaCl2; beads soaked in 1 wt% chitosan in glacial acetic acid, washed and vacuum-dried overnight. Mean bead diameter reported about 2 mm.
Reported result: Composite preparation improves recoverability of the clay nanosheets and creates a rough, dense bead surface. The article describes oxygen-containing functional groups and surface-charge/texture changes as potentially important for adsorption.
Value / units: Alginate 5 wt%; CMC 2 wt%; chitosan 1 wt%; CaCl2 2 wt%; mean bead diameter ≈2 mm
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–4; Sections 2.2–2.3; Fig. 1 and related ESI figures
Caveat / follow-up: Preparation includes mineral exfoliation, Fe/Cu nanoparticle formation, polymer encapsulation, acid treatment, washing and drying; no product yield, chemical/energy inventory, metal leaching or quantified preparation cost is reported in the supplied main PDF.

Evidence domain: Batch removal and fitted equilibrium capacity
Experimental design / conditions: Authors report optimum batch conditions around initial NOR concentration 20 mg/L, pH 6 and 300 min contact; the abstract also states sorbent concentration 2000 mg/L and sorbent dosage 0.15 g. Table 4 reports sorbent concentration 0.15 g/L; methods and kinetic/pH experiments elsewhere use 0.30 g in 200 mL. Keep the source's condition variants distinct until reconciled.
Reported result: Abstract/conclusion report about 86% NOR removal. The Langmuir model gives fitted qmax = 354.9 ± 41 mg/g (R² = 0.92; separation factor RL = 0.238). This is a fitted maximum, not the observed uptake under the optimum single-concentration removal test.
Value / units: ≈86% removal; Langmuir fitted qmax = 354.9 ± 41 mg/g; R² = 0.92; RL = 0.238
Model / metric: Percentage removal separated from fitted Langmuir qmax
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 1 (abstract); pp. 5–8; Table 2; Fig. 4; Table 4; conclusion
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; requires quantitative verification
Caveat / follow-up: Do not use 354.9 mg/g as observed uptake. Reported bead dose/concentration varies by section. At 20 mg/L initial concentration, 86% removal implies residual NOR ≈2.8 mg/L, but the method reports UV–vis LOD 2.72 mg/L and LOQ 8.24 mg/L; verify whether the reported residual quantification is below the stated LOQ.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetics assessed from 30–300 min at 20 mg/L NOR; equilibrium isotherms tested across 10–100 mg/L; model fits reported for pseudo-first-order (PFO), pseudo-second-order (PSO), intraparticle diffusion, Langmuir, Freundlich and Temkin.
Reported result: Kinetic table lists PFO qe(cal) = 107.339 mg/g (R² = 0.986) and PSO qe(cal) = 200 mg/g (R² = 0.935); text says PFO fit is better. Langmuir fitted qmax = 354.9 ± 41 mg/g (R² = 0.92) versus Freundlich R² = 0.82 and Temkin R² = 0.92. Model-derived qe values should not be presented as independent observed capacities.
Value / units: PFO qe(cal) 107.339 mg/g, R² 0.986; PSO qe(cal) 200 mg/g, R² 0.935; Langmuir qmax 354.9 ± 41 mg/g
Model / metric: Kinetic-fit estimates and isotherm-fit parameters, not interchangeable with measured qexp
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; model consistency flagged
Caveat / follow-up: The PSO qe(cal) of 200 mg/g exceeds the simple mass-balance ceiling for a 20 mg/L batch if the stated sorbent concentration is 0.15 g/L (133 mg/g), and the methods/figure captions report different bead concentrations. Check the original methods, figure captions and ESI before using kinetic capacities quantitatively. Table 3 thermodynamic units/magnitudes also warrant checking.

Target / co-contaminant: Norfloxacin (NOR); competing salts, humic acid and polyethylene microplastics
Evidence domain: Water chemistry, matrix effects and spiked-water performance
Experimental design / conditions: Tests report NaCl and CaCl2 concentrations up to 1.0 M; separate tests add humic acid and polyethylene microplastics. Tap, lake and groundwater from a university campus were spiked with NOR at 20 mg/L. Hospital wastewater was simulated rather than a test of untreated native hospital effluent.
Reported result: Reported NOR removal decreased with increasing salt concentration: from 86.07% to 16.59% for NaCl and to 13.44% for CaCl2. Removal exceeded 80% at lower stated humic-acid additions but fell to about 60% at the highest stated addition. The paper reports only about 24–28% removal for the spiked tap, groundwater and lake samples, attributing losses to matrix ions/organic matter.
Value / units: 86.07% to 16.59% (NaCl); 13.44% at highest CaCl2; ≈24–28% in spiked natural-water matrices; NOR spike 20 mg/L
Model / metric: Percentage removal under synthetic and matrix-spiked batch tests
Caveat / follow-up: The 20 mg/L spike is far above reported environmental trace concentrations and does not establish performance at native trace levels. The paper's displayed units for humic acid/microplastic additions require checking against the figure/ESI; do not silently normalize possibly inconsistent source units.

Adsorbent / material: Fe/Cu CNS composite beads; recovery/reuse and treated-solution toxicity assessed
Evidence domain: Mechanistic interpretation, degradation contribution, reuse and residual toxicity
Experimental design / conditions: Authors used XPS/FTIR to investigate interactions; TOC and high-resolution LC–MS to assess residual organic carbon and transformation products. Beads were eluted using 0.1 M HCl for 12 h, rinsed three times and reused. Scenedesmus sp. algal viability was measured over 72 h.
Reported result: After 300 min the paper reports 86.06% NOR removal but 72.84% TOC removal and discusses demethylation, defluorination, piperazine-ring opening and oxidation. The reported algae viability was 77% for treated NOR solution versus 36% for untreated NOR control. The paper states beads could be used for five adsorption–desorption cycles with minimal decline, without a fully tabulated numeric cycle series in the main text.
Value / units: NOR removal 86.06%; TOC removal 72.84%; algae viability 77% treated versus 36% untreated; 0.1 M HCl, 12 h elution; five cycles stated
Model / metric: Combined removal; TOC/LC–MS transformation evidence; qualitative reuse statement
Caveat / follow-up: This is not a purely adsorption-only removal system: the authors attribute part of NOR removal to catalytic transformation/mineralization. Keep degradation and adsorption endpoints separate; the toxicity test suggests reduced effect but does not establish that every transformation product is harmless.

Adsorbent / material: Ash sawdust and mixed-species timber sawdust, unmodified and chemically modified
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — raw lignocellulosic/timber waste, with separate chemically modified variants
Experimental design / conditions: Sawdust ground and sieved to 210–300 µm, washed five times with distilled water and dried at 90 °C for 20 h. Modified sawdust underwent sequential treatments with 10 wt% H3PO4, 20 wt% H2SO4 and 2.8 wt% KOH in ethanol; each treatment was mixed for 4 h at room temperature and 2 h at 60 °C, followed by washing to neutral pH and drying at 60 °C for 24 h.
Reported result: Modified ash and mixed sawdust BET surface areas were 2.0451 and 2.1827 m²/g, respectively, versus 0.7052 and 0.8261 m²/g for the corresponding unmodified forms. Modification increased surface area by roughly threefold but absolute BET areas remained low.
Value / units: BET: ash 0.7052→2.0451 m²/g; mixed 0.8261→2.1827 m²/g; target particle size 210–300 µm
Caveat / follow-up: Multiple acid/base solutions, ethanol, repeated washing and drying add chemical, water and energy requirements; the paper does not quantify chemical use per mass of product, process yield, washwater treatment, regeneration cost or life-cycle impacts.

Adsorbent / material: Modified ash sawdust, modified mixed sawdust and powdered activated carbon (AC) control
Continuum stage: Stage 1 with chemically modified timber-waste variants
Experimental design / conditions: Glass column internal diameter 22 mm packed with approximately 1 g adsorbent; 100 mL vancomycin solution per run; continuous filtrate flow maintained for 100 min; room temperature 20 ± 1 °C. Fig. 5 comparison used 2.0 g adsorbent and 100 mg/L vancomycin.
Reported result: At 100 mg/L initial vancomycin, removal was 63.0 ± 2.3% with modified mixed sawdust, 56.6 ± 5.1% with modified ash sawdust and 98.2 ± 2.9% with powdered AC. Unmodified sawdust removal was reported below 15%.
Model / metric: Fixed-bed/filtration removal percentage, distinct from batch isotherm data
Caveat / follow-up: This is a proof-of-concept model-water test at high vancomycin concentrations, not actual wastewater or trace-level field validation. Performance was lower than powdered AC under the stated comparison conditions.

Adsorbent / material: Modified ash sawdust, modified mixed sawdust and powdered AC
Continuum stage: Stage 1 with chemically modified timber-waste variants
Experimental design / conditions: At 20 ± 1 °C, 100 min and 100 mg/L vancomycin, the study compared 1.0 and 2.0 g adsorbent loads. Isotherm tests separately used 25 mL antibiotic solutions from 30 to 150 mg/L with about 500 mg sawdust; mixtures were stirred for 2 h at 22 ± 1 °C and filtered after 48 h.
Reported result: At 2.0 g, observed capacities were 2.79 mg/g for modified ash, 3.11 mg/g for modified mixed sawdust and 9.33 mg/g for AC. At 1.0 g, corresponding capacities were 3.58, 4.76 and 9.23 mg/g. Increasing sawdust amount improved percentage removal but reduced uptake per gram. The authors estimate 1 g modified ash could treat approximately 330 L at 0.0085 mg/L, extrapolated from the reported 2.79 mg/g capacity.
Value / units: 2 g: 2.79 mg/g (modified ash); 3.11 mg/g (modified mixed); 9.33 mg/g (AC). 1 g: 3.58, 4.76 and 9.23 mg/g, respectively.
Model / metric: Observed uptake per adsorbent mass and removal percentage
Caveat / follow-up: The 330 L estimate is a theoretical extrapolation to trace concentration, not a tested treatment volume. Source-water concentrations in the experiments (30–150 mg/L for isotherms; 100 mg/L comparison) are orders of magnitude above the cited treated-effluent concentration.

Evidence domain: Fitted adsorption isotherms and capacity plausibility
Experimental design / conditions: Langmuir and Freundlich models fitted to batch equilibrium data from 30–150 mg/L vancomycin. Table 3 gives Langmuir qmax, KL, R² and χ² along with Freundlich KF, n, R² and χ².
Reported result: Table 3 reports qmax = 5.252 mg/g for unmodified ash and 12,179.5 mg/g for modified ash, with modified-ash Langmuir R² = 0.943. Yet observed column capacities were 2.79–3.58 mg/g for modified ash, and the plotted batch uptake is roughly up to 4 mg/g over the studied range.
Value / units: Langmuir qmax: 5.252 mg/g (unmodified ash); 12,179.5 mg/g (modified ash); measured capacities ≈2.79–4 mg/g
Model / metric: Fitted Langmuir capacity versus observed uptake
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; high-priority source inconsistency
Caveat / follow-up: The modified-ash qmax is physically implausible relative to the entire measured uptake range and should not be cited as a valid capacity. The Langmuir expression/table may contain a transcription or calculation problem. Preserve the discrepancy and verify against author correction/underlying data before any comparison.

Adsorbent / material: Modified timber sawdust; powdered AC benchmark
Continuum stage: Stage 1 with chemical modification; possible end-of-life energy recovery
Experimental design / conditions: Study reports heating values for sawdust before/after adsorption and discusses thermal conversion for energy production; no cost model or full life-cycle assessment is presented.
Reported result: Sawdust heating values were 15.5–18.5 MJ/kg, approximately 65–90% of reported AC values. Authors propose that spent sawdust may be thermally converted for energy, but do not demonstrate a full-scale thermal treatment or quantify contaminant fate during it. Cost values for AC in the introduction are literature values, not a cost comparison conducted by this study.
Value / units: Sawdust heating value 15.5–18.5 MJ/kg; cited AC values 20.5–23 MJ/kg
Caveat / follow-up: No measured manufacturing cost, chemical consumption per unit product, regeneration process, true wastewater validation or life-cycle assessment. Thermal recovery of antibiotic-loaded media is a proposal, not proven contaminant-safe disposal.

Adsorbent / material: Sulfonated graphene oxide (SGO) prepared from graphite flakes
Experimental design / conditions: SGO synthesized by a modified Hummers-type process: 3 g graphite added to a 9:1 mixture of concentrated H2SO4 and H3PO4, followed by 18 g KMnO4 addition at 30 °C and 24 h stirring. Product was quenched with water/H2O2, washed sequentially with 7.7 mol/L HCl, deionized water, ethanol and diethyl ether, then dried at 60 °C.
Reported result: The process introduces oxygenated/sulfonated surface functionality that the authors associate with strong ciprofloxacin interactions. The method requires concentrated acids, a large oxidant dose, organic-solvent washing and substantial purification.
Value / units: 3 g graphite; 18 g KMnO4; 30 °C; 24 h; H2SO4/H3PO4 (9:1); 7.7 mol/L HCl wash
Caveat / follow-up: No product yield, chemical recovery, washwater treatment, cost per gram, life-cycle analysis, or assessment of oxidant/acid waste is reported. High adsorption performance alone does not establish that this synthesis route is sustainable.

Evidence domain: Observed uptake and fitted Langmuir capacity
Experimental design / conditions: Batch test used 10 mg SGO with 50 mL of 50 µmol/L ciprofloxacin, pH 4.0, 150 rpm and 240 min. Concentration-series tests used 10–100 µmol/L at 0.2 g/L SGO; equilibrium temperature tests covered 25–40 °C.
Reported result: Table 1 reports observed qe(exp) values of 45.45, 121.06, 237.12, 326.06 and 402.58 µmol/g at initial CIP concentrations of 10, 25, 50, 75 and 100 µmol/L. The reuse section instead reports 239.39 µmol/g as the initial uptake at 50 µmol/L. Fitted Langmuir qm is reported as 1000 µmol/g (331.35 mg/g) at each tested temperature, with R² = 0.9998.
Value / units: Observed qe(exp): 45.45–402.58 µmol/g; fitted qm = 1000 µmol/g = 331.35 mg/g
Model / metric: Observed equilibrium uptake distinguished from fitted Langmuir maximum
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 3, 7–10 and 14–15; Table 1; Table 2; Fig. 15
Caveat / follow-up: Do not report 1000 µmol/g as observed uptake. If the isotherm used the stated 0.2 g/L SGO and initial concentrations up to 100 µmol/L, the simple mass-balance ceiling at the highest C0 is 500 µmol/g; the fitted qm is an extrapolation beyond the measured range and requires verification of dose/fit setup and ESI. Table 1 and reuse text also differ slightly at the 50 µmol/L condition.

Target / co-contaminant: Ciprofloxacin (CIP); effects of pH, concentration, temperature and coexisting ions
Experimental design / conditions: C0 10–100 µmol/L; SGO 0.2 g/L; pH 4.0; temperature 25–40 °C; kinetics tracked over 0–240 min. Cation-interference tests used Na+, K+, Mg2+ and Ca2+ at 0.1 M.
Reported result: The authors report rapid initial uptake, with the curve becoming nearly constant after about 60 min, although 240 min was used for later equilibrium tests. qe(exp) rose from 45.45 to 402.58 µmol/g as C0 rose from 10 to 100 µmol/L, while percentage removal fell from 97.32% to 81.28%. From 25 to 40 °C, Table 1 reports qe(exp) increasing from 237.12 to 244.24 µmol/g. Coexisting ions reduced uptake/removal in the order Ca2+ > Mg2+ > K+ > Na+.
Value / units: C0 10–100 µmol/L; SGO 0.2 g/L; pH 4; 25–40 °C; ions 0.1 M; qe(exp) 45.45–402.58 µmol/g
Model / metric: Observed uptake, percent removal and kinetic model-fit outputs
Caveat / follow-up: Experiments are batch tests in prepared aqueous solutions, not real wastewater. Do not treat a high removal percentage at low C0 as equivalent to a high mass-normalized capacity; preserve the concentration and dose conditions for each metric.

Adsorbent / material: Ciprofloxacin-loaded and regenerated sulfonated graphene oxide (SGO)
Experimental design / conditions: Loaded SGO was treated with 50 mL DMF containing 1 M HCl; desorption test used 0.01 g loaded SGO. The solid was rinsed to neutral pH, dried at 100 °C and reused for five adsorption–desorption cycles. Cycle tests used 0.2 g/L SGO, 50 µmol/L CIP, pH 4 and 25 °C.
Reported result: The paper reports 98.11% CIP release within 10 min and >99.14% within 240 min. Uptake values for fresh/direct and first through fifth reuse were 239.39, 237.94, 233.27, 231.46, 229.91 and 229.29 µmol/g; fifth-use uptake is about 95.8% of the reported initial value.
Value / units: Desorption: 98.11% at 10 min; >99.14% at 240 min; uptake retention ≈95.8% after five cycles
Model / metric: Desorption percentage and measured per-cycle uptake
Caveat / follow-up: Regeneration relies on strongly acidic DMF, followed by neutralization rinses and drying. Solvent recovery, solvent/acid consumption, disposal of desorbed CIP, and regeneration cost were not quantified; strong lab-scale reuse results do not by themselves establish operational sustainability.

Experimental design / conditions: Authors combine FTIR, SEM/EDX and DFT modelling; they discuss electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions. Isotherm data were analysed with Freundlich, Temkin, Dubinin–Radushkevich and Langmuir models.
Reported result: The article reports pseudo-second-order as the best-fitting kinetic model and Langmuir as the best-fitting isotherm model (R² = 0.9998). Authors report thermodynamic ΔG from −27.50 to −29.22 kJ/mol and ΔH = 6.35 kJ/mol, interpreting uptake as spontaneous and endothermic. The study's measurements were duplicate runs.
Value / units: Langmuir R² = 0.9998; ΔG = −27.50 to −29.22 kJ/mol; ΔH = 6.35 kJ/mol; n=2 reported
Model / metric: Kinetic/equilibrium model fit, thermodynamic interpretation and characterization-supported mechanism
Caveat / follow-up: Kinetic/isotherm fit does not uniquely establish a molecular mechanism. No real-water validation, process-cost accounting or life-cycle assessment is reported. The small replication count and extrapolated qm should be considered when judging evidence strength.

Target / co-contaminant: Trimethoprim (TMP; antibiotic); diclofenac (DCF; non-antibiotic NSAID comparator)
Adsorbent / material: Unmodified low-processing biosorbents: orchard-pruning biochar, brown macro-algae (Fucus vesiculosus), and oak wood chippings
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — unmodified natural waste/biomass for algae and wood; Stage 3 — standard biochar
Evidence domain: Feedstocks, baseline characterization and batch study design
Experimental design / conditions: The selected materials were ground and sieved to 0.25–0.8 mm, washed three times separately with methanol and Milli-Q water, and dried at 105 °C. Biochar originated from orchard pruning residues pyrolyzed at 500 °C. Reported BET areas: biochar 8.89 m²/g, wood chips 1.77 m²/g, macro-algae 0.29 m²/g. pHpzc: biochar 9.1, wood 5.7, algae 5.5. Tests were batch and triplicate; most baseline runs used pH 7 at 20 °C.
Reported result: The article examines DCF and TMP. DCF is an NSAID, not an antibiotic; only TMP belongs in antibiotic-specific evidence counts. Materials receive limited processing for the experiments, but the biochar has already undergone pyrolysis and all feedstocks were washed, ground, sieved and dried.
Value / units: BET area: 8.89, 1.77 and 0.29 m²/g (biochar, wood, algae); pHpzc: 9.1, 5.7 and 5.5
Model / metric: Primary comparative characterization and batch-study protocol
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–4; Section 2.2–2.5; Fig. 1; Fig. S2 cited by article
Caveat / follow-up: Supporting information was not provided. Preserve TMP as the antibiotic endpoint and DCF as a non-antibiotic comparator. Unit glyphs in the published tables are µg/g and µg/L; OCR can misread the µ symbol as m, so use the rendered PDF tables rather than unverified extracted text.

Adsorbent / material: Biochar, Fucus vesiculosus macro-algae and oak wood chippings
Continuum stage: Stage 1 for algae/wood; Stage 3 for standard biochar
Evidence domain: Observed uptake and kinetic model fitting at low initial concentration
Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic tests at C0 = 500 µg/L TMP, pH 7, 20 °C, 100 mL solution, 2 g/L biosorbent, 300 rpm, and up to 24 h; triplicate batch experiments. Table 1 source units are µg/g, confirmed from the rendered PDF image (PDF p. 5).
Reported result: Observed TMP equilibrium uptake Qe,exp: biochar 2.20×10² µg/g (=0.220 mg/g); macro-algae 2.38×10² µg/g (=0.238 mg/g); wood chippings 1.58×10² µg/g (=0.158 mg/g). The pseudo-second-order model fits each reported kinetic series with R² = 0.999 and calculated qe values close to the experimental values.
Value / units: Biochar 220 µg/g; macro-algae 238 µg/g; wood chips 158 µg/g (0.220, 0.238 and 0.158 mg/g, respectively)
Model / metric: Observed equilibrium uptake distinct from fitted kinetic qe
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 5; Table 1; Fig. 2; methods on PDF p. 3
Caveat / follow-up: These measured uptakes are from a 500 µg/L test and are not the fitted isotherm Qm values. Source values are µg/g, not mg/g. DCF values in the same table are not antibiotic results.

Target / co-contaminant: Trimethoprim (TMP); DCF results excluded from antibiotic-only comparisons
Adsorbent / material: Biochar, macro-algae and oak wood chippings
Evidence domain: Isotherms, unit normalization and mass-transfer interpretation
Experimental design / conditions: Langmuir/Freundlich fits used concentration-series tests different from the 500 µg/L kinetic study. Published Table 3 shows Qm in µg/g. Figure 4 shows different x-axis concentration ranges by material; TMP isotherm tests extend as high as 400,000 µg/L for macro-algae, while the biochar and wood-chipping plot ranges are lower.
Reported result: Langmuir Qm for TMP: biochar 2.08×10³ µg/g (=2.08 mg/g; R²=0.987); macro-algae 7.14×10⁴ µg/g (=71.4 mg/g; R²=0.994); wood chippings 8.33×10³ µg/g (=8.33 mg/g; R²=0.932). For wood chips, the Freundlich model fits better than Langmuir (R²=0.996 vs 0.932). Authors identify intraparticle diffusion as the main rate limitation for biochar, while final adsorptive attachment is important for macro-algae and wood chips.
Value / units: TMP Qm: 2.08, 71.4 and 8.33 mg/g after explicit conversion from 2.08×10³, 7.14×10⁴ and 8.33×10³ µg/g
Model / metric: Fitted Langmuir Qm and model-fit R²; distinct from observed kinetic uptake
Caveat / follow-up: The very different isotherm concentration ranges mean the fitted Qm values are not an equal-condition material ranking and should not be conflated with low-concentration kinetic uptake. Maintain the published µg/g units before conversion. Only TMP is an antibiotic; DCF is an NSAID.

Evidence domain: Feedstock, activation chemistry and preparation burden
Experimental design / conditions: Coconut husk was washed, dried at 105 °C to constant mass, pyrolyzed at 400 °C for 1 h in a low-cost homemade reactor, crushed/blended and sieved. Activation used 50 g biochar in 500 mL of 0.2 M HNO3 with stirring for 2 h at 25 °C. About 2–5 mL of 0.5 M NaOH was added to return the material to its stated original pH of 10; material was filtered and oven-dried at 105 °C for 12 h.
Reported result: The authors report acid activation improved amoxicillin removal relative to the unactivated biochar, and discuss development of pores and reactive surface groups. BET surface area, total pore volume and pore diameter were not measured in the study; the authors identify these as useful future measurements.
Value / units: Pyrolysis 400 °C/1 h; 50 g biochar per 500 mL 0.2 M HNO3; activation 2 h at 25 °C; drying 105 °C/12 h
Model / metric: Primary preparation protocol and qualitative characterization
Caveat / follow-up: No biochar yield, acid/alkali consumption per unit product, washwater volume/treatment, measured production cost, regeneration cost or life-cycle assessment is provided. The authors' low-cost/sustainable label is not supported by a quantitative process inventory.

Evidence domain: Observed removal, solution pH, contact time and dose effects
Experimental design / conditions: Main methods describe typical batch tests with 25 mg biochar in 50 mL AMX solution, 50 mg/L, initial pH adjusted to 7, 25 °C and 6 h. Separate tests varied pH 1–11, contact time 0–24 h, initial concentration 20–70 mg/L and dose 2–20 mg. pHpzc reported as 6.25.
Reported result: For the reported time series, AMX removal reached about 90% by 10 min and about 99% by 40 min, stayed near 98% through 8 h, then declined to around 80% by 24 h. Removal peaked around pH 3 at 98.9%, remained relatively stable pH 5–7 and declined in alkaline conditions. Figure 10 shows plotted uptake rising roughly from 37 mg/g at 20 mg/L to about 136 mg/g at 70 mg/L; removal was about 93.5% at 20 mg/L and about 98% at 50–70 mg/L. Figure 11 shows capacity falling as dose increased (approximately 580 mg/g at 4 mg to about 120 mg/g at 20 mg), while removal remained around 97–98%.
Value / units: About 99% removal by 40 min; pH ≈3; plotted uptake ≈37–136 mg/g over C0 20–70 mg/L; pHpzc 6.25
Model / metric: Reported observed percentage removal and plotted uptake; not the disputed kinetic-table uptake
Caveat / follow-up: The abstract's initial-concentration range (0.5–2.5 mg/L) conflicts with methods/results stating 20–70 mg/L. The work uses artificially polluted/synthetic water, not a demonstrated untreated real-wastewater matrix. Do not silently reconcile the concentration ranges.

Experimental design / conditions: Paper reports a kinetic experimental qe of 245.9 ± 1.4 mg/g, a pseudo-second-order calculated qe = 243.902 mg/g (R²=0.999), and a Langmuir fitted qmax = 239.230 mg/g (R²=0.995). PFO R²=0.100; Freundlich R²=0.092 and Temkin R²=0.130. The stated typical batch condition is 25 mg adsorbent + 50 mL at 50 mg/L AMX.
Reported result: Authors identify PSO as the better kinetic fit and Langmuir as the best isotherm fit. The reported kinetic qe and fitted qmax are both around 240–246 mg/g.
Value / units: qe(exp) = 245.9 ± 1.4 mg/g; PSO qe(calc)=243.902 mg/g; Langmuir qmax=239.230 mg/g
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7 and 10–11; Table 1; Table 2; Fig. 12
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; high-priority quantitative caveat
Caveat / follow-up: If the stated 25 mg/50 mL/50 mg/L batch condition applies, the total initial AMX mass is 2.5 mg and the mass-balance ceiling is 100 mg/g, which cannot support qe≈245.9 mg/g. Figure 10 values at 20–70 mg/L also differ from the kinetic table, and fitted qmax is slightly below the reported experimental qe. Treat these table values as unresolved until the exact kinetic conditions/raw data or a correction is available; do not use the 245.9 mg/g value as a verified cross-paper benchmark.

Experimental design / conditions: Four adsorption/desorption cycles were performed. The solid was rinsed with 0.05 M NaOH after filtration and dried at 110 °C before reuse. Main conclusion states the study is limited to AMX adsorption in artificially polluted water.
Reported result: The first cycle reportedly reached 98.6% removal. The article describes a 5% capacity drop by cycle 2 and a near-20% drop by cycle 4, but also states fourth-cycle removal efficiency was 72.2%, a larger decline than the accompanying description suggests.
Value / units: Four cycles; 0.05 M NaOH desorption; first-cycle removal 98.6%; fourth-cycle removal reported 72.2%
Model / metric: Removal efficiency across reuse cycles, distinct from adsorbent mass-normalized capacity
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 10; Fig. 13; conclusion on PDF p. 11
Caveat / follow-up: The description of a near-20% loss appears inconsistent with the stated change from 98.6% to 72.2% removal. No spent-adsorbent contaminant fate, leaching, regeneration cost, real wastewater validation or LCA is reported.

Target / co-contaminant: Ciprofloxacin (CIP), gatifloxacin (GAT), and Cu²⁺ in binary tests
Adsorbent / material: PGOT@GEL: phosphorus-doped graphene oxide functionalized with triethylenetetramine and incorporated into an AMPS/modified β-cyclodextrin hydrogel
Experimental design / conditions: GO produced by modified Hummers-type oxidation of graphite; P doping used H3PO2 at 80 °C for 5 h. TETA was grafted by an EDC/NHS-assisted amidation route; β-cyclodextrin was modified in DMF with triethylamine/acryloyl chloride; AMPS and A-β-CD were then free-radically polymerized with crosslinker/promoter/emulsifier/initiator at 75 °C for 2 h. Final product was washed and dried.
Reported result: The hydrogel was designed to improve recovery of graphene oxide while providing phosphorus-, nitrogen-, sulfonic-acid-, and β-cyclodextrin-related functional groups. This is a multistep engineered material, unlike raw biomass or standard biochar.
Value / units: P doping 80 °C/5 h; polymerization 75 °C/2 h; GO oxidation and multiple reagent/washing steps
Model / metric: Primary synthesis description; no normalized process-cost metric
Caveat / follow-up: No product yield, reagent/energy consumption per mass of adsorbent, solvent recovery, waste treatment, production cost or LCA is reported. The description of the hydrogel as environmentally friendly does not substitute for a process inventory.

Evidence domain: Observed uptake, fitted Langmuir capacities and RSM optimization
Experimental design / conditions: Single-solute batch studies varied pH, dose, contact time, concentration, temperature and ions; supplemental material contains some detailed conditions and response tables, but it was not supplied. The reported RSM optimum for CIP is 296.52 mg/L initial concentration, pH 6.70, dose 5.08 mg and 298.88 K.
Reported result: At pH 7, CIP uptake was reported as 192.24 mg/g with 96.12% removal; GAT uptake was 171.84 mg/g with 85.92% removal at pH 6. Fitted Langmuir qmax values were 821.24 mg/g for CIP (R²=0.9908) and 755.96 mg/g for GAT (R²=0.9923). RSM predicted 800.60 mg/g CIP uptake and the follow-up experiment reportedly gave 807.54 mg/g.
Value / units: CIP qmax 821.24 mg/g; GAT qmax 755.96 mg/g; pH-optimized reported uptake 192.24 and 171.84 mg/g; RSM observed 807.54 mg/g at C0 296.52 mg/L
Model / metric: Observed uptake and removal separated from fitted Langmuir qmax and RSM-predicted values
Caveat / follow-up: The RSM validation used a high initial CIP concentration (296.52 mg/L), not an environmentally trace concentration. qmax and optimized RSM uptake are not interchangeable with the pH-test uptake. Supplementary information containing some detailed conditions was not supplied.

Evidence domain: Solution pH, kinetics, temperature and ionic-strength effects
Experimental design / conditions: pH tests across 1–12; kinetic tests described through 120 min; isotherms measured at 298, 308 and 318 K. Interference tests included Na2SO4, NaCl and CaCl2; full detailed concentrations are not available in the main article text provided here.
Reported result: CIP uptake was highest near pH 7 and GAT near pH 6. The authors report adsorption approaching equilibrium after about 120 min. At 298 K, reported ionic effects retained 96.63% of initial CIP uptake with Na2SO4, 96.75% with NaCl and 92.27% with CaCl2. Higher temperature reduced adsorption, and the authors describe the process as exothermic.
Value / units: Approx. equilibrium by 120 min; retained CIP adsorption: 96.63% (Na2SO4), 96.75% (NaCl), 92.27% (CaCl2)
Model / metric: Observed batch uptake/removal and model fits; not continuous-flow performance
Caveat / follow-up: Some operating details are in the unprovided supplementary information. High removal at optimized batch conditions does not establish performance at trace concentrations or in continuous flow. Kinetic and isotherm fits alone do not prove a unique molecular mechanism.

Target / co-contaminant: Ciprofloxacin (CIP) and copper (Cu²⁺) in binary systems
Evidence domain: Competitive/co-adsorption and interaction of antibiotic with metal ion
Experimental design / conditions: Binary CIP–Cu²⁺ and Cu²⁺–CIP tests used adsorption-capacity ratios (Rq) to compare single-solute and combined systems. The paper varies Cu²⁺ concentrations up to 100 mg/L and CIP concentrations up to 100 mg/L; detailed design is described in figures and supporting information.
Reported result: CIP adsorption showed a promotional/synergistic ratio Rq of about 1.0061–1.1417 as Cu²⁺ concentration increased from 0 to 30 mg/L. Cu²⁺ uptake showed Rq about 1.0070–1.2044 as CIP concentration increased; reported enhancement weakened at higher concentrations, consistent with site limitation/competition. The authors propose positively charged CIP–Cu²⁺ complexes and additional CIP oxygen-bearing sites as contributors.
Value / units: Rq(CIP) 1.0061–1.1417; Rq(Cu²⁺) 1.0070–1.2044; tested co-solute concentrations up to 100 mg/L
Model / metric: Relative adsorption-capacity ratio for co-adsorption, not removal of a single antibiotic
Caveat / follow-up: This is a co-contaminant interaction study under relatively high prepared-solution concentrations. Do not interpret synergy in these tests as a universal beneficial matrix effect or as evidence of performance at trace environmental concentrations.

Adsorbent / material: PGOT@GEL hydrogel; recovered and reused sorbent
Evidence domain: Water-matrix application, regeneration and plant-toxicity assay
Experimental design / conditions: The paper compares CIP removal in deionized, tap, farmland and lake-water conditions (Fig. 12); some test details are in supplementary material. Seven reuse cycles were run, with methanol soaking for 12 h after adsorption, followed by water washing and drying. Rice seedling growth and chlorophyll were compared across CIP-only, CIP-plus-hydrogel and blank groups.
Reported result: CIP removal was reported as greater than 89% across the four water conditions. After seven cycles, reported removal performance was about 90.53% of the initial removal. The rice-seedling assay showed less growth/chlorophyll impairment in the CIP-plus-PGOT@GEL group than with CIP alone.
Value / units: >89% reported removal in each of four water conditions; ≈90.53% of initial removal retained after seven cycles; 12 h methanol regeneration
Model / metric: Water-matrix removal and cycle performance; plant response is a separate endpoint
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 10–12; Figs. 12–13; conclusion on PDF pp. 14–15
Caveat / follow-up: The main text does not provide all challenge concentrations and water-matrix details; do not label this as proof of trace-level untreated wastewater treatment until supporting data are inspected. Methanol use, recovery, waste handling and reuse cost are unquantified. The plant assay does not prove all transformation products or spent media are non-toxic.

Target / co-contaminant: CIP and GAT; Cu²⁺ in binary tests
Evidence domain: Proposed interaction mechanisms and feasibility limits
Experimental design / conditions: Authors used FTIR/XPS and pH-dependent comparison experiments to discuss electrostatic interactions, hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions. The co-adsorption system additionally invokes coordination/bridging interactions.
Reported result: FTIR and XPS peak shifts were interpreted as evidence of hydrogen bonding, π–π interactions and electrostatic interactions between PGOT@GEL and fluoroquinolones. The authors propose that Cu²⁺ forms positively charged complexes with CIP and that CIP can provide extra coordination sites for Cu²⁺. The hydrogel decreased CIP-associated damage in a rice seedling test.
Value / units: Qualitative mechanism evidence and biological-response comparison; no shared quantitative mechanism constant
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanism assignments remain interpretations of characterization and perturbation tests; no quantitative chemical inventory or life-cycle cost is provided. Avoid inferring that adsorption destroys the antibiotic or makes spent media safe.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash and mussel shell from forestry/agro-food side streams
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — minimally processed natural residues/by-products; ash is a combustion residue
Experimental design / conditions: Oak ash from combustion of oak logs; mussel shell supplied at <1 mm; pine bark crushed and sieved through 0.63 mm mesh. Single-solute batch adsorption/desorption at 25 °C, triplicate, antibiotic concentrations 0–600 µmol/L (25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600). 0.5 g sorbent was mixed with 10 mL of 0.005 M CaCl2 for 48 h. Antibiotics quantified by HPLC-UV.
Reported result: The paper compares three antibiotics across three low-processing sorbents and evaluates both adsorption and release. Material chemistry differs strongly: reported water pH was approximately 3.99 for pine bark, 9.39 for mussel shell and 11.31 for oak ash; oak ash also had high calcium and non-crystalline Fe/Al fractions.
Value / units: C0 = 25–600 µmol/L; sorbent = 0.5 g per 10 mL; 0.005 M CaCl2; 25 °C; 48 h
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2–4; Sections 2.1–2.5; Fig. 1; Supplementary Table S1 referenced
Caveat / follow-up: Supplementary information, including full physicochemical Table S1, was not supplied. This is primarily a retention-in-soil/side-stream valorization study, not a wastewater column demonstration. Do not equate its percentage retention with a treatment-plant removal result.

Adsorbent / material: Pine bark, oak ash and mussel shell
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — natural by-products and combustion residue
Experimental design / conditions: Single-solute systems at seven added concentrations from 0 to 600 µmol/L, 25 °C, 48 h. Fig. 1 reports adsorbed amount (µmol/kg sorbent) and percentage retained.
Reported result: Oak ash was the best AMX sorbent, with adsorption percentages close to 100% across tested concentrations; pine bark and mussel shell generally retained less than 20% AMX. Pine bark retained nearly 100% CIP and TMP across the tested concentration range. For CIP at the highest added concentrations, oak ash and mussel shell reached roughly 70% and 80% retention, respectively; TMP retention by oak ash fell below 30% at the highest concentrations, and mussel shell was generally below 20%.
Value / units: Up to ≈100% retention for AMX on oak ash and for CIP/TMP on pine bark; ≈70% CIP on ash and ≈80% on shell at high addition
Model / metric: Observed single-solute percent retention, separate from fitted qmax
Caveat / follow-up: Tests used added concentrations up to 600 µmol/L and a CaCl2 background electrolyte. No binary/tertiary competition test was conducted in this paper; conclusions about mixture performance remain future work.

Adsorbent / material: Oak ash, mussel shell and pine bark
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — natural by-products and combustion residue
Evidence domain: Isotherm fitting and fitted capacity plausibility
Experimental design / conditions: Freundlich, Langmuir and linear partition models were fitted to single-solute data. Table 1 reports qmax in µmol/kg, KL in L/µmol, and linear Kd in L/kg, together with parameter errors and R².
Reported result: The only reported AMX Langmuir qmax was 14,909 µmol/kg for oak ash (reported error 4,359; R²=0.93). The TMP Langmuir qmax for pine bark was 76,429 µmol/kg (reported error approximately 4.6×10⁴; R²=0.99). CIP on pine bark retained 100% at all tested concentrations, so modelling was not possible. The authors state that Langmuir fitting had high errors for most sorbent–antibiotic pairs and that saturation may not have been reached.
Value / units: qmax: AMX/oak ash 14,909 µmol/kg; TMP/pine bark 76,429 µmol/kg with very large error; no CIP/pine-bark fit
Model / metric: Fitted Langmuir qmax, not observed uptake
Caveat / follow-up: Under the highest test point (600 µmol/L × 10 mL / 0.5 g), the maximum mass-balance uptake for complete removal is 12,000 µmol/kg. The fitted TMP/pine-bark qmax of 76,429 µmol/kg substantially exceeds the experimentally accessible loading and has very large parameter error, so it must not be treated as a validated observed capacity. Abstract-level approximate capacities and Table 1 fitted qmax are different metrics.

Adsorbent / material: Adsorbate-loaded pine bark, oak ash and mussel shell
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — natural by-products and combustion residue
Experimental design / conditions: After adsorption, the residual sorbent was weighed and stirred in 10 mL of fresh 0.005 M CaCl2 for 48 h at 25 °C; three replicates were used. Release was reported in µmol/kg and percentage.
Reported result: AMX desorption from oak ash was close to 0%; release could reach around 80% from mussel shell and around 60% from pine bark at selected additions. CIP desorption was often high at low additions but fell below 10% for all three materials at the two highest additions. TMP desorption from pine bark was very low (maximum 6.29% at 25 µmol/L; <5% across the reported discussion), whereas mussel shell could release nearly all retained TMP.
Value / units: AMX: ~0% release from ash; up to 80% shell and 60% bark. CIP: <10% release at two highest additions. TMP: max 6.29% from bark at 25 µmol/L
Model / metric: Desorption percentage and released amount, not multi-cycle regeneration efficiency
Caveat / follow-up: The procedure is a single release test in CaCl2, not repeated sorbent regeneration. Low release indicates retention under these laboratory conditions but does not establish contaminant destruction or safe end-of-life handling.

Continuum stage: Stage 1 — natural by-products and combustion residue
Experimental design / conditions: Authors relate antibiotic speciation to material pH, exchangeable Ca and non-crystalline Fe/Al, and discuss electrostatic interactions, calcium cation bridges, and hydrogen bonding. Material/adsorbate pKa discussion appears in the results.
Reported result: The authors propose that alkaline, calcium-rich oak ash forms cationic bridges that favor AMX retention and suppress release. Pine bark's acidic conditions and organic carboxyl/hydroxyl groups are proposed to favor hydrogen bonding with CIP and TMP. The conclusion proposes application to agricultural soils to limit antibiotic mobility into water and the food chain.
Value / units: Proposed mechanisms: Ca-mediated bridging for AMX/ash; hydrogen bonding for CIP/TMP on pine bark
Model / metric: Mechanistic interpretation based on material properties and adsorption/desorption patterns
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanisms are proposed interpretations, not isolated direct measurements of each interaction. The work suggests soil retention/valorization; no full life-cycle analysis, process-cost inventory, long-term soil leaching study or real wastewater treatment trial is reported in the supplied main paper.

Adsorbent / material: Natural clay minerals (sepiolite, stevensite, illite, beidellite, low-charge and high-charge montmorillonites), synthetic ferrihydrite/goethite, and calcined sewage sludge
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural minerals/clays; engineered inorganic hydroxides and calcined residual are separate higher-processing comparators
Experimental design / conditions: Natural mineral materials included commercial mineral deposits/clays with some impurities. Ferrihydrite was synthesized by precipitation of Fe(NO3)3 with NaOH, aging and washing before freeze-drying/grinding; goethite similarly required pH 12, 72 h aging at 65 °C, washing/dialysis and freeze-drying. Calcined sewage sludge originated from a wastewater-treatment sludge gasification residue and was calcined at 800 °C, crushed to <2 mm.
Reported result: The paper intentionally studies materials in a largely unpurified/natural state for their potential as lower-cost sorbents. It compares mineralogy, cation exchange capacity, BET-specific surface area and point of zero salt effect (PZSE) as explanatory properties.
Value / units: Synthetic ferrihydrite/goethite preparation; calcined sludge at 800 °C; sludge particle size <2 mm
Model / metric: Primary characterization and sorption study preparation record
Caveat / follow-up: Synthetic hydroxides and calcined sludge should not be grouped with untreated natural clays when discussing processing burden. No full production cost or life-cycle inventory is supplied; detailed crystal-chemical supplementary material was not included in the uploaded file.

Adsorbent / material: Low-charge montmorillonite (LC Mnt), high-charge montmorillonites, stevensite, sepiolite, illite, beidellite, ferrihydrite, goethite and calcined sewage sludge
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural minerals/clays, with synthetic hydroxide and calcined residue comparators
Evidence domain: Observed uptake at controlled concentrations and pH
Experimental design / conditions: Triplicate batch isotherms at pH 4, 6 and 8, 25 °C, 0.1 M NaCl aqueous media and initial TC concentrations 33.2, 131.6, 322.6, 625.0 and 1176.5 mg/L. Fig. 7 plots observed sorbed amount against initial concentration and pH.
Reported result: LC Mnt showed the highest observed TC uptake at all tested concentrations: 13.2, 51.2, 125.5, 242 and 381.2 mg/g for initial TC concentrations 33.2, 131.6, 322.6, 625.0 and 1176.5 mg/L. At the highest concentration, high-charge montmorillonite with low Fe content reached 342.14 mg/g. Ferrihydrite, goethite and calcined sludge had lower uptake at high TC concentrations; ferrihydrite and illite reached around 8–10 mg/g at the lowest concentration near pH 8.
Value / units: LC Mnt observed uptake 13.2–381.2 mg/g over C0 33.2–1176.5 mg/L; HC Mnt NFe 342.14 mg/g at 1176.5 mg/L
Model / metric: Observed batch uptake (not fitted maximum capacity)
Caveat / follow-up: Even the lowest test concentration (33.2 mg/L = 33,200 µg/L) is far above the paper's cited typical effluent level (<1 µg/L), so results do not validate performance at trace environmental concentrations. Treat the high observed uptake values as high-loading laboratory results, not field capacities.

Adsorbent / material: Mineral sorbents listed in Table 3 and Table 4
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural minerals/clays and inorganic comparators
Experimental design / conditions: Freundlich and Langmuir equations were fitted separately at pH 4, 6 and 8. Table 3 reports Freundlich Kf, n and R²; Table 4 reports a Langmuir K parameter and Cm in cmol/kg alongside each material's CEC.
Reported result: The authors note high fit R² values for most materials but caution that R² alone cannot uniquely identify the better model. LC Mnt had Langmuir Cm of 116, 87.6 and 89.8 cmol/kg at pH 4, 6 and 8 against CEC 83 cmol/kg. Sepiolite had much larger fitted Cm values (392, 160, 125 cmol/kg) than its listed CEC (20 cmol/kg); the paper notes such anomalously high Cm values can indicate near-linear fitting rather than a reliable saturation capacity.
Value / units: Langmuir Cm: LC Mnt 116/87.6/89.8 cmol/kg (pH 4/6/8); sepiolite 392/160/125 cmol/kg; CEC values differ
Model / metric: Model parameter Cm in cmol/kg, not mg/g; separate from experimentally observed qe
Caveat / follow-up: Do not convert or compare Cm as if it were qmax in mg/g without a justified stoichiometric/unit conversion. Very high fitted values for some minerals are inconsistent with CEC and/or linear-isotherm behavior; rely on observed uptake at stated concentrations for transparent comparisons.

Adsorbent / material: Montmorillonite/smectites, sepiolite, stevensite, illite, ferrihydrite and goethite
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural mineral adsorbents; synthetic ferrihydrite/goethite are separate comparators
Evidence domain: Solution chemistry and proposed adsorption mechanisms
Experimental design / conditions: pH 4, 6 and 8; 0.1 M NaCl; mineral properties including CEC, BET surface area, XRD mineralogy and PZSE were examined. TC speciation varies from cationic below pH ≈3.3, zwitterionic at pH ≈3.3–7.7 and anionic above pH ≈7.7 as described by the authors.
Reported result: LC Mnt retained high uptake with relatively little pH dependence. The authors propose that its less tightly stacked 2:1 layers make internal layer surface more accessible. Sepiolite shows strong uptake attributed to external surface area, while low-loading uptake by ferrihydrite and illite is associated with available surface and acid-base properties. At pH 8, non-iron high-charge montmorillonite showed a marked adsorption decrease.
Value / units: Study pH 4/6/8; background 0.1 M NaCl; PZSE values for smectites approximately pH 8.2–8.4
Model / metric: Authors' mechanism interpretation supported by sorption curves and mineral characterization
Caveat / follow-up: The paper reports batch mineral-water tests rather than actual wastewater trials. Mechanistic explanations are inferred from mineral chemistry and curve trends; no direct molecular-scale proof or column/regeneration results are reported.

Adsorbent / material: Natural clays versus synthetic iron hydroxides and calcined sewage sludge
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — mineral adsorbents across different preparation intensities
Experimental design / conditions: The study compares observed uptake and model parameters across C0 33.2–1176.5 mg/L and pH 4–8; it does not report regeneration or continuous-flow treatment. Materials were not purified, but some required synthesis or thermal processing.
Reported result: LC Mnt offered the highest high-loading uptake across the tested pH range. The authors also highlight that illite, sepiolite and ferrihydrite display useful adsorption intensity at low-to-medium concentrations relative to other tested minerals, suggesting possible prefilter or permeable-reactive-barrier use for future testing.
Value / units: Maximum observed uptake ≈381.2 mg/g for LC Mnt at initial TC 1176.5 mg/L; no demonstrated column performance
Model / metric: High-concentration batch performance plus proposed, not demonstrated, application
Caveat / follow-up: The author's phrase 'low concentration' is relative to this study's isotherm range and still refers to tens of mg/L at the lowest point. No real wastewater, trace-level, regeneration, disposal, chemical consumption per kg or life-cycle cost data are provided.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics including tetracycline (TC), ciprofloxacin (CIP), amoxicillin (AMX), levofloxacin, ceftriaxone, erythromycin, norfloxacin, ofloxacin, doxycycline, cefotaxime and sulfamethoxazole
Adsorbent / material: Chitosan-based composites: magnetic oxides, biochar/carbon materials, graphene oxide, clays, silica, MOFs, hydrogels and crosslinked/grafted chitosan
Continuum stage: Stage 2–4 depending on composite; review covers modified biopolymers and biopolymer-based composites, not a single adsorbent
Experimental design / conditions: Narrative review of published studies; no original adsorption experiments in this paper. The review discusses chitosan made from chitin and modification routes including grafting, crosslinking, blending and incorporation of nanomaterials/MOFs.
Reported result: The review organizes literature by antibiotic family and discusses how chitosan's amino/hydroxyl groups, pH-sensitive charge and low water stability/solubility motivate modification. It highlights improved separability, surface properties and reusability reported for some composites, but these outcomes depend on the specific formulation and method.
Value / units: Review covers 11 antibiotic categories and several classes of chitosan composites
Model / metric: Secondary literature synthesis, not original experimental evidence
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1–5; Sections 1–2; Fig. 2; contents on p. 2
Evidence status: Full text reviewed — review article; supporting source only
Caveat / follow-up: Do not count this as a primary experimental paper or place its compiled qmax values into primary-study rankings without tracing the cited original studies. Q1 status and final source role remain to be verified.

Adsorbent / material: Selected chitosan composite adsorbents reported in review Table 2
Continuum stage: Stage 2–4 — modified chitosan/mineral, magnetic and carbon composites
Experimental design / conditions: Review Table 2 compiles maxima and optimum pH from cited primary studies. Examples include chitosan-g-AMPS (806.60 mg/g, pH 3), MMICs-Fe3+ (516.29 mg/g, pH 7–8), MOF-Cs (495.04 mg/g, pH 8–9), MSCsG (183.47 mg/g, pH 6) and Cs-olive pomace (1.6 mg/g, pH 8).
Reported result: The review illustrates a wide spread in reported TC capacities among chitosan composite formulations, from 1.6 to 806.60 mg/g in the selected entries. These values are transcribed from the review's table and are not newly measured in this article.
Value / units: Review-reported qmax: Cs-g-AMPS 806.60 mg/g; MMICs-Fe3+ 516.29 mg/g; MOF-Cs 495.04 mg/g; MSCsG 183.47 mg/g; Cs-olive pomace 1.6 mg/g
Model / metric: Secondary summary of fitted maxima; source-study conditions differ
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 5; Table 2; narrative on pp. 5–7
Evidence status: Extracted — review-level values; primary sources must be traced
Caveat / follow-up: The listed studies use different adsorbent dose, concentration, pH, temperatures and model conventions; do not compare their qmax as a like-for-like ranking. Verify each number, metric and condition against its original paper before manuscript use.

Adsorbent / material: Magnetic chitosan–graphene oxide, MgO/chitosan/graphene oxide, Fe–chitosan nanoparticles, chitosan/biochar and related composites
Continuum stage: Stage 2–4 — modified chitosan, magnetic nanocomposites and carbon composites
Evidence domain: Secondary compiled capacities and pH effects for ciprofloxacin
Experimental design / conditions: Review Table 3 compiles qmax and optimum pH from cited studies; it is not a harmonized experiment. Examples include MgO/Cs/GO (1111 mg/g, pH 7), magnetic chitosan-grafted GO (MCsGO, 282.9 mg/g, pH 4–9), Fe-CS NCs (142.85 mg/g, pH 6), and Cs/BC (>76 mg/g, pH 3).
Reported result: The review emphasizes that CIP speciation and chitosan composite surface charge vary with pH, while GO, magnetic oxides and biochar introduce additional surface area, binding sites and separation options. The reported maxima span a very broad range.
Value / units: Review-reported qmax: MgO/Cs/GO 1111 mg/g; MCsGO 282.9 mg/g; Fe-CS NCs 142.85 mg/g; Cs/BC >76 mg/g
Model / metric: Secondary literature summary; not independent test data
Evidence status: Extracted — review-level values; primary sources must be traced
Caveat / follow-up: The exceptionally high 1111 mg/g value should be verified in the cited original work and its concentration/dose mass balance before use. Do not rank these materials from review table entries alone; confirm whether each endpoint is adsorption-only.

Adsorbent / material: Chitosan-stabilized bimetallic Fe/Ni nanoparticles (Cs-Fe/Ni), as summarized in review
Evidence domain: Mixed removal endpoint and possible degradation pathway
Experimental design / conditions: The review summarizes a cited primary study by Weng et al. (2013). It reports AMX removal in single-solute and AMX/Cd²⁺ binary solutions and describes Fe corrosion, electron production and hydrogen-radical-mediated cleavage of the AMX β-lactam bond.
Reported result: Review-reported AMX removal was 93% in the single solution and 68.9% in the binary solution. The review describes a reductive degradation pathway as part of the explanation, so the endpoint should not automatically be treated as adsorption alone.
Value / units: 93% AMX removal alone; 68.9% in mixed AMX/Cd²⁺ solution
Model / metric: Secondary reported removal percentage; combined adsorption/reductive transformation may contribute
Evidence status: Extracted — review-level summary; original study required
Caveat / follow-up: Do not include this removal percentage in an adsorption-only performance ranking until the Weng et al. primary study is reviewed and the contributions of adsorption and reductive degradation are separated.

Adsorbent / material: Chitosan-based composites and their magnetic, carbon, mineral, MOF and oxide additives
Evidence domain: Cross-cutting mechanisms, matrix effects and regeneration
Experimental design / conditions: Narrative discussion synthesizes studies that vary pH, adsorbent dose, ionic strength, competing pollutants and material composition. The paper contains antibiotic-specific sections and tables across pp. 5–15.
Reported result: The review repeatedly emphasizes pH-dependent antibiotic speciation, interactions with chitosan amine/hydroxyl groups, electrostatics, hydrogen bonding and π–π interactions when carbon/graphene components are present. Magnetic particles are discussed as a means to improve solid recovery. It also notes limitations of unmodified polymers in complex wastewater and the use of grafting/crosslinking/composites to improve stability and properties.
Value / units: Qualitative cross-cutting synthesis; no one common test condition or standardized metric
Model / metric: Review synthesis, not primary mechanism verification
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 4–5 and 8–15; Tables 2–7 and antibiotic-specific sections
Caveat / follow-up: The review aggregates heterogeneous studies and sometimes discusses removals involving redox, Fenton-like, photocatalytic or other transformation processes. Trace every mechanism/capacity cited in the manuscript to its primary paper and distinguish adsorption, degradation, percentage removal and desorption.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics; review emphasizes tetracycline, ciprofloxacin, amoxicillin and other antibiotic classes
Adsorbent / material: Chitosan-based composites including magnetic chitosan, chitosan–MOF, chitosan–carbon, chitosan–clay, oxide and hydrogel composites
Continuum stage: Stages 2–4 depending on composite; review covers modified biopolymers and engineered composites
Evidence domain: Review methodology, evidence scope and selection criteria
Experimental design / conditions: The review searched Google Scholar, ScienceDirect, Scopus and PubMed for 2018–2025 publications. It reports 477 records identified, 342 removed before title/abstract screening, 135 screened, 38 excluded for insufficient data, 97 full texts assessed, 23 excluded and 74 studies included (59 batch, 15 dynamic). Inclusion focused on peer-reviewed English-language experimental studies of chitosan combined with adsorbents for antibiotic removal from water.
Reported result: The review provides a recent map of batch and fixed-bed literature and explicitly separates dynamic-column operation from batch equilibrium tests. Its PRISMA flow diagram is on PDF p. 2.
Value / units: 477 identified; 74 included; 59 batch studies and 15 dynamic studies
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1–2; Section 2; Fig. 1 / PRISMA diagram
Evidence status: Full text reviewed — review article; supporting source only
Caveat / follow-up: Do not count this as a primary experiment. The review excludes studies from journals with impact factor <3; that filter can affect coverage and needs to be noted if discussing its search method. Its compiled evidence still requires primary-paper checking for units, conditions, endpoint and mass balance.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics, especially tetracycline (TC), ciprofloxacin (CIP), amoxicillin (AMX), trimethoprim (TMP), sulfamethoxazole (SMX) and other examples
Adsorbent / material: Chitosan composites with MOFs, magnetic oxides, graphene oxide, biochar, cellulose/alginate, clays and other phases
Continuum stage: Stages 2–4 — modified chitosan and biopolymer-based composites
Evidence domain: Secondary batch-study capacities and model trends
Experimental design / conditions: The review compiles capacities, fitted isotherms, kinetic models and conditions from primary studies in antibiotic-specific tables (including Tables 1–3, PDF pp. 6–8). One example is Fe3O4/MOF/grafted chitosan for TMP: reported Langmuir qmax 391.90 mg/g at pH 8, initial concentration 0.26–0.34 mg/L and dosage 0.8 g/L; reported kinetic qe 383.22 mg/g at C0=0.3 mg/L.
Reported result: The review states tetracycline is the most commonly studied antibiotic and chitosan–MOF composites include some of the highest reported capacities. It reports pseudo-second-order (PSO) as the most frequent best-fitting kinetic model and Langmuir as a common best-fitting isotherm.
Value / units: Example secondary value: TMP qmax 391.90 mg/g and kinetic qe 383.22 mg/g (as reported by review; original source must be checked)
Model / metric: Secondary synthesis of fitted qmax, qe and model-fit statistics
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 5–9; Tables 1–3; kinetic discussion on PDF p. 9
Caveat / follow-up: Values represent different primary studies and are not standardized. In particular, high reported qe values at low initial concentrations must be checked against dose, volume and mass balance in the original papers. A PSO fit does not, by itself, prove chemisorption; do not reproduce the review's kinetic-model interpretation as direct mechanistic proof.

Target / co-contaminant: Tylosin (TYL), amoxicillin (AMX), erythromycin (ERY), doxycycline (DC), sulfamethoxazole (SMX), ofloxacin (OFL), tetracycline (TC), oxytetracycline (OTC), norfloxacin (NOR), levofloxacin and ciprofloxacin, among others
Adsorbent / material: Chitosan-containing composite adsorbents reported in fixed-bed columns
Continuum stage: Stages 2–4 depending on the material; column data include biopolymer, carbon and multicomponent composites
Evidence domain: Secondary fixed-bed breakthrough and exhaustion data
Experimental design / conditions: Review Table 6 summarizes fixed-bed data from 15 selected dynamic studies, listing flow rate, bed height, influent concentration, breakthrough/exhaustion times, volumes, model and q0. Examples include chitosan–cellulose composite for TYL (Q=5 mL/min, bed 5 cm, C0=10 mg/L, breakthrough 146 min, exhaustion 736 min, reported q0=47.2 mg/g); PVP–chitosan–ZnFe2O4 for AMX (Q=0.5 mL/min, C0=40 mg/L, breakthrough 115 min, q0=218.9 mg/g); and chitosan–cellulose nanocomposite microspheres for SMX (Q=4 mL/min, bed 1.5 cm, C0=10 mg/L, breakthrough 102.5 min, exhaustion 797.5 min, q0=117.4 mg/g).
Reported result: The compiled dynamic literature shows that fixed-bed behaviour depends on flow rate, influent concentration and bed design. In the review's cited tylosin example, increasing flow from 4 to 6 mL/min reduced saturation time from 620 to 446.67 min, while the volume treated to saturation rose from 2480 to 2680 mL.
Value / units: Review-reported q0 examples: TYL 47.2 mg/g; AMX 218.9 mg/g; SMX 117.4 mg/g; values are source-study-specific
Model / metric: Secondary reported fixed-bed capacities and breakthrough/exhaustion metrics
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 13–16; Fig. 7; Table 6; flow-rate discussion on PDF p. 13
Evidence status: Extracted — review-level dynamic data; original studies needed
Caveat / follow-up: Do not blend q0 with batch qmax or qe; these are different metrics and test geometries. Conditions are heterogeneous and some Table 6 cells are blank or compressed in the review layout. Verify any selected dynamic-study values against the primary paper before manuscript quotation or ranking.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics in batch and fixed-bed operation
Adsorbent / material: Chitosan-based composites; review compares batch and packed-column systems
Evidence domain: Scale-up, utilization, regeneration and operating trade-offs
Experimental design / conditions: The review compares batch and dynamic systems in Table 7 (PDF p. 16) and discusses breakthrough curves, mass-transfer zones, flow rate, bed height, inlet concentration, pressure drop, channeling and clogging.
Reported result: Batch studies offer comparatively simple, controlled screening and isotherm/kinetic measurements; fixed-bed studies are more relevant to continuous operation and scale-up but are more complex and can leave parts of the bed underused within the mass-transfer-zone framework. The review identifies only 15 dynamic studies versus 59 batch studies among its 74 selected papers.
Value / units: 59 batch vs 15 dynamic studies in the review
Model / metric: Review comparison of operating modes, not new experimental data
Caveat / follow-up: The review describes dynamic systems as closer to real wastewater operation but this does not mean the summarized columns necessarily used real wastewater. Check matrix composition, regeneration method, spent-media fate, and cost/energy data for each primary study; the review does not establish a common techno-economic comparison.

Adsorbent / material: Untreated barley husks and eggshells compared with activated carbon
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — untreated agricultural/food waste; activated carbon is comparator
Evidence domain: Source identity, feedstock characteristics and preparation
Experimental design / conditions: The paper uses a commercial 500 mg levofloxacin tablet to prepare stock solution (not a pure analytical standard). Sorbents had particle size 0.6–1 mm. Table 1 reports BET surface area: barley husk 0.302 m²/g, eggshell 0.163 m²/g and activated carbon 1100 m²/g; ash contents 19.6%, 84% and 5%, respectively. Tests generally used 30 °C and 200 rpm.
Reported result: The barley-husk material was tested as-received after size classification as a low-processing waste sorbent. The paper's internal journal imprint is December 2014, Volume 20, Number 12; the uploaded filename incorrectly contains '(2023)'.
Value / units: Particle size 0.6–1 mm; BET area: barley 0.302 m²/g, eggshell 0.163 m²/g, activated carbon 1100 m²/g
Model / metric: Primary study metadata and material characterization
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1, 5 and 11; Table 1; methods Section 3.1
Caveat / follow-up: Use 2014, not the filename's 2023, as the publication year; the screening register already preserves this correction. Tablet excipients can affect solution composition/UV measurements and the paper does not clearly document an independent active-ingredient assay or blank correction for all excipients.

Adsorbent / material: Barley husks, eggshells and activated carbon
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — untreated barley husks and eggshell waste; activated carbon comparator
Evidence domain: Observed removal, dosage and pH response
Experimental design / conditions: The abstract reports 74% removal for activated carbon and 71% for barley husks, each at 5 g/L, and 42% for eggshells at 50 g/L. Batch tests used 150 mg/L LEVX for pH/time experiments at 30 °C and 200 rpm. The paper reports approximate time to constant uptake as 50 min for barley husks, 110 min for activated carbon and 40 min for eggshells.
Reported result: At pH 7, the paper reports 74% removal with activated carbon and 71% with barley husks at equal 5 g/L dosage, while eggshells reached 42% only at ten times that dosage. Uptake reportedly increased from pH 4 to 7: activated carbon 3.8 to 5.2 mg/g, barley husks 2.1 to 3.7 mg/g and eggshells 1.1 to 1.5 mg/g.
Value / units: Removal: AC 74% at 5 g/L; barley husk 71% at 5 g/L; eggshell 42% at 50 g/L; pH-7 uptake 5.2, 3.7 and 1.5 mg/g respectively
Model / metric: Reported removal percentages and uptake trends, not fitted qmax
Caveat / follow-up: The water was synthetic and highly spiked (150 mg/L for key tests), not real wastewater or trace-level effluent. Removal percentages are not directly comparable without accounting for the tenfold higher eggshell dose.

Adsorbent / material: Barley husks, eggshells and activated carbon
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — untreated waste materials; activated carbon comparator
Evidence domain: Isotherm fitting and reported maximum capacities
Experimental design / conditions: Isotherm experiments used 100 mL LEVX at initial concentrations 25, 50, 75, 100, 125 and 150 mg/L, pH 7, 3 h, 30 °C and 200 rpm. Activated carbon and barley husks dosage was 0.5 g/100 mL (5 g/L); eggshell dosage was 5 g/100 mL (50 g/L).
Reported result: Table 2 reports Langmuir q_m values of 34.211 mg/g for activated carbon, 125.735 mg/g for barley husks and 5.6423 mg/g for eggshells; Langmuir R² values were 0.995, 0.988 and 0.995, respectively. The paper calls Langmuir the best fitting model.
Value / units: Langmuir q_m: AC 34.211 mg/g; barley husks 125.735 mg/g; eggshells 5.6423 mg/g
Model / metric: Fitted Langmuir maximum capacity, distinct from measured removal or observed qe
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 11; Table 2; Fig. 4 on PDF p. 14
Caveat / follow-up: At the maximum isotherm C0=150 mg/L with 100 mL and 0.5 g sorbent, the maximum possible observed qe is 30 mg/g for AC/barley husks; the eggshell dose has a ceiling of 3 mg/g. The fitted q_m for barley (125.735 mg/g) is far above the experiment's accessible loading and should not be treated as a verified capacity. A fitted asymptote may extrapolate beyond the tested range, but here it is weakly constrained by the available mass balance.

Adsorbent / material: Barley husks, eggshells and activated carbon
Continuum stage: Stage 1 — untreated waste materials; activated carbon comparator
Evidence domain: Kinetic model, process mass balance and internal consistency
Experimental design / conditions: The paper describes a separate 1 L kinetic setup at C0=150 mg/L and target Ce/C0=0.05. It reports dosage values of 20.745 g activated carbon, 30.722 g barley husks and 720 g eggshells. Table 3 reports PFO qe values of 30.66, 23.81 and 17.12 mg/g and PSO-calculated qe values of 4.71, 6.87 and 0.21 mg/g, respectively.
Reported result: The paper reports PSO fits with R²=0.9988 for activated carbon, 0.9966 for barley husks and 0.9846 for eggshells, versus PFO R²=0.7224, 0.7022 and 0.8099.
Value / units: Separate target-Ce/C0 setup uses dose 20.745/30.722/720 g per 1 L at 150 mg/L; reported qe values diverge sharply by model
Model / metric: PFO and PSO fitted qe, with cross-check against stated kinetic dose/mass balance
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 7 and 12; Section 4.3; Table 3; Figs. 6–10
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; high-priority unresolved caveat
Caveat / follow-up: The stated 1 L setup contains 150 mg LEVX, of which at most 142.5 mg can be removed to reach Ce/C0=0.05. With the stated doses, qe cannot exceed about 6.87 mg/g for AC, 4.64 mg/g for barley husks and 0.198 mg/g for eggshells. Several reported kinetic values (including PFO qe and barley PSO qe=6.87 mg/g) exceed these ceilings, some by a wide margin. Do not use Table 3's qe values without resolving the mismatch between described batch setups, dosage units and table entries.

Adsorbent / material: Raw Tunisian clays AM, HJ1 and HJ2; each also activated with Na2CO3 (base) or HCl (acid)
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural mineral clays; acid/base-activated derivatives are more processed comparators
Evidence domain: Material origin, preparation and processing–cost trade-off
Experimental design / conditions: Raw clays were suspended in distilled water, sieved at 50 µm and dried at 60 °C. Base activation mixed 30 g clay with 1.5 g Na2CO3 in 300 mL water at 75 °C for 1 h; activated material was settled and dried at 60 °C without washing. Acid activation used 3 N HCl at 75 °C for 4 h, followed by distilled-water washing to pH 6 and drying at 60 °C.
Reported result: Raw clays contained 14–20% organic matter and had pH 8.39–9.08, electrical conductivity 446–495 dS/m and eCEC 80.65–97.45 cmolc/kg as reported. Their mineral composition varied: AM had high calcite, HJ1 more kaolinite/sepiolite and HJ2 32% microcline. Activation materially altered pH and EC but added chemical, heating, washing and drying steps.
Value / units: Activation: 5% Na2CO3, 75 °C/1 h or 3 N HCl, 75 °C/4 h; raw pH 8.39–9.08; OM 14–20%
Model / metric: Primary material characterization and preparation protocol
Caveat / follow-up: The EC unit and reported magnitude are unusually high but should be retained as published pending source verification rather than silently corrected. Supplementary Table S1 was not included in the uploaded PDF. The paper gives no reagent cost, washwater treatment, yield, or life-cycle inventory.

Adsorbent / material: Raw and acid-/base-activated AM, HJ1 and HJ2 Tunisian clays
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clays and chemically activated derivatives
Evidence domain: Observed adsorption under varying concentration and solution chemistry
Experimental design / conditions: Triplicate batch tests used 0.5 g clay with 10 mL solution containing 0.005 M CaCl2 and 25, 50, 100, 200, 400, 600, 800 or 1000 µmol/L TC, at 25±2 °C in the dark, shaken at 50 rpm for 24 h. Solution pH after contact was reported around 6–10.
Reported result: Raw clays generally showed adsorption percentages close to 100% at the higher TC additions. The maximum observed adsorption was 12,672.7 µmol/kg when 1000 µmol/L TC was added. Raw clays were similar in overall performance; acid/base activated clays were also effective but could show lower adsorption at the lowest TC concentration, where removal dropped to about 75%.
Value / units: Maximum observed uptake 12,672.7 µmol/kg at C0=1000 µmol/L; 0.5 g clay/10 mL; 24 h; 25±2 °C
Model / metric: Observed adsorbed amount and percentage removal, separate from fitted isotherm capacities
Caveat / follow-up: Even the test range (25–1000 µmol/L, roughly 11–444 mg/L TC) is much higher than trace environmental concentrations; near-100% retention under these conditions is not proof of trace-level wastewater performance. The authors explicitly report no significant pH effect on adsorption in their design (ANOVA p=0.981).

Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clays versus chemically activated derivatives
Evidence domain: Adsorption versus desorption; reversibility and hysteresis
Experimental design / conditions: After adsorption, desorption was tested by adding 10 mL fresh 0.005 M CaCl2 and applying the same agitation/centrifugation/filtration procedure. Fig. 4 and Tables 6–7 report released fractions, fitted desorption parameters and hysteresis indices.
Reported result: Desorption percentages were always below 10% and mostly below 4%; highest release (near 10%) occurred at the two lowest TC additions. Average hysteresis index values reported in Table 7 were approximately 0.956–0.973 across clay/activation combinations. The authors interpret this as strong retention and relatively irreversible adsorption under their test conditions.
Value / units: Desorption <10%, most values <4%; average hysteresis index about 0.956–0.973
Model / metric: Observed desorption percentage and hysteresis index; not repeated regeneration-cycle retention
Caveat / follow-up: Low release in a single CaCl2 desorption step does not show antibiotic destruction or safe end-of-life handling. No repeated regeneration cycles, leachate toxicity, real-water test or spent-clay disposal assessment is reported.

Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clays and activated derivatives
Evidence domain: Isotherm fit quality and fitted-capacity interpretation
Experimental design / conditions: The authors fitted Freundlich, Langmuir, Linear, Sips and Temkin models to adsorption and desorption datasets. Table 5 reports fitted adsorption parameters and Table 6 fitted desorption parameters. The maximum observed adsorbed amount was 12,672.7 µmol/kg; several fitted Sips qm estimates are around 12,000–14,000 µmol/kg.
