Reported result: The Sips model was reported as the best overall fit for adsorption and desorption, with higher R² and smaller reported errors than competing models. All reported Sips heterogeneity parameters were greater than 1 for adsorption; raw clays were generally described as more heterogeneous than activated variants.
Value / units: Observed max 12,672.7 µmol/kg; fitted Sips qm examples span roughly 7,040–13,978 µmol/kg, source table values vary by clay/activation
Model / metric: Fitted isotherm parameters; do not conflate with directly observed uptake
Caveat / follow-up: The paper's supplementary material was not provided, and some table layout is dense. Keep units in µmol/kg and do not convert to mg/g without molecular-weight-based conversion. The Sips fit describes empirical heterogeneity but does not alone establish a unique molecular mechanism or field performance.

Adsorbent / material: Raw and activated AM, HJ1 and HJ2 clays
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — low-processing minerals; activated variants have additional chemical burden
Evidence domain: Effectiveness of activation and practical transferability
Experimental design / conditions: The paper compares raw clays with HCl- and Na2CO3-activated forms under the same batch design and reports pH/EC for the activated materials in Table 4.
Reported result: The authors conclude that acid/base activation was not necessary to improve TC adsorption/desorption and could even decrease capacity. Raw clays were already effective across the studied range; activated samples showed broadly similar high-concentration removal, with lower adsorption for some activated clays at the lowest TC concentration.
Value / units: Activated-clay pH: Na2CO3 variants ≈9.99–10.18; HCl variants ≈3.33–4.49; activated EC 3.03–44.4 dS/m as reported
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 8–10; Table 4; conclusions on PDF p. 12
Caveat / follow-up: No measured process cost or life-cycle data are given, but the absence of performance improvement alongside added acid/base, heat, washing (for acid activation) and drying supports treating activation as additional burden rather than an assumed benefit. Results are from artificial batch solutions, not real wastewater or continuous flow.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics; review covers biochar-based adsorbents for antibiotic wastewater remediation
Adsorbent / material: Biomass-derived biochar and hybrids from agricultural, forestry, livestock and sludge feedstocks
Continuum stage: Stages 3–4 — standard biochar through activated, doped, plasma/electrochemically treated and MOF/MXene hybrid materials
Evidence domain: Review framework for precursor and thermochemical processing routes
Experimental design / conditions: Review article covering pyrolysis, gasification, hydrothermal carbonization (HTC), torrefaction and subsequent activation/modification strategies. The review describes pyrolysis as typically about 300–900 °C; slow pyrolysis uses longer residence time (>1 h) and lower heating rates (3–10 °C/min), while HTC operates in water at about 120–260 °C and 2–10 MPa, commonly 30 min–8 h. HTC can process wet biomass without pre-drying but produces a hydrochar with typically lower fixed carbon and pore surface area than pyrochar.
Reported result: The review links feedstock and processing parameters to the final pore structure, surface area, surface chemistry and biochar yield. It presents HTC as potentially advantageous for wet feedstocks and pyrolysis as a common route for producing more highly carbonized porous materials.
Value / units: Pyrolysis typically 300–900 °C; HTC 120–260 °C and 2–10 MPa; HTC 30 min–8 h; slow pyrolysis >1 h
Model / metric: Secondary synthesis of production routes and material properties; no original experimental batch
Evidence status: Full text reviewed — review article; supporting source only
Caveat / follow-up: The source does not provide a harmonized process inventory, yield, energy consumption or cost per kg for all routes. Treat the process ranges as review summaries, not universal design specifications. Do not equate stated low-cost/green benefits with a quantified life-cycle advantage.

Target / co-contaminant: Sulfamethoxazole (SMX), ciprofloxacin (CIP), tetracycline (TC) and other antibiotics in cited studies
Adsorbent / material: Physically activated, chemically activated, ball-milled, plasma-treated, electrochemically modified, atom-doped and composite biochars
Experimental design / conditions: Secondary review of modification routes. Examples include steam activation; acid/base/oxidant and metal-salt treatments; ball milling; plasma and electrochemical modification; heteroatom doping; and hybrids with MOFs or MXenes. Physical activation is described at roughly 700–1100 °C. The review cites steam-activated sludge biochar with BET area 1583.07 m²/g and SMX uptake of 204.07 mg/g in 90 min; it also cites NH3 plasma treatment raising CIP removal from 31.8% to 85.7% for corn-straw biochar.
Reported result: Modification may create pores and functional groups and improve antibiotic uptake, but the review also notes trade-offs: strong acids/bases and metal impregnation create chemical waste; nitric-acid oxidation can add acidic groups while damaging structure or lowering surface area; ball-milled biochar may be highly water-dispersible; plasma/electrochemical methods can require specialized equipment and higher initial investment.
Value / units: Example review-reported values: steam-activated biochar BET 1583.07 m²/g and SMX uptake 204.07 mg/g/90 min; NH3 plasma-treated biochar CIP removal 31.8%→85.7%
Model / metric: Secondary reported example values; not a harmonized comparison or independent measurements
Caveat / follow-up: Trace any selected numerical example to its cited primary paper before ranking. The source reports different antibiotics, concentrations and materials, so example values are not like-for-like. Processing burden, yield, waste treatment, regeneration and LCA are not normalized across the examples.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics; table also includes at least one non-antibiotic contaminant entry
Adsorbent / material: Biochar-derived adsorbents including doped, magnetic, activated and composite biochars
Evidence domain: Secondary capacity overview and capacity-ranking caution
Experimental design / conditions: Table 3 compiles published qmax values from different cited sources rather than a common experimental comparison. Examples include N,S co-doped biochar for TC (1480.10 mg/g), corncob-xylose-residue biochar for SMX (1429 mg/g), porous graphitic biochar for TC (1122.20 mg/g), and dyeing-sludge-derived biochar for TC (1081.30 mg/g). Table 3 also contains an alkali-modified biochar entry for bisphenol A (BPA), which is not an antibiotic.
Reported result: The review illustrates the very broad spread of reported fitted capacities across biochar formulations. The spread reflects different adsorbates and primary-study conditions and should be used as a literature-navigation aid, not as evidence of a single standardized material ranking.
Value / units: Review-table examples: TC 1480.10 mg/g (N,S co-doped biochar); SMX 1429 mg/g (corncob xylose residue biochar); TC 1122.20 mg/g (porous graphitic biochar); TC 1081.30 mg/g (dyeing-sludge biochar)
Model / metric: Review-compiled qmax values from primary studies
Evidence status: Extracted — review table; primary studies not revalidated here
Caveat / follow-up: Do not place these qmax values in the master primary-study ranking without tracing the cited originals and checking concentration range, units, dose/volume mass balance, fitting quality and whether removal includes transformation. Table 3 appears to mix a non-antibiotic BPA entry into an otherwise antibiotic-focused capacity summary, so table scope should be interpreted carefully.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics in aqueous media; possible coexisting cations and natural organic matter
Adsorbent / material: Biochar with native and engineered surface functionalities; DFT-studied biochar–antibiotic pairs
Continuum stage: Stages 3–4 — standard biochar and functionalized/doped biochars
Experimental design / conditions: Review discusses electrostatic interaction, ion exchange, π–π interaction, surface complexation, capillary diffusion, cation bridging and hydrogen bonding. It summarizes density functional theory (DFT) calculations as a way to inspect electron-level interactions and identify functional groups that may provide favorable binding sites.
Reported result: The review emphasizes that uptake depends on feedstock chemistry, pyrolysis/activation conditions, antibiotics' speciation and matrix ions. It notes cited studies with mixed findings for Na+, Ca2+ and Mg2+ effects, and describes humic acid as either an adsorbing phase or a bridge on the biochar surface in some systems.
Value / units: Qualitative mechanism synthesis; no universal mechanism constant
Model / metric: Review of experimental and DFT-based interpretations
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 13–18; mechanism and DFT discussion; Figs. 9–11
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanistic interpretations may be system-specific and some are computationally inferred. Do not treat a DFT interaction energy or a fitted kinetic model as proof of a unique mechanism without primary experimental context. Verify any exact mechanism claim against the original paper.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics and potential residual contaminants associated with spent biochar
Adsorbent / material: Raw, modified and composite biochars, including biochar incorporating MOFs or MXenes
Continuum stage: Stages 3–4 — conventional through advanced engineered biochar
Evidence domain: Scale-up, reproducibility, environmental safety and future research
Experimental design / conditions: Review conclusion and challenge section discuss variable feedstock and pyrolysis conditions, lack of standardized material descriptors, potential residual phenolic compounds, PAHs or metal species, chemical waste from modification, and long-term stability and safety of spent adsorbent. The authors recommend standardization of porosity, H/C–O/C ratios, particle size and surface functionality, plus pilot-scale testing.
Reported result: The review recommends safer modification chemistry, application-specific quality indicators, molecular modelling integrated with experiments, pilot-scale validation and assessment of long-term spent-adsorbent safety.
Value / units: Proposed descriptors include porosity, H/C ratio, O/C ratio, particle size and surface functionality
Model / metric: Review-derived research gaps and recommended evaluation framework
Caveat / follow-up: The article does not itself provide a cross-material techno-economic or life-cycle assessment. Use these as identified research gaps, not as quantitative evidence that any particular route is more sustainable.

Continuum stage: Stage 3 — activated carbon and biochar, including physically/chemically modified variants
Experimental design / conditions: Structured review focused on tetracycline adsorption by biomass-derived AC and BC. The stated search uses Scopus and Google Scholar title/abstract/keyword fields with the Boolean query: (“activated carbon”) AND (“biochar”) AND (“tetracycline” AND “adsorption”) AND (“biomass”). The review evaluates feedstock, synthesis/activation, characterization, kinetics/isotherms, and reported performance.
Reported result: The article offers a TC-specific synthesis comparing how biomass choice, pore structure, surface area and functionality relate to adsorption and discusses environmental occurrence and antimicrobial-resistance implications.
Value / units: Search sources explicitly stated: Scopus and Google Scholar; scope restricted to tetracycline
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 2; Section 2; environmental concentration comparison in Table 1, PDF p. 3
Evidence status: Full text reviewed — review article; supporting source only
Caveat / follow-up: The search requires all four terms and is therefore potentially restrictive; studies focused on AC alone or biochar alone may be missed if metadata do not contain both. No PRISMA flow or total included-paper count is stated in the inspected method section. Do not generalize this TC-focused review to every antibiotic class.

Adsorbent / material: Biomass-derived activated carbon and biochar with surface oxidation, amination, metal-oxide loading, pore engineering and composite formation
Continuum stage: Stage 3 — activation/engineered surface chemistry; some composites approach Stage 4
Evidence domain: Surface chemistry, pore-size engineering and adsorption mechanisms
Experimental design / conditions: Review sections cover surface modification by oxidation, amination and metal-oxide loading; pore-size modification for the relatively large TC molecule; and multifunctional composites. It describes OH, COOH, NH2 and phosphate-containing groups as able to tune surface charge and interactions, and discusses π–π electron donor–acceptor interactions, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, surface complexation and pore filling.
Reported result: The review links accessible pore size and developed surface chemistry to TC uptake, while noting that the exact effect depends on pH, ionic strength, temperature and TC speciation. An example cited in the text reports 1357.5 mg/g Langmuir-estimated capacity for a biochar made from Schizochytrium limacinum, although the cited study's Freundlich model was reported as the better fit.
Value / units: Review-reported example: 1357.5 mg/g Langmuir-estimated TC capacity for Schizochytrium limacinum biochar
Model / metric: Review-reported fitted capacity; primary-study verification needed
Caveat / follow-up: The high capacity is secondary and appears alongside a statement that Freundlich fit the same study better (R²=0.96). Check the primary data, fit quality and mass balance before use. Do not interpret the review's generalization that a better pseudo-second-order fit proves chemisorption as mechanistic proof.

Target / co-contaminant: Tetracycline in aqueous and wastewater conditions
Adsorbent / material: Activated carbon, biochar and engineered AC/BC composites
Continuum stage: Stage 3 — conventional and modified carbonaceous adsorbents
Evidence domain: Transferability, regeneration, safety and techno-economic gaps
Experimental design / conditions: The review's future-scope and conclusion sections discuss reproducibility of material synthesis, real wastewater matrices, coexisting ions, natural organic matter, microbial activity, repeated adsorption–desorption cycles, leaching of incorporated metal species, pilot-scale testing, techno-economic analysis (TEA) and life-cycle assessment (LCA).
Reported result: The review concludes that laboratory results alone do not establish field feasibility and recommends greener scalable synthesis, continuous/semi-continuous reactors, real-water tests, stability checks and TEA/LCA.
Value / units: No common TEA/LCA metric or harmonized pilot dataset provided
Caveat / follow-up: The review provides recommendations rather than a completed cross-material economic or environmental assessment. Keep its real-world limitations distinct from experimentally demonstrated performance in individual primary papers.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotic families, including β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, sulfonamides, tetracyclines, macrolides and multi-antibiotic systems
Adsorbent / material: Agricultural biomass, biochar, activated carbon, chitosan beads, bentonite, zeolites and carbon nanomaterials
Continuum stage: Stages 1–4 — raw biomass through pyrolyzed, activated and composite carbonaceous materials
Evidence domain: Review scope, material classification and outcome distinctions
Experimental design / conditions: Broad narrative review of antibiotic classes, biomass/biochar adsorbents, adsorption theory, kinetic and isotherm models, regeneration and engineering applications. The review includes a comparative table of remediation methods (Table 2, PDF p. 6), material/antibiotic summaries (Table 6, PDF pp. 26–29), and a fixed-bed engineering discussion.
Reported result: The review spans many antibiotic families and sorbent classes, including agricultural biomass and biochar. It notes the importance of distinguishing direct antibiotic concentration measurements from proxy indicators such as chemical oxygen demand (COD), because high COD removal does not necessarily demonstrate high antibiotic removal.
Value / units: Table 6 compiles many individual primary-study results; no common cross-study condition
Model / metric: Secondary narrative synthesis and review tables
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1–2, 6–8 and 26–31; Tables 2 and 6; Section 10
Evidence status: Full text reviewed — review article; supporting source only
Caveat / follow-up: This paper is not a primary experiment and the inspected sections do not establish a reproducible systematic-search flow. Its tables combine heterogeneous conditions and sometimes broad removal mechanisms. Trace any capacity, mechanism or removal claim used in the manuscript to its cited primary study.

Adsorbent / material: Raw agricultural biomass, biosorbents, biochar and activated carbon prepared from different waste feedstocks
Continuum stage: Stages 1–3 — unmodified biomass through carbonized/activated waste-derived adsorbents
Evidence domain: Secondary adsorption-performance examples and comparison limits
Experimental design / conditions: Review Table 6 lists study-specific feedstocks, antibiotics, initial concentration (IC), adsorbent dose (AD), time, pH, temperature, capacity/removal, kinetic and isotherm models, and proposed mechanisms. Values are compiled from separate primary studies under differing designs.
Reported result: The table illustrates that many feedstocks and antibiotic classes have been investigated, but their reported values span different endpoint types and operating ranges. The review discusses Langmuir, Freundlich, Sips, Temkin and other models and notes the importance of kinetic and isotherm interpretation.
Value / units: Table 6 includes reported mg/g capacities and removal percentages; no single standardized comparison value
Evidence status: Extracted — review-level summary; primary sources not revalidated here
Caveat / follow-up: Do not combine removal percentages, observed uptake, fitted qmax and column capacity into one ranking. Each cited primary paper must be checked for units, mass balance, initial concentration, adsorbent dose and whether degradation or other processes contribute.

Adsorbent / material: Regenerable biomass-derived adsorbents, biochar and activated carbon; fixed-bed configurations
Continuum stage: Stages 1–4 depending on preparation and composite formation
Experimental design / conditions: The review discusses thermal and solvent regeneration, acid–base regeneration, and fixed-bed configurations in series or parallel with mass-transfer zones. Figure 4 (PDF p. 31) shows pressure and gravity fixed-bed filter examples. The text emphasizes flow, pressure drop and bed design as influences on operating performance.
Reported result: The review notes that repeated cycles can reduce adsorbent performance and that chemical/thermal regeneration must be selected with regard to material stability. Fixed beds can support continuous treatment, but the design must account for breakthrough, regeneration scheduling and operating conditions.
Value / units: Conceptual engineering discussion; no one common regeneration cycle metric
Model / metric: Review synthesis of regeneration/column engineering, not a new column experiment
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 29–31; Section 8 and Section 9; Fig. 4
Caveat / follow-up: Review-level engineering descriptions do not establish that each cited sorbent has been validated in actual wastewater. For practical claims, verify primary column tests, bed geometry, breakthrough conditions, regeneration reagent, spent-sorbent fate and process economics.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics and sequestered residues after adsorption
Adsorbent / material: Biomass/biochar-derived sorbents and chemically modified adsorbents
Evidence domain: Cross-cutting gaps in real water, modifying-agent burdens and spent-media management
Experimental design / conditions: The concluding discussion (PDF pp. 30–31) identifies limited reporting of used adsorbent/adsorbed antibiotic fate, extensive use of synthetic aqueous systems, matrix effects in real waters, environmental problems from some modifying agents and cost/complexity of modification. It proposes greater emphasis on engineering-scale use, green modifiers, and machine-learning prediction.
Reported result: The authors state that the majority of reviewed experiments used synthetic aqueous environments and that disposal/fate of spent adsorbents and residual solutions is often unclear. They also emphasize that modification may enhance performance while introducing economic and environmental burdens.
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 30–31; Section 10, concluding remarks and future perspectives
Caveat / follow-up: These are the review authors' synthesis statements rather than a newly counted estimate from our own screening. Use them as a source-supported rationale for our own matrix, regeneration, cost and spent-media columns; verify any specific claim against the relevant primary studies.

Adsorbent / material: Kaolin (KN), calcium-crosslinked sodium alginate–kaolin composite beads (KN@Alg), and granular activated carbon (AC) comparator
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clay; biopolymer composite adds processing and crosslinking
Experimental design / conditions: KN was used as received. KN@Alg was made by dispersing 2 g sodium alginate in 100 mL water for 2 h, adding 2 g kaolin, homogenizing, extruding drops into 0.5% CaCl2 to form beads, then rinsing thoroughly with distilled water. Beads were about 1 mm diameter. Batch comparison included AC, pristine KN and KN@Alg.
Reported result: Alginate immobilizes kaolin as recoverable beads, addressing powder recovery/pressure-drop challenges and improving capacity relative to pristine KN. This composite requires polymer, calcium chloride, water, stirring/homogenization, bead formation and washing; the preparation is more involved than using kaolin directly.
Value / units: 2 g SA + 2 g KN; 100 mL water; 0.5% CaCl2; bead diameter ≈1 mm
Caveat / follow-up: The bead formulation should be classified as a processed biopolymer–clay composite, not as raw natural clay. The paper gives reagent prices and an estimated adsorbent cost but not a full independent life-cycle inventory or pilot-scale capital/operating assessment.

Adsorbent / material: AC, pristine kaolin (KN) and kaolin–alginate beads (KN@Alg)
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clay versus calcium-crosslinked clay–biopolymer composite
Evidence domain: Observed batch uptake and removal response
Experimental design / conditions: Batch tests used 10 mL solutions with adsorbent dosages 0.4–4 g/L, pH 2–12, temperatures 298–328 K, contact time 5 min–7 h and initial CTC concentrations 20–100 mg/L. Kinetic/isotherm tests used pH 6 and 298 K; 0.8 g/L AC versus 4 g/L KN and KN@Alg. Concentration was measured by UV absorbance at 365 nm after centrifugation.
Reported result: At 4 g/L, KN and KN@Alg removal efficiencies were 55.04% and 68.44%. At the selected isotherm condition, observed capacities were AC 102.96 mg/g, KN 42.76 mg/g and KN@Alg 68.74 mg/g. Optimum reported capacity was pH 8 for KN (42.76 mg/g) and pH 6 for KN@Alg (68.74 mg/g).
Value / units: Observed/isotherm uptake: AC 102.96 mg/g; KN 42.76 mg/g; KN@Alg 68.74 mg/g. Removal at 4 g/L: KN 55.04%, KN@Alg 68.44%
Model / metric: Observed uptake and percentage removal; not the fitted Langmuir asymptote
Caveat / follow-up: Adsorbent dosages differ between AC (0.8 g/L in isotherm/kinetic tests) and KN/KN@Alg (4 g/L); comparisons must retain the dose. The fitted Langmuir qmax values are higher than observed uptakes (AC 176.151, KN 55.178, KN@Alg 79.679 mg/g); keep fitted and observed metrics separate. Laboratory initial CTC concentrations are well above typical trace environmental concentrations.

Adsorbent / material: KN@Alg beads compared with KN and AC
Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic measurements: C0=100 mg/L, pH 6; AC dose 0.8 g/L, KN and KN@Alg 4 g/L; 298 K; 5 min–7 h. Isotherms used C0 10–100 mg/L at pH 6 and 298 K. Kinetic fits included PFO, PSO, Elovich and intraparticle diffusion; isotherms included Langmuir, Freundlich and Temkin.
Reported result: Experimental equilibrium uptake was 104.720 mg/g AC, 45.300 mg/g KN and 68.700 mg/g KN@Alg. The paper's kinetic table gives KN@Alg PSO-calculated qe=144.307 mg/g with R²=0.838, far above its experimental qe=68.700 mg/g, whereas the PFO-calculated qe=70.616 mg/g is much closer. In Table 2, fitted Langmuir qmax values were 176.151, 55.178 and 79.679 mg/g for AC, KN and KN@Alg; the Temkin model is reported to have the highest R² for the three materials.
Value / units: Experimental qe: AC 104.720, KN 45.300, KN@Alg 68.700 mg/g; fitted Langmuir qmax: 176.151, 55.178, 79.679 mg/g
Model / metric: Experimental equilibrium uptake, model-calculated qe and fitted isotherm qmax are separate metrics
Caveat / follow-up: The KN@Alg PSO qe estimate (144.307 mg/g) is over twice the experimental equilibrium uptake (68.700 mg/g), and that model's R² is only 0.838. Do not repeat claims that the best-fitting kinetic model proves chemisorption; model fit alone is not direct mechanistic proof. Negative ΔG for KN@Alg is reported only at 298 K; calculated ΔG becomes positive at 308 and 318 K, so spontaneity is temperature-limited in the paper's own table.

Adsorbent / material: KN@Alg beads, pristine kaolin and AC
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — composite bead regeneration versus clay and activated-carbon comparators
Experimental design / conditions: Four adsorption–regeneration cycles were performed. The eluents tested included distilled water, 0.1 M HCl and 0.1 M NaCl; the methods describe a regeneration solution containing 0.1 M HCl, 0.1 M NaCl and distilled water, with 1 h contact, followed by thorough water washing.
Reported result: KN@Alg retained its structure in SEM after four cycles and its CTC removal efficiency declined by 14.19%. The paper reports more pronounced losses for pristine KN (20.67%) and AC (48.24%) over the corresponding comparisons.
Value / units: Four cycles; KN@Alg removal-efficiency decline 14.19%; KN 20.67%; AC 48.24%
Model / metric: Regeneration-cycle removal performance, not contaminant destruction
Caveat / follow-up: Regeneration transfers desorbed CTC into an eluent unless that stream is subsequently treated. Four cycles are a short laboratory reusability test, not long-term durability or full regeneration cost. Verify the exact eluent description against the supplementary methods before detailed protocol replication.

Adsorbent / material: KN@Alg beads in SPE cartridges and continuous glass bead column
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — shaped clay–biopolymer composite for dynamic treatment
Evidence domain: Water-matrix test, continuous-flow performance and reported material cost
Experimental design / conditions: SPE cartridge held 40 beads in a 6 mL cartridge; 5 mg/L CTC solution was prepared in distilled, tap and river water and passed at 1 drop/s. Continuous column was 1.5 cm ID × 15 cm height with 1 cm quartz sand layer, treating 5 mg/L CTC-contaminated river water at 1 mL/min. Column maintained performance over 20 bed volumes. The paper calculated sorbent cost including chemicals and energy and assumed four reuse cycles.
Reported result: After three SPE elution cycles, reported removal was 96.5% for distilled water, 94.2% for tap water and 93.7% for river water. The continuous column reported 93.6% removal over 20 bed volumes. The paper reports CTC removal cost of 0.095 US$/g for KN@Alg versus 0.15 US$/g for AC.
Value / units: 5 mg/L spiked CTC; column Q=1 mL/min; 20 bed volumes; 93.6% column removal; reported cost KN@Alg 0.095 US$/g vs AC 0.15 US$/g
Model / metric: Spiked-water application test and author-estimated adsorbent cost
Caveat / follow-up: These were 5 mg/L CTC-spiked water matrices, not proof of performance on naturally contaminated, trace-level wastewater. The cost estimate is narrow and assumes four cycles; the stated electricity price unit (US$/g) is unusual and should be verified before reuse. The reported cost does not establish a full plant-scale TEA or life-cycle advantage.

Adsorbent / material: Natural bentonite (NB) after laboratory purification; acid-activated bentonite (AAB)
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural clay versus acid-activated mineral; NB itself was pretreated/purified
Experimental design / conditions: Natural bentonite collected in Matrouh, Egypt, was dried, crushed, ground and sieved. It was then lab-purified by repeated washing and treatment with 0.1 N sodium acetate/acetic acid at pH≈5 and H2O2, followed by centrifugation and washes with 0.01 N NaCl and Milli-Q water. AAB was made by mixing NB with 0.5 M HCl at a 1:2 weight-to-volume ratio, heating at 70±1 °C for 4 h, rinsing repeatedly until chloride removal (AgNO3 test), drying at 60 °C for 24 h, and grinding/sieving to 100 µm.
Reported result: Acid activation increased the BET surface area by more than twofold and changed the oxide/mineral composition, including lower Al2O3, Fe2O3 and MgO percentages and higher SiO2. XRD/FTIR indicate alteration and partial dissolution but not complete destruction of the layered clay structure.
Value / units: AAB treatment: 0.5 M HCl, 70 °C, 4 h, clay:acid solution ratio 1:2; 100 µm final sieve
Caveat / follow-up: Do not call NB completely untreated natural bentonite: it had substantial purification, oxidant treatment and multiple washes. AAB adds acid, heating and additional washing/drying; the article does not provide a full chemical/washwater cost or life-cycle inventory.

Continuum stage: Stage 2 — purified natural clay and acid-activated derivative
Evidence domain: Observed batch adsorption and concentration/pH response
Experimental design / conditions: Batch experiments used CIP solution initially at 30 mg/L for optimization; pH range 3–9; dose varied 0.1–0.8 g/L. Kinetic experiments used 5–240 min; isotherm tests used 5–200 mg/L CIP. Selected later conditions included 0.2 g/L dose, pH≈5.5 and 180 min.
Reported result: The fitted/experimentally compared maximum monolayer capacities were 126.56 mg/g for NB and 305.20 mg/g for AAB; Table 4 reports experimental values 126.53 and 300.03 mg/g. Acid activation increased capacity by roughly 2.4-fold and lowered the clay dose needed to reach a strong removal response (AAB equilibrium response was reached at about 0.3 g/L versus 0.7 g/L for NB in the dosage test).
Value / units: Langmuir qmax: NB 126.56 mg/g; AAB 305.20 mg/g; qmax(exp) table: NB 126.53, AAB 300.03 mg/g; selected dose 0.2 g/L
Model / metric: Langmuir fitted maximum and source-reported experimental maximum; distinguish from percentage removal
Caveat / follow-up: The tests used synthetic aqueous CIP at mg/L concentrations, not real wastewater or trace environmental levels. Capacity values are condition-dependent; do not treat this single-study acid-activation benefit as proof that activation is generally cost-effective across clays.

Evidence domain: Kinetic fits, isotherms and proposed sorption mechanisms
Experimental design / conditions: Kinetics at CIP 30 mg/L, 0.2 g/L clay, pH≈5.5, 5–240 min, with equilibrium within 120 min and about 80% of uptake in the first 30 min. Nonlinear PFO, PSO and intraparticle diffusion models were tested. Langmuir, Freundlich and Sips models were fitted to 5–200 mg/L isotherm data.
Reported result: Experimental kinetic qe values were 85.56 mg/g for NB and 134.74 mg/g for AAB. PSO fits gave R²=0.999 and 0.994, respectively, with calculated qe close to experimental values (87.80 and 134.70 mg/g). Langmuir was reported as the best isotherm model, with R²=0.990 for NB and 0.987 for AAB. Proposed mechanisms include cation exchange/interlayer complexation, hydrogen bonding, electrostatic attraction, intercalation and pore filling.
Value / units: Kinetic qe(exp): NB 85.56 mg/g, AAB 134.74 mg/g; PSO R² 0.999/0.994; isotherm Langmuir R² 0.990/0.987
Model / metric: Measured kinetic uptake, model-fitted kinetics and fitted isotherm are different evidence types
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 9–11 and 14–15; Tables 3–4; Figs. 6 and 8
Caveat / follow-up: The authors interpret PSO fit as chemisorption, but a better-fitting PSO model is not by itself direct proof of a unique molecular mechanism. Mechanistic claims should rely also on the paper's XRD/FTIR/SEM and pH evidence and remain system-specific.

Experimental design / conditions: NaCl ionic strength was varied from 0 to 0.5 M. Regeneration of batch adsorbents used 0.1 M NaOH or 0.1 M HCl, with 4 h elution followed by washing/drying and five adsorption–desorption cycles.
Reported result: Increasing NaCl inhibited CIP sorption: removal fell from 59.8% to 16.1% for NB and from 95.3% to 75.5% for AAB between 0 and 0.5 M NaCl. NaOH was more effective than HCl for regeneration. With NaOH, reported CIP sorption/removal performance declined from 59.9% to 48.1% for NB and from 97.3% to 88.5% for AAB by cycle 5. With HCl, AAB fell from 96.9% to 58.3% by cycle 5.
Value / units: 0–0.5 M NaCl; NaOH five-cycle performance: NB 59.9→48.1%; AAB 97.3→88.5%; HCl AAB 96.9→58.3%
Model / metric: Observed removal/sorption performance over cycles, not antibiotic degradation
Caveat / follow-up: Strong salt sensitivity is relevant to real-water transferability. Regeneration uses corrosive 0.1 M eluents and repeated washing; spent eluate and salt/chemical consumption are not comprehensively assessed. Low post-regeneration performance loss does not mean CIP was destroyed.

Continuum stage: Stage 2 — acid-activated clay applied in continuous flow
Evidence domain: Breakthrough, loading, flow rate and column regeneration
Experimental design / conditions: Glass column 5 mm internal diameter × 130 mm length. AAB loadings 25 or 50 mg, influent CIP 10 or 20 mg/L and flow rates 1.5 or 3 mL/min; pH≈5.5. Column regeneration used 0.1 M NaOH and was tested for three cycles.
Reported result: At 50 mg AAB, 20 mg/L CIP and 1.5 mL/min, the first-cycle column reported qbed=97.12 mg/g, total uptake=4.86 mg, removal efficiency=37.99%, breakthrough time 40 min and total run time 400 min. Increasing the flow to 3 mL/min lowered qbed to 66.81 mg/g and removal to 36.05%; increasing influent from 10 to 20 mg/L lowered removal from 45.89% to 37.99%. Across regeneration cycles, Table 6 gives qbed values 97.12, 61.85 and 28.14 mg/g, totaling 187.11 mg/g.
Value / units: First cycle qbed 97.12 mg/g; Table 6 three-cycle total 187.11 mg/g; first-cycle removal 37.99%
Model / metric: Fixed-bed capacity (qbed) and removal efficiency, not batch Langmuir qmax
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; internal consistency caveat
Caveat / follow-up: An internal source discrepancy needs preserving: Table 6 lists 97.12+61.85+28.14=187.11 mg/g total across three cycles, but the conclusion states total column sorption capacity of 178.11 mg/g. Use the table sum only with the discrepancy noted until clarified. The laboratory column's reported total removal is moderate (37.99% first cycle), despite high batch qmax; column qbed and batch qmax must not be conflated.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple antibiotics, including SMX, CIP, enrofloxacin, cephalexin and tetracyclines
Continuum stage: Stage 3 — biochar and modified biochar from waste biomass
Experimental design / conditions: Review states that an in-depth Google Scholar assessment identified 88 research articles published during 2004–2024 on waste-biomass-derived biochar for antibiotic remediation in water. It reviews antibiotic toxicity, precursor selection, biochar preparation, kinetics, isotherms, thermodynamics and regeneration.
Reported result: The review offers a broad narrative synthesis of several antibiotic classes and focuses specifically on waste-derived and modified biochar rather than all possible adsorbent families.
Value / units: 88 articles identified from 2004–2024 via Google Scholar (as stated by authors)
Model / metric: Narrative review / literature survey, not a primary experimental dataset
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 1–4; Abstract, Introduction and “Need for this review”; Fig. 1
Evidence status: Full text reviewed — review article; supporting source only
Caveat / follow-up: The inspected methodology describes an in-depth Google Scholar assessment rather than a reproducible systematic-review/PRISMA workflow. Do not infer exhaustive coverage or count its compiled numbers as new experimental observations.

Target / co-contaminant: SMX, CIP, enrofloxacin, cephalexin, tetracyclines and other antibiotics
Adsorbent / material: Waste-derived biochar and modified biochar compared with other adsorbent classes
Continuum stage: Stage 3 — biochar; advanced chemical modification may approach Stage 4
Experimental design / conditions: Review Table 1 compiles adsorbent type, study/operating parameters, adsorption efficiency and capacity from separate source papers; Table 3 summarizes favoured kinetic/isotherm models and maximum capacities. Entries differ in concentration, dose, pH, temperature, units and target antibiotic.
Reported result: The review cites examples including modified Chinese-herbal-medicine-residue biochar with 80% tetracycline removal at 0.8 g/L and fish-scale-derived activated carbon with Langmuir capacities of 80.826–108.021 mg/g at 30–50 °C. These are source-study summaries, not results measured in this review.
Value / units: Secondary examples: 80% TC removal; fish-scale carbon qmax 80.826, 86.394 and 108.021 mg/g at 30, 40 and 50 °C
Model / metric: Review-compiled values, not a harmonized comparison
Caveat / follow-up: Do not rank heterogeneous review-table numbers as like-for-like capacities. Check each cited primary source for exact units, fitted versus observed uptake, dose/concentration mass balance and whether the endpoint is adsorption rather than degradation or combined removal. The review's table includes mixed unit formats, so verify transcription before manuscript quotation.

Target / co-contaminant: Antibiotics adsorbed onto biochar or modified biochar
Evidence domain: Preparation burden, regeneration, spent-media and real-water limitations
Experimental design / conditions: The review discusses biochar preparation and modifications and summarizes available regeneration/reuse studies. Its challenges/future section notes declining adsorption capacity, energy-intensive regeneration, secondary waste generation, predominance of batch tests at high initial antibiotic concentrations and the need for actual wastewater and pilot-plant studies.
Reported result: The authors recommend better regeneration/recycling, testing actual wastewater, pilot-scale deployment and exploring additional waste biomass precursors. These observations align with implementation gaps in the processing–cost–performance framework.
Value / units: Qualitative synthesis; no harmonized full-cost or LCA result
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 20–23; “Reusability of exhausted adsorbents,” “Challenges and future perspectives,” and Conclusion
Caveat / follow-up: Claims of low cost, low energy or sustainability are not supported by a common process inventory in this review. Treat them as qualitative framing unless source studies quantify energy, chemical input, yield, regeneration burden and spent-media fate.

Adsorbent / material: Poplar-sawdust biochar (BC), nickel ferrite (NiFe2O4; NFO), and magnetic NiFe2O4/biochar composite (NFO/BC)
Experimental design / conditions: Poplar sawdust was washed, dried, and pyrolysed at 700 °C for 1 h. To prepare NFO/BC, 0.1 g BC was sonicated in 50 mL water for 30 min; 0.1 mmol Ni(NO3)2·6H2O and 0.2 mmol Fe(NO3)3·9H2O were added, ammonia was used to raise pH to about 11, and the mixture was hydrothermally treated in a PTFE-lined autoclave at 180 °C for 12 h. Product was centrifuged and washed at least three times with deionized water and ethanol, then vacuum-dried at 80 °C for 12 h.
Reported result: Ferrite loading adds metal salts, concentrated ammonia, autoclave heating, centrifugation and repeated solvent washing. The biochar acts as a carrier to improve ferrite dispersion; ferrite adds magnetic separability.
Value / units: Pyrolysis 700 °C/1 h; hydrothermal synthesis 180 °C/12 h; pH≈11; final drying 80 °C/12 h
Caveat / follow-up: Classify as engineered ferrite/biochar, not conventional biochar. The paper provides no full process yield, reagent/washwater cost, Ni/Fe leaching assessment or life-cycle inventory; magnetic recovery is a handling advantage, not by itself proof of sustainability.

Continuum stage: Stage 4 — engineered magnetic biochar composite, compared with unmodified biochar and ferrite
Experimental design / conditions: BET area, average pore size and pore volume were measured for BC, NFO and NFO/BC; room-temperature magnetization was measured by vibrating sample magnetometry. The composite was characterized by XRD, FTIR, XPS, SEM/EDX and thermogravimetric analysis.
Reported result: BET areas: BC 422.5 m²/g, NFO 111.6 m²/g, NFO/BC 356.1 m²/g. Average pore sizes: 3.16, 7.95 and 3.88 nm; pore volumes 0.33, 0.21 and 0.27 cm³/g, respectively. NFO/BC saturation magnetization was 15.2 emu/g, which the authors state was sufficient for magnetic separation.
Value / units: BET area (m²/g): BC 422.5, NFO 111.6, NFO/BC 356.1; pore volume (cm³/g): 0.33, 0.21, 0.27; Ms=15.2 emu/g
Caveat / follow-up: The composite's BET area is below that of BC alone, although above NFO; its improved removal should not be attributed simply to a larger surface area than BC. Magnetic recovery and composite synergy require separate assessment from capacity.

Adsorbent / material: NFO/BC composite, compared with BC and NFO
Evidence domain: Observed removal, dosage and pH response
Experimental design / conditions: Baseline TC solution was 20 mg/L. Dosage was varied from 0.2 to 2.0 g/L; pH response was tested across acidic, neutral and alkaline conditions. Isotherm experiments used 20 mL TC solution at 5–200 mg/L with 20 mg adsorbent for 24 h. Kinetic tests used 20 mg adsorbent in 20 mL of 20 mg/L TC at pH 6.
Reported result: NFO/BC removal reached 93.9% at 1.0 g/L; raising dose from 0.2 to 1.0 g/L increased removal from 37% to 93.9%, with little cost justification for further dose increases. Maximum removal reported at pH 7 was 92.4%; removal at pH 3 was 75.5%.
Value / units: TC removal 93.9% at 1.0 g/L; pH 7 removal 92.4%; pH 3 removal 75.5%; isotherms 5–200 mg/L
Model / metric: Observed removal percentage under stated conditions; not qmax
Caveat / follow-up: The test is a prepared aqueous system using mg/L TC, not a real wastewater or trace-level environmental demonstration. Preserve concentration, pH and dose alongside the removal percentage.

Evidence domain: Fitted capacity, matrix effects and regeneration
Experimental design / conditions: Langmuir and Freundlich models were fitted to equilibrium data. Humic acid and inorganic salts were added to simulated water to examine interference. Four adsorption–desorption cycles were performed, with deionized water used for desorption between cycles.
Reported result: The paper reports a Langmuir maximum capacity of 420.41 mg/g for TC. Increasing humic-acid dosage significantly reduced removal. NaCl was reported to have little effect, while at 0.5% salt conditions Mg2+ and Ca2+ reduced removal/capacity to 59.8% and 63.8% of the original condition. NFO/BC removal remained about 72% after the fourth cycle.
Value / units: Reported Langmuir qmax=420.41 mg/g; after cycle 4 removal ≈72%; at 0.5% Mg/Ca salt conditions performance ≈59.8%/63.8% of baseline
Model / metric: Fitted Langmuir qmax; interference test and cycle reuse performance
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 8–10; Figs. 4–6; supplementary Tables S1–S4 (not in uploaded PDF)
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; supplementary tables not supplied
Caveat / follow-up: The exact fitting table and temperature-specific thermodynamics are in supplementary material not included in the uploaded file. Treat 420.41 mg/g as a fitted qmax, not observed uptake. Four cycles leave a notable performance decline; no real-water, column, regeneration-effluent or leaching assessment was reported.

Adsorbent / material: Separate chitosan beads and alginate beads
Evidence domain: Preparation, material form and pH response
Experimental design / conditions: Chitosan (≥75% deacetylated) was dissolved in 1% acetic acid at 1 g/50 mL; alginate was dissolved in ultrapure water at 1 g/50 mL. Solutions were dripped into separate coagulation baths: 1 M NaOH for chitosan and 20% CaCl2 for alginate. Beads rested 48 h and were washed to neutral pH. pH optimization used 300 mg/L amoxicillin and 1 g adsorbent with McIlvaine buffer.
Reported result: Both bead types had optimum reported pH 4. At pH 4, observed capacity was 80.4±0.2 mg/g for chitosan and 74.2±0.3 mg/g for alginate. Alginate beads were reported to dissolve above pH 6. The two polymers were prepared as separate beads, not a mixed chitosan–alginate composite.
Value / units: At pH 4: chitosan 80.4±0.2 mg/g; alginate 74.2±0.3 mg/g; initial amoxicillin 300 mg/L
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): Preprint PDF pp. 4–5 and 8–9; Fig. 1; Table 1
Evidence status: Uploaded Research Square preprint reviewed; published-version abstract cross-check confirms headline pH-4 capacity values; published full tables not fully assessed
Caveat / follow-up: Published journal abstract now independently confirms the headline pH-4 capacities (alginate 74.2±0.3 mg/g; chitosan 80.4±0.2 mg/g). The uploaded full text remains the preprint, and the published article's full methods/tables/supplement were not fully accessible in the inspected view. Keep the caveat on commercial-capsule assay/excipient controls; do not assume fitted-model, kinetic asymptote or thermodynamic details were unchanged without a full published-version check.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetic experiments followed pH optimization. The paper fits Boyd external-diffusion and Weber–Morris intraparticle-diffusion models and reports triplicate experiments.
Reported result: Text/conclusion report chitosan uptake 78.6 mg/g after 200 min and alginate uptake 71.3 mg/g after 250 min. Boyd's model was reported as the better fit for chitosan (external diffusion), whereas Weber–Morris fit better for alginate (internal diffusion). Table 2 gives a fitted Weber–Morris q∞ of 136.75±8.2 mg/g for alginate, much larger than the text's 71.3 mg/g kinetic uptake.
Value / units: Text kinetic uptake: chitosan 78.6 mg/g at 200 min; alginate 71.3 mg/g at 250 min; fitted alginate q∞=136.75±8.2 mg/g
Model / metric: Reported kinetic uptake versus intraparticle-diffusion fitted asymptote
Evidence status: Extracted — preprint data with internal model/metric discrepancy
Caveat / follow-up: Do not use fitted q∞ as observed equilibrium capacity. The difference from the stated kinetic uptake needs clarification, and should be checked in the final published version before manuscript use.

Experimental design / conditions: Isotherms were run at 278, 293 and 308 K (5, 20 and 35 °C) across initial amoxicillin concentrations of 50–300 mg/L. Langmuir and Freundlich models were compared; experiments were reportedly conducted in triplicate.
Reported result: Langmuir qmax for chitosan was 98.4±0.8, 102.2±0.9 and 94.4±0.7 mg/g at 5, 20 and 35 °C. For alginate, it was 60.8±1.2, 104.3±0.8 and 99.0±0.7 mg/g. The authors nevertheless state that Freundlich generally fit better, with R² around 0.990–0.996 in reported conditions. ΔH was positive: 20.6±0.8 kJ/mol (chitosan) and 13.8±0.4 kJ/mol (alginate); ΔG was reported negative across tested temperatures.
Value / units: Langmuir qmax (mg/g): chitosan 98.4/102.2/94.4; alginate 60.8/104.3/99.0 at 278/293/308 K
Model / metric: Langmuir-fitted qmax; paper reports Freundlich as generally better fit
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): Preprint PDF pp. 5–6 and 11–14; Fig. 6; Tables 3–4
Evidence status: Extracted — preprint data; published version not cross-checked
Caveat / follow-up: Keep the Langmuir qmax explicitly as fitted and note the paper's preference for Freundlich. High mg/L batch concentrations and lack of real wastewater/regeneration tests limit practical interpretation. Validate values against the published version before final citation.

Adsorbent / material: Chitosan, chemically/physically crosslinked chitosan, graft copolymers, magnetic composites, porous polymer blends, hydrogels and chitosan–MOF/carbon/clay composites
Continuum stage: Stage 2–4 depending on degree of modification and composite components
Experimental design / conditions: Narrative overview of in vitro adsorption and in silico studies. The article classifies chitosan modifications (crosslinking and grafting), chitosan composite architectures, effects of solution physicochemistry, and computational work. Tables 2–3 compile tetracycline and ciprofloxacin adsorption studies.
Reported result: The review identifies chitosan's amino and hydroxyl groups as key contributors to adsorption interactions, while emphasizing poor mechanical properties and acid instability as motivations for crosslinking or composite formation. It focuses on four antibiotic examples, rather than a systematic survey of every antibiotic class.
Value / units: Review scope: four focal antibiotics; no new experimental capacity
Evidence status: Full text reviewed — supporting review only
Caveat / follow-up: The inspected paper does not provide a PRISMA-style reproducible screening flow. Values in its tables come from different primary studies under heterogeneous conditions; use for discovery and mechanism framing, not as a standardized capacity ranking.

Adsorbent / material: Chitosan and chemically modified/crosslinked chitosan-based materials
Continuum stage: Stage 2–4 — from biopolymer beads to engineered composites
Experimental design / conditions: Review discusses physical crosslinking (e.g., ionic bonds, tripolyphosphate) and chemical crosslinking with aldehydes, epoxides and other reagents; it also reviews graft copolymerization and magnetic/porous composites.
Reported result: Crosslinking can improve mechanical strength, stability and porosity, but may consume chitosan amino groups and reduce accessible active sites. Some agents have toxicity concerns; the review recommends considering less harmful crosslinkers such as genipin or natural acids where feasible. Magnetic particles can simplify recovery after adsorption.
Caveat / follow-up: Do not assume any modification is automatically greener or higher-performing. Reagent toxicity, yields, washing, residue disposal, mechanical durability and regeneration need assessment at primary-study level; the review does not provide a common process-cost or LCA comparison.

Adsorbent / material: Chitosan and its carbon-, clay-, magnetic-, MOF- and polymer-based composites
Evidence domain: Solution chemistry and proposed adsorption interactions
Experimental design / conditions: The review compiles source studies where pH, antibiotic speciation, surface charge, functional groups, porosity and co-components influence adsorption. It discusses electrostatic attraction/repulsion, hydrogen bonding, π–π and hydrophobic interactions, and host–guest inclusion.
Reported result: The review describes pH-dependent adsorption as a consequence of the changing charge states of both the antibiotic and chitosan/composite surface. It notes that tetracycline and ciprofloxacin often show lower adsorption at strongly acidic/basic conditions, depending on the particular material, due to repulsion, protonation/deprotonation or structural instability.
Value / units: Qualitative synthesis; no universal pH optimum
Model / metric: Review of mechanisms and source-study observations
Caveat / follow-up: Mechanisms and pH optima remain material- and water-specific. Do not convert compiled mechanisms into proof for a particular primary paper without its experimental characterisation; high fitted capacity does not identify a unique mechanism.

Target / co-contaminant: Mainly tetracycline and ciprofloxacin interactions with chitosan–MOF/composite materials
Adsorbent / material: Simplified molecular models of chitosan, chitosan–ZIF-8 and ZnCo-ZIF–chitosan
Continuum stage: Stage 2–4 — computational interpretation of engineered biopolymer composites
Evidence domain: In silico mechanism evidence and limitations
Experimental design / conditions: Review discusses DFT and molecular docking studies. Example tetracycline/ZIF-8–chitosan work used a simplified chitosan trimer and a reduced ZIF-8 model; structures were optimized, docked, re-optimized and evaluated with binding-energy calculations. Other work used solvent models and dispersion corrections for ciprofloxacin/composite interactions.
Reported result: One cited modelling study suggested tetracycline binding was stronger at the ZIF-8 component than at chitosan, with electrostatics as a major contribution. The review describes computations as qualitative insight to interpret experiments and notes that models simplify real aqueous interfaces.
Caveat / follow-up: DFT/docking results depend on chosen protonation states, model size, solvent treatment and geometry. They cannot substitute for experimental real-water, regeneration or matrix testing; verify the original computational paper before quoting energies or mechanism strengths.

Adsorbent / material: Calcium-montmorillonite from Ningcheng, Inner Mongolia; acid/solvent-treated nano-montmorillonite derivative
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural mineral with a chemical/solvent-assisted nano-treatment; not completely untreated clay
Experimental design / conditions: Starting calcium-montmorillonite had reported CEC 97.9 mmol/100 g. Nano-montmorillonite preparation used 8.6 g of a reagent named inconsistently in the method text as butyl acetic acid/butyl acetate, 25 mL water, 22 mL HCl and 32 mL absolute ethanol at 60 °C for 4 h to form a gel. Then 5 g clay was added and stirred at 60 °C for another 4 h, followed by filtration, washing and drying.
Reported result: Preparation creates a nano-treated clay through acid/solvent gel formation and a second heated clay-treatment step. It is more processed than simply sieving or using natural montmorillonite as received.
Value / units: CEC 97.9 mmol/100 g; 60 °C for two 4 h stages; 22 mL HCl; 32 mL ethanol; 5 g clay
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PMC full-text HTML; Experimental instruments and materials; Preparation of nano-montmorillonite
Caveat / follow-up: Method text names the first reagent inconsistently; resource table identifies butyl acetate. No treatment yield, acid/solvent consumption per kg product, washwater treatment, production cost, solvent recovery, regeneration or life-cycle analysis is reported.

Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural mineral and chemically/solvent-treated nano-clay
Evidence domain: Batch study design and reported time/concentration response
Experimental design / conditions: Specific factor tests used 0.03 g clay in 50 mL solution. Kinetics: C0=200 mg/L and pH 4; concentration tests: C0=20, 40, 60, 80, 120, 300 and 500 mg/L at pH 4; pH tests: C0=200 mg/L over pH 1–10; cation tests: C0=200 mg/L, pH 1 and 0.1 mol/L Na+ or Ca2+. Experiments were at 25 °C, 180 rpm and away from light. These conditions are not fully harmonized with the conclusion's stated optimal dosage of 0.03 g/L.
Reported result: The paper reports adsorption becoming approximately stable after 60 min. The concentration series states that adsorption amount approached a plateau, with 500 mg/g reported at an equilibrium concentration of 120 mg/L.
Value / units: Kinetic condition: 0.03 g/50 mL, C0=200 mg/L, pH 4, 25 °C; concentration series C0=20–500 mg/L; reported stability around 60 min
Model / metric: Observed batch response; reported concentration labels and dosage need reconciliation
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PMC full-text HTML; Adsorption experiment; Fig. 3A–B
Caveat / follow-up: The methods say 0.03 g per 50 mL (0.6 g/L), while the conclusion calls the optimum dosage 0.03 g/L. These differ twenty-fold. The concentration-series discussion distinguishes initial concentration from equilibrium concentration, but the conclusion's 120 mg/L wording appears to blur them. Do not synthesize the optimum claim until reconciled.

Evidence domain: Observed versus fitted capacity and mass-balance plausibility
Experimental design / conditions: The paper reports a maximum adsorbed amount of 500 mg/g when equilibrium concentration reaches 120 mg/L; the conclusion describes >90% removal at an initial concentration of 120 mg/L, pH 1, 60 min and dosage 0.03 g/L. Table 3 reports Langmuir qm=558.184 mg/g (R²=0.974) and Freundlich KF=200.706 mg/g, 1/n=0.170 (R²=0.846). The abstract/conclusion elsewhere states a maximum capacity of 526 mg/g.
Reported result: Three different maximum-related quantities appear: 500 mg/g in the results discussion, 526 mg/g in abstract/conclusion, and fitted Langmuir qm=558.184 mg/g. They should not be treated as interchangeable. The methods' dosage 0.03 g per 50 mL corresponds to 0.6 g/L, not 0.03 g/L.
Value / units: Reported result 500 mg/g; conclusion 526 mg/g; Langmuir fitted qm=558.184 mg/g (R²=0.974)
Model / metric: Reported uptake/maximum versus fitted Langmuir asymptote
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PMC full-text HTML; Fig. 3B; Langmuir/Freundlich model discussion; Table 3; Conclusion
Evidence status: Extracted — primary study; high-priority source caveat
Caveat / follow-up: If 120 mg/L is the initial concentration and 0.03 g sorbent is used in 50 mL, only 6 mg TC is present, so mass-balance qe cannot exceed 200 mg/g. Thus >90% removal at those conditions is incompatible with q=526 mg/g or the stated 500 mg/g value. The latter may refer to a different concentration/equilibrium point; precise condition labels need reconciliation. Do not silently correct it.

Target / co-contaminant: Tetracycline (TC); competing sodium and calcium ions
Continuum stage: Stage 2 — natural and treated mineral clay
Experimental design / conditions: pH tests used C0=200 mg/L TC, 0.03 g sorbent in 50 mL; electrolyte tests used 0.1 mol/L Na+ or Ca2+ at pH 1. The paper relates TC speciation to pH and clay interlayer cation exchange.
Reported result: Reported adsorption capacity was 296.7 mg/g at pH 1 and 132.3 mg/g at pH 10. Addition of Na+ reduced the reported capacity to 254.1 mg/g, while Ca2+ reduced it to 147.3 mg/g; authors infer stronger competition from divalent Ca2+.
Value / units: pH 1: 296.7 mg/g; pH 10: 132.3 mg/g; with Na+: 254.1 mg/g; with Ca2+: 147.3 mg/g
Model / metric: Reported adsorption amount/capacity under individual batch conditions
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PMC full-text HTML; Fig. 3C–D; Adsorption mechanism discussion
Caveat / follow-up: Tests were performed in simulated aqueous solutions, not demonstrated real wastewater. The 0.1 M cation condition is a strong competitive-electrolyte challenge and should not be treated as normal environmental-water performance.

Experimental design / conditions: The authors used SEM, XRD, FTIR and contact-angle analysis, alongside kinetic and equilibrium model fitting. Reported BET area was 247 m²/g, total pore volume 9.84 cm³/g, average particle size 364 nm; the measured contact angle rose from 33° before adsorption to 46.5° after adsorption.
Reported result: The article reports a pseudo-first-order kinetic fit (R²=0.986) and Langmuir fit (R²=0.974). It proposes interlayer intercalation/cation exchange and electrostatic attraction under acidic conditions, with interlayer-spacing and wettability changes interpreted as evidence of uptake.
Value / units: BET 247 m²/g; pore volume 9.84 cm³/g; particle size 364 nm; contact angle 33°→46.5°; PFO R²=0.986; Langmuir R²=0.974
Model / metric: Primary characterization and empirical model fits
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PMC full-text HTML; Fig. 4; Fig. 5A; Table 3; Fig. 6
Caveat / follow-up: A better pseudo-first-order fit does not prove a unique mechanism. No actual wastewater, column trial, repeated regeneration, process cost, solvent recovery or end-of-life test is reported.

Adsorbent / material: Separate chitosan beads and alginate beads
Experimental design / conditions: PubMed record for the published journal article (Epub 2024-10-28) and a ResearchGate publisher preview were checked on 2026-10-27. Abstract reports pH optimum 4 for both bead types; capacities are reported using 1 g adsorbent. The complete published methods/tables/supplement were not fully accessible in the inspected view.
Reported result: Published-version abstract confirms the same headline pH-4 capacities as the uploaded preprint: alginate 74.2 ± 0.3 mg/g; chitosan 80.4 ± 0.2 mg/g. The abstract also reports external diffusion governs alginate uptake and internal diffusion governs chitosan uptake. This confirms the headline abstract values only, not all preprint tables or model parameters.
Value / units: Alginate 74.2 ± 0.3 mg/g; chitosan 80.4 ± 0.2 mg/g; optimum pH 4; 1 g adsorbent as stated by abstract
Model / metric: Published-version abstract corroboration of reported adsorption capacities; not a full-text table audit
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PubMed abstract: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39466532/ (lines 233–239); ResearchGate publisher preview: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/385318818_Adsorption_of_amoxicillin_by_chitosan_and_alginate_biopolymers_composite_beads (abstract lines 124–169)
Evidence status: Published-version abstract and publisher preview checked; full methods/tables not fully assessed
Caveat / follow-up: Headline pH-4 capacities are corroborated by the published abstract, reducing the risk that those headline values were unique to the preprint. Do not assume preprint details for fitted Langmuir/Freundlich values, diffusion-table asymptotes, thermodynamics, detailed methods or supplementary results were all retained unchanged; recheck the published full text/supplement before using those details.

Target / co-contaminant: TC, CIP, SMX; IBP is non-antibiotic
Experimental design / conditions: Uploaded full text che mod bio 1.pdf, PDF pp. 4–6. Main text section 3.2 describes kinetic experiments at C0=20 mg/L, pH 7 and contact up to 24 h, with equilibrium around 6 h.
